slides.title:
Section I:
Inspector Roles & Duties
content: Learning Objective 1 — Describe the basic roles & duties of an inspector.

slides.title: Shared Responsibilities
content:
Fire department may share inspection responsibilities 

With building or code enforcement department

Jurisdiction must establish clear inspection guidelines or MOUs regarding procedures

slides.title: Building Departments & Inspections 1
content:
In some jurisdictions, fire inspection & code enforcement responsibility may be assigned to the building department

Inspectors are usually civilian employees

Generally responsible for reviewing & approving all new construction & alterations to existing structures

slides.title: Building Departments & Inspections 2
content:
Inspector should be able to:

Read & understand construction documents

Issue permits related to bbuildings & their use

Perform field inspections to verify approved plans are followed in the construction & alteration process

Recommend to the building official the issuance of the certificate of occupancy

slides.title: Code Enforcement Department  (1 of 2)
content: Some jurisdictions may have a separate code enforcement department

slides.title: Inspectors Scope of Power (Insurance)
content:
Insurance inspector’s scope & power to make improvements or enforce corrections varies widely

Insurance company’s policies & procedures dictate the working relationship between the insured & inspector

Inspector must always follow appropriate insurance company policies & procedures for handling noted hazards

slides.title: Inspectors Scope of Power (Private)
content:
Private inspectors should

Have good working relationships with the public sector inspectors within the jurisdiction because it may be necessary to work together

Regularly communicate about facility & process changes that will affect fire & life safety

slides.title: Inspector Training & Professional Development (3 of 3)
content:
Initial training may include: 
basic fire behavior
HazMat, 
building construction
strategies & tactics

AHJ may require continuing education & recertification

slides.title: Inspection Categories (1 of 5)
content: Inspectors may be authorized to perform several categories of fire and life safety inspections

slides.title: Inspection Categories (3 of 5)
content:
Inspectors must know jurisdictions:
applicable statutes
codes
regulations
ordinances
permitting processes

slides.title: NOTE 2
content: When dealing with federal properties, inspectors need to understand federal rules & regulations.

slides.title: Discussion Question 1
content: What categories of inspection do you expect to perform with your organization?

slides.title:
Section II:
Codes & Standards
content: Learning Objective 2 — Describe the different types of codes & standards.

slides.title: Types of Codes & Standards (1 of 4)
content:
Model codes — Set of requirements similar to a standard
These requirements are generally called prescriptive codes
Consensus organization develops model codes that contain agreed-upon requirements for fire protection, building construction, structural safety, building sanitation, & life safety
Only enforceable when the AHJ adopts them

slides.title: Types of Codes & Standards (2 of 4)
content:
The AHJ may adopt a model code without changes

The code may be amended to address specific local conditions & needs

Inspector must be thoroughly familiar with the locally adopted code, its amendments, & policies

Codes are legal documents that govern activities at various levels of government

slides.title: Types of Codes & Standards (3 of 4)
content:
Building & fire codes or standards may be classified as either

Prescriptive code/standard
Describes in detail the types of materials that can be used & how they must be assembled

Performance-based code/standard
Describes an acceptable level of performance that an assembly, material, or system must meet without stating how the item is assembled & gives the designer greater freedom than a prescriptive-based code/standard does

slides.title: Types of Codes & Standards (4 of 4)
content:
Before the creation of standardized model codes, jurisdictions developed their own sets of codes

Led to a wide variety of acceptable minimum levels of safety

Created some confusion among manufacturers & contractors who sold materials in multiple jurisdictions

As a result, organizations were formed to write consensus or model codes that could be applied universally

slides.title: Review Question 1
content: What are the differences between codes & standards?

slides.title:
Section III:
Consensus Standards
content:
Learning Objective 3 — Describe the organizations that publish consensus standards.

Learning Objective 4 — Describe the development & adoption processes for national codes & standards.

slides.title: Consensus Standards (1 of 2)
content: “Standard” refers to a variety of rules, guidelines, product specifications, &/or procedures
Published by various organizations related to building construction, fire & life safety, & hazardous processes
Document drafted, developed, & published by a committee of volunteer experts through consensus decision-making procedures of the American National Standards Institute (ANSI)

slides.title: Model Building Code Organizations
content:
NFPA & ICC® are the two main model building code organizations in the United States

Canadian Commission on Building & Fire Codes (CCBFC) develops & maintains Codes Canada publications

slides.title: Model Building Code Organizations (Con’t.)
content:
Codes developed by these organizations are used to regulate building components, fire protection, & life safety systems

To assist an inspector in interpreting model codes
Explanatory commentaries & handbooks are available for some codes

Consensus organizations also provide training sessions & workshops

slides.title: Review Question 2
content: What organizations produce model building codes?

slides.title: Review Question 3
content: Why is public input important in the NFPA & ICC® code modification cycles?

slides.title:
Section IV:
Application of Codes & Standards
content:
Section IV:
Application of Codes & Standards
Learning Objective 5 — Describe the different ways that codes & standards are applied.

slides.title: Application of Codes & Standards
content:
Some jurisdictions use locally developed codes, most jurisdictions adopt model codes
Inspector should be familiar with model codes & standards referenced in the adopted code

Elements of adopted electrical, plumbing, & mechanical codes that reference the fire code or are referenced by the fire code are also important

Most model codes are revised regularly, typically every 3 to 5 years

Fire & life safety inspectors must know the adopted editions of codes & standards in their jurisdiction

slides.title: Consistent Codes & Standards (1 of 3)
content:
Inspector should continually monitor applicable code provisions enacted at all levels of government

Prevents conflicts between various codes

Fire & life safety codes must be consistent with other codes to avoid: 
duplication 
or attempting to enforce contradictory regulations

Interpretation of fire & life safety codes must be clear & consistent within the purpose & intent of the actual fire codes

slides.title: Consistent Codes & Standards (3 of 3)
content:
Additional methods for keeping current with building changes include

Monitoring business license applications

Monitoring issuance of business occupancy & activity permits

Conducting annual occupancy inventory survey

Monitoring new electrical service applications

Be aware that some facilities may have to meet multiple code requirements

slides.title: Multiple Codes- Example
content:
Hospital is example of a facility that may need to meet several codes
May have to meet locally adopted building & fire codes
Portion of the same facility may have to meet NFPA 101® because of health care licensing requirements in that area
Additions constructed at different times may be constructed under different editions of a particular code or ordinance
Usually, all sections of the facilities must comply with current edition means of egress requirements
Inspector may have to enforce the more restrictive code requirement or coordinate enforcement efforts

slides.title: Multiple Code Compliance (2 of 2)
content: Inspectors from different departments must maintain open lines of communication & work to produce equivalent, alternate solutions

slides.title: NOTE 4
content: Unless inspectors are specifically given the authority, they cannot apply current building code requirements to existing structures.

slides.title: Review Question 4
content: How can existing structures be affected by new codes?

slides.title:
Section V:
Legal Authority & Liability
content:
Learning Objective 6 — Identify the types of legislation & laws inspectors need to be aware of.

Learning Objective 7 — Explain the legal status of inspectors.

Learning Objective 8 — Describe the different types of liability that can affect inspectors.

Learning Objective 9 — Explain when outside technical assistance may be necessary to aid an inspector.

slides.title: Scope of Power
content:
Some AHJs have almost unlimited power to develop, enact, & enforce fire codes

Others may be required to enforce a code established by state/province, county, or regional government

Some organizations may not have any power to modify or amend provisions of the fire code

Codes are usually the result of a cooperative effort among community stakeholders, AHJ, legislative body

Legal counsel should provide information on the inspector’s authority & liability as defined by the law

slides.title: Federal Laws (2 of 3)
content:
Agency that sets standards is usually responsible for their enforcement

Federal buildings & some state/provincial-owned buildings located within a jurisdiction are not required to comply with local codes

Military bases that have their own fire departments & fire prevention staff follow Unified Facilities Criteria (UFC) from the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD), Portions of the IFC®, NFPA standards

Combination of UFC, NFPA standards, & local code adaptations is often used in local, federally owned buildings

slides.title: Labor, Insurance, & Health laws
content:
Sometimes encompass fire & life safety inspection responsibilities

Inspector’s responsibility to communicate the local jurisdiction’s authority

Communication is necessary to form an effective working relationship between local & state/provincial agencies

Each inspector must be familiar with his or her state/provincial adoption regulations & know how oversight works

slides.title: Local Laws & Ordinances (2 of 2)
content:
Regulations adopted by reference &/or by enabling acts

Adoption by reference — Local jurisdiction follows state/provincial laws exactly as written

Enabling acts — Local jurisdiction uses state/provincial laws as their basis, but allow additions/deletions to regulations or ordinances based on local needs or preferences

slides.title: Discussion Question 2
content: How are local laws & ordinances adopted in your jurisdiction?

slides.title: Public Sector Authorization (2 of 3)
content:
Fire codes authorize inspectors to:

interrupt business operations

stop work on construction

evacuate & close a building that presents imminently dangerous conditions

slides.title: Conﬂicts Between Public & Private Requirements
content:
Insurance companies often dictate protection requirements for insured risks that are more stringent than local fire codes or ordinances

Life safety code issues always have precedence over property conservation considerations

Public inspector must point out these issues to the building owner/occupant & insurance inspectors to ensure that life safety is paramount

Insurance inspectors should work with municipal inspectors to ensure that the insurance requirements meet or exceed the locally adopted fire code

slides.title: Review Question 5
content: What factors can determine an inspector’s legal status in the public & private sectors?

slides.title: Supreme Court Cases
content:
In the US, inspectors have a right of entry, but property owners also have certain rights under the Fourth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution

Two U.S. Supreme Court cases set federally protected constitutional limits on the authority of fire inspectors to enter a business or a private dwelling:

See v. City of Seattle (387 U.S. 541) & Camara v. Municipal Court of City/County of San Francisco (387 U.S. 523)

Inspector always has the authority to enter the premises if exigent circumstances exist

slides.title: Exigent Circumstances
content:
Situations of urgency, such as emergency conditions, that demand unusual or immediate action & allow people to circumvent usual procedures

Would cause a reasonable person to believe that prompt action is necessary to prevent physical harm

Court has also ruled that if a hazard is obvious & in public view, inspectors have the right to enter the premises

slides.title: For Canada (3 of 3)
content:
AHJ may provide a refusal form for inspectors to use when a property owner or occupant refuses their right to enter a property — Provides information for obtaining a warrant to enter at a later time

Occasionally, it is practical to obtain written permission to enter a site before the inspection

Use of a consent-to-enter form will remove questions regarding the original authorization to enter & perform an inspection

Any form developed for these purposes should be approved by the jurisdiction’s legal counsel & authorized by the fire chief

slides.title: Review Question 6
content: How can exigent circumstances affect an inspector’s ability to enter & inspect a premise?

slides.title: Review Question 7
content: What are some examples of practices that may lead to a civil rights violation?

slides.title: Indemnification (1 of 2)
content:
Most jurisdictions indemnify inspection personnel or provide liability insurance to protect them in areas where they may be held liable

To indemnify the inspector means that the AHJ assumes the responsibility for any claims against the individual

Procedures for indemnification generally depend on prevailing state law

Inspectors need to determine whether they are indemnified or protected by liability insurance when performing official duties

Liability insurance provided by jurisdictions protects the inspector from costs involved with providing legal counsel or court judgments

slides.title: Indemnification (2 of 2)
content:
If inspectors discover violations in a property but fail to perform a follow-up inspection to verify the violations are corrected, they can be held liable if a fire related to the violations occurs

Inspectors can also be held liable for resulting deaths or injuries that can be attributed to any outstanding code violations

Inspectors who take on a special duty or obligation to a person can be held liable

Liability results if an inspector places a person in potential harm or danger through incorrect/unsafe advice or act outside the scope of his/her authority

slides.title: Review Question 8
content: What is the difference between malfeasance & negligence?

slides.title: Discussion Question 3
content: Does your organization have agreements with third parties for technical assistance?

slides.title:
Section VI:
Legal Procedures
content:
Learning Objective 10 — Explain the general official actions to ensure code compliance.

Learning Objective 11 — Identify the inspector’s role within types of legal proceedings.

slides.title: Compliance Procedures
content:
Official actions vary by jurisdiction & are dictated by local codes & ordinances

Inspectors must understand procedures & thoroughly & accurately document all actions taken

Inspector & any other inspection personnel involved in an inspection &/or subsequent action may find themselves involved in legal proceedings
Inspectors may be considered witnesses or courtroom advisors to the prosecution

If there are questions regarding an inspector’s authority or the meaning of the code, it is best to seek advice from legal counsel before taking action

slides.title: NOTE 3
content: Because procedures for issuing sanctions differ, each jurisdiction should have a written procedure that details the process.

slides.title: Review Question 9
content: What actions may be taken during compliance procedures?

slides.title: Civil Proceedings (1 of 2)
content:
May be the result of a noncriminal violation, but usually involve one party filing suit against another party

Suit may allege a breach of contract or be filed for other reasons

slides.title: Summary Offenses (1 of 2)
content:
Lowest form of offense in most legal systems

Minor infractions of laws or local ordinances

Person who commits a summary offense is typically given a written citation of the violation when the violation occurs

Offender has the choice of paying the fine that accompanies the citation or challenging the citation before a judge

slides.title: Summary Offenses (1 of 2)
content:
Most common forms of summary offenses include speeding or parking violations

In some jurisdictions, unauthorized controlled burns are considered summary offenses

The inspector may be involved in writing the citations

slides.title: Evidentiary Requirements (1 of 3)
content:
An inspector’s job is to keep accurate notes about the inspection process
Accurate record-keeping is important for an efficient program 
Notes & photographs may be needed as evidence in a trial someday

For either digital or paper inspection records, inspection visits must include
Notes about conditions found on the premises & document any violations

Notes, plus photographs of violations, provide a record for the inspection department & owner

slides.title: Evidentiary Requirements (2 of 3)
content:
After visit is complete, inspector can print a copy of the inspection form for the owner to sign or e-mail it as a record of the visit

Depending on their severity, violations are given several time frames for abatement, such as 30 days, 60 days, or immediately for severe hazards

Inspectors must know legal requirements for entering premises
Hazards in plain sight during an inspection may be recorded
Evidence obtained without a scheduled visit or warrant may be inadmissible in court if the matter comes to a trial

slides.title: Preliminary Hearings
content:
Takes place before a judge

Prosecutor’s office required to establish that a crime has been committed with probable cause to believe the defendant committed the offense

If sufficient evidence is presented, the judge concludes the defendant must stand trial

During a preliminary hearing regarding an arson prosecution, most jurisdictions will require a fire origin & cause expert to establish that the fire in question was the result of a crime (typically intentionally & maliciously set) prior to a determination of probable cause

slides.title: Felony Trial (1 of 2)
content:
Defendant has the constitutional right to a trial before a jury

Defendant sometimes waives this right, & a bench trial takes place with only the judge making the determination as to the defendant’s guilt or innocence

Burden of proof is higher at the criminal trial stage
Prosecutor’s office must present enough evidence to convince the judge/jury that the defendant is guilty beyond a reasonable doubt
Reasonable doubt standard does not require 100% certainty but does require level of proof beyond that which a “reasonable” person would have after hearing evidence

slides.title: Felony Trial (2 of 2)
content:
Prosecution presents evidence first

Defendant & defense attorneys then present evidence in support of their not guilty position after the prosecutor finishes or “rests”

Witnesses are often called upon to testify to facts indicating that a crime has taken place or that a person is responsible for the crime

slides.title: Testimony
content:
Affirmation or declaration made under oath, typically in a court of law

All verbal information provided in a trial is sworn or affirmed testimony

Generally divided into two categories
Fact witness
Expert witness

In order to preserve the case & be as helpful as possible, inspector should understand basic courtroom procedures

slides.title: Inspector Testimony (2 of 2)
content:
Verify that all physical evidence, exhibits, photographs, notes, reference materials, & other materials pertinent to the case have been reviewed by the prosecutor & have been brought to court

Answer all questions factually & truthfully

Anticipate personal attacks or challenges to credibility

Never become argumentative on the witness stand

Maintain professionalism in presentation & expression — Use appropriate body language & nonverbal communication

slides.title: Fact Witness
content:
Answers questions posed by an attorney regarding what they have seen, heard, touched, smelled, or tasted

Testimony presents information to the judge or jury regarding “facts” without the witness being allowed to provide his or her own interpretation of those facts

Example of fact testimony (also known as lay testimony) would be a witness’s description of seeing a structure built without a permit & with no regard for building & fire codes

Witness would not be allowed to provide further testimony such as which codes or code sections were violated

slides.title: Expert Witness
content:
An expert witness is allowed, at the court’s discretion, to provide opinion testimony

Generally defined as a person with sufficient skill, knowledge, or experience in a given field capable of drawing inferences or reaching conclusions or opinions that an average person would not be competent to reach

Prior to being admitted as an expert, qualifications must be established through interview &/or resume

Evidence upon which an inspector bases an expert opinion must be relevant & reliable, thereby allowing it to be admissible

slides.title: Review Question 10
content: What are the differences between testifying as a fact witness & as an expert witness?

slides.title: Learning Objectives 1-5
content:
Explain the basic principles of fire science
Describe how thermal energy impacts fire behavior
Explain the function of fuel within the combustion process
Explain the function of oxygen within the combustion process

slides.title: Learning Objectives 6-9

slides.title:
Section I:
Fire Science
content: Objective 1 – Explain the basic principles of fire science

slides.title: Physical Science Terminology
content:
Physical science is the study of matter and energy
Includes chemistry and physics
World is made up of matter: physical materials that occupy space and have mass
Matter can undergo many types of physical and chemical changes
This chapter concentrates on changes related to fire

slides.title: Oxidation
content:
Chemical reaction involving the combination of an oxidizer with other materials
Can happen slowly, like when oxygen combines with iron to form rust
Can happen rapidly, like the combustion of methane

slides.title: Energy
content:
Capacity to perform work
Work occurs when
Force is applied to object over a distance
Substance undergoes a chemical, biological, or physical change
In the case of heat, work means increasing a substance’s temperature
Forms of energy are classified as potential or kinetic

slides.title: Potential Energy
content: Represents the amount of energy that an object can release at some point in the future

slides.title: Kinetic Energy
content:
Energy that a moving object possesses
While a fuel such as wood is not “moving,” molecules within fuel begin to vibrate when heat is introduced

slides.title: Exchange of Energy (1 of 2)
content:
Chemical and physical changes almost always involve exchange of energy
Fuel’s potential energy releases during combustion and converts to kinetic energy
Reactions that emit energy as they occur are exothermic
Fire is an exothermic chemical reaction that releases energy in form of heat and sometimes light

slides.title: Exchange of Energy (2 of 2)
content:
Reactions that absorb energy as they occur are endothermic reactions
Converting water from liquid to a gas requires input of energy resulting in endothermic physical reaction
Converting water to steam is a tactic for controlling and extinguishing some types of fires

slides.title: Fire Triangle and Tetrahedron (1 of 2)
content:
Models explain elements of fire and how to extinguish it
Triangle model shows three elements necessary for combustion
Fuel
Oxygen 
Heat
Remove any one of these elements and fire will be extinguished

slides.title: Fire Triangle and Tetrahedron (2 of 2)
content:
Fire tetrahedron model includes chemical chain reaction
Uninhabited chemical chain reaction must be present for a fire to occur
Includes chemical chain reaction to explain flaming or gas-phase combustion
Fire is example of gas-phase combustion

slides.title: Ignition (1 of 2)
content:
Fuels must be in gaseous state to burn
Piloted ignition is the most common form of ignition
Mixture of fuel and oxygen encounter heat source with sufficient heat to start combustion reaction
Autoignition has no external flame or spark to ignite fuel gases
Fuel’s surface is heated until combustion reaction 
Energy released from combustion transfers to remaining fuel

slides.title: Ignition (2 of 2)
content:
Transfer produces additional fuel vapors or gases, which also ignite
Exchange of energy from burning gases to fuel creates sustained combustion reaction
Autoignition temperature (AIT)
Minimum temperature at which a fuel in the air must be heated to start self-sustained combustion
AIT of a substance is always higher than its piloted ignition temperature

slides.title: Review Question 1
content: What is the difference between piloted ignition and autoignition?

slides.title: Combustion
content:
Fire and combustion are similar conditions, but combustion can occur without visible flames
There are two types of combustion
Flaming
Nonflaming

slides.title: Flaming Combustion (1 of 3)
content:
Also known as gas-phase combustion
Commonly referred to as fire
Produces a visible flame above the material’s surface
Occurs when a gaseous fuel mixes with oxygen in the correct ratio and heats to ignition temperature
Requires liquid or solid fuels to convert to a gas through addition of heat
When heated, both liquid and solid fuels will emit vapors that mix with oxygen, producing flames above the material’s surface if gases ignite

slides.title: Nonflaming Combustion
content:
Also known as solid-phased or condensed-phase combustion
Occurs more slowly and at lower temperature, producing smoldering glow in a material’s surface
Burning may be localized on or near the fuel’s surface where it is in contact with oxygen
Examples of nonflaming or smoldering combustion include burning charcoal or smoldering wood or fabric

slides.title: Products of Combustion (1 of 5)
content:
As fuel burns, its chemical composition changes, producing new substances

Products of combustion are often described as heat and smoke
Exposure to toxic gases in smoke and/or lack of oxygen cause most fire deaths
Smoke is an aerosol comprised of gases, vapor, and particulates

slides.title: Products of Combustion (3 of 5)
content: Structure fires involve two basic types of fuels

slides.title: Products of Combustion (4 of 5)
content: Reactions with limited air supply result in a higher level of incomplete combustion, which produces more smoke

slides.title: Products of Combustion (5 of 5)
content:
Combustion process consumes oxygen from the air, removing it from the environment
As part of chemical reaction, consumed oxygen combines with carbon in smoke to form combustion products like carbon monoxide (CO) or carbon dioxide (CO2)
Low oxygen concentrations alone can result in hypoxia or death
Toxic gases in combination with a low oxygen concentration can further reduce survival time
Concentrations of combustion products and/or low oxygen concentrations can cause asphyxiation

slides.title: Common Products of Combustion and Their Toxic Effects
content: Common Products of Combustion and Their Toxic Effects

slides.title: Carbon Monoxide (CO)
content:
Toxic and flammable product of incomplete combustion of organic (carbon-containing) materials
Almost every fire produces this colorless, odorless gas
Released when an organic material burns in an atmosphere with a limited supply of oxygen
Often identified as cause of death in civilian fatalities

slides.title: Pressure Differences (2 of 3)
content:
Heat from a fire increases pressure of surrounding gases
Increased pressure seeks to expand and equalize with areas of lower pressure
Heated gases rise and travel up and out
Cool air travels toward fire
Exchange of air creates convective flow

slides.title: Pressure Differences (3 of 3)
content: Small changes to the gas pressure within a structure can dramatically affect fire behavior

slides.title: Review Question 2
content: How does fire influence the pressure of the surrounding gases?

slides.title:
Section II:
Thermal Energy (Heat)
content: Objective 2 — Describe how thermal energy impacts fire behavior.

slides.title: Thermal Energy (Heat) (1 of 3)
content:
Working knowledge of fire dynamics requires an understanding of temperature, energy, and power or heat release rate (HRR)
To use these terms correctly, an inspector must know how they differ 
Power is the rate at which energy transfers
Another way to describe power is the rate at which energy converts from one form to another
The standard international (SI) unit for power is the watt (W)
One watt is 1 joule per second (J/s)

slides.title: Difference Between Heat Release Rate and Temperature (1 of 4)
content: Difference Between Heat Release Rate and Temperature (1 of 4)

slides.title: Difference Between Heat Release Rate and Temperature (2 of 4)
content: Difference Between Heat Release Rate and Temperature (2 of 4)

slides.title: Difference Between Heat Release Rate and Temperature (3 of 4)
content: Difference Between Heat Release Rate and Temperature (3 of 4)

Temperature can be measured using several different scales
Most common are Celsius and Fahrenheit
People use freezing and boiling points of water as points of comparison between these two scales
Temperature does NOT accurately predict or measure heat transfer

slides.title: Difference Between Heat Release Rate and Temperature (4 of 4)
content: Difference Between Heat Release Rate and Temperature (4 of 4)

One candle burns at the same temperature as ten candles burning separately
However, the heat release rate of the ten candles is ten times greater than one candle at the same temperature
Increased heat release rate results in an increased heat transfer rate to other objects
Heat flux measures heat transfer per unit area and is measured in kilowatts per square meter

slides.title: Review Question 3
content: What is the difference between heat and temperature?

slides.title: Sources of Thermal Energy
content:
Transfer heat and cause the temperature of a substance to increase
Frequently the ignition source of structure fires
Common sources of heat that result in the ignition of a fuel include:
Chemical Energy
Electrical Energy
Mechanical Energy

slides.title: Chemical Energy (1 of 4)
content:
Most common source of heat in combustion reactions
Potential for oxidation exists when any combustible fuel is in contact with oxygen
Oxidation process almost always results in production of thermal energy

slides.title: Electrical Energy
content:
Can generate temperatures high enough to ignite any combustible materials near the heated area
Electrical heating can occur in several ways, including
Resistance
Overcurrent or overload
Arcing
Sparking

slides.title: Mechanical Energy (1 of 2)
content:
Friction or compression generates mechanical energy
Movement of two surfaces against each other creates friction that generates heat and/or sparks
Compressing a gas also generates heat
Diesel engines use this principle to ignite fuel vapors without spark plugs

slides.title: Mechanical Energy (2 of 2)
content:
When a compressed gas expands, the gas absorbs heat
This heat absorption explains why the cylinder feels cool after a CO2 extinguisher is discharged

slides.title: Heat Transfer (1 of 2)
content: Transfer of heat from one point to another is part of thermodynamics

slides.title: Heat Transfer (2 of 2)
content:
Rate of heat transfer depends on temperature differences between objects and thermal conductivity of their materials
Greater the temperature difference, greater the transfer rate
Material with higher thermal conductivity transfers heat more quickly than other materials

slides.title: Conduction (1 of 2)
content:
Transfer of heat through and between solid objects
Occurs when material is heated as result of direct contact with heat source
Caused by increased molecular motion and collisions between substance’s molecules
More closely packed molecules of substance are, more readily it conducts heat

slides.title: Conduction (2 of 2)
content:
Heat transfer due to conduction depends upon the
Area being heated
Temperature difference between heat source and material being heated
Thermal conductivity of heated material
Insulating materials slow heat conduction between solids
Good insulators do not conduct heat well because material’s physical makeup disrupts transfer of heat
Best insulators use fine particles or fibers with void space filled with gas such as air
Gases do not conduct heat well because their molecules are far apart

slides.title: Convection (1 of 2)
content:
Transfer of thermal energy due to the circulation or movement of liquid or gas
Convection usually involves heat transfer through movement of hot smoke and fire gases
Heat flows from hot fire gases to cool structural surfaces, building contents, and air
May occur in any direction

slides.title: Convection (2 of 2)
content:
Buoyancy of smoke and fire gases cause vertical movement
Lateral movement is usually result of pressure differences (movement from high to low pressure)

slides.title: Radiation (1 of 2)
content:
Transmission of energy as electromagnetic waves without an intervening medium
Radiant heat can become dominant mode of heat transfer as fire grows in size, can ignite objects located far from fire
Radiant heat transfer significantly affects fire development and spread in compartments

slides.title: Factors Influencing Radiant Heat Transfer
content:
Nature of exposed surfaces
Dark-colored materials emit and absorb heat more effectively than light-colored materials
Smooth or highly-polished surfaces reflect more radiant heat than rough surfaces
Distance between heat source and exposed surfaces
Temperature of heat source
Radiant heat transfer primarily depends on temperature of heat source
As temperature and HRR of heat source increases, so does radiant energy

slides.title: Interaction Among the Methods of Heat Transfer
content: Interaction Among the Methods of Heat Transfer

Heat transfer methods tend to occur together
As fire radiates heat, it causes convection of heat through hot fuel gases and conducts heat through burning materials or metals involved in fire
Heat is transferred by convection and radiation to walls and ceilings, heating those surfaces
Heat is conducted through wall or ceiling until temperature of opposite side equals temperature of heated side
A heated surface will then radiate heat that can lead to ignition, combustion, convection, and so on
Cycle continues until it is interrupted

slides.title:
Section III:
Fuel
content: Objective 3 – Explain the function of fuel within the combustion process

slides.title: Fuel (1 of 4)
content:
Oxidized or burned material or substance in combustion process
Can be in any of three physical states of matter
Gas
Liquid
Solid
Fuel in combustion reaction is known as reducing agent

slides.title: Vapor Density
content:
Describes density of gases in relation to air
Air has vapor density of 1
Gases with vapor density less than 1 will rise
Gases with vapor density greater than 1 will sink
Vapor densities are based on assumption that density is measured at standard temperature and pressure
Heated gases expand and become less dense

slides.title: Specific Gravity
content:
Specific gravity is ratio of mass of given volume of liquid compared to mass of equal volume of water at same temperature
Scientists assign water specific gravity of 1
Liquids with specific gravity less than 1 are lighter than water and float on its surface
Liquids with specific gravity greater than 1 are heavier than water and sink

slides.title: Vaporization (1 of 2)
content:
To burn, liquids must vaporize
Vaporization is transformation of liquid to vapor or a gaseous state
Unlike solids, liquids retain their state of matter partly due to standard atmospheric pressure
For vaporization to occur, the escaping vapors must be at a greater pressure than atmospheric pressure
Pressure that vapors escaping from liquid exert is known as vapor pressure, which indicates how easily a substance evaporates into air
Flammable liquids with higher vapor pressure present special hazard because they produce flammable gases at lower temperatures

slides.title: Vaporization (2 of 2)
content:
Substance’s vapor pressure and amount of thermal energy applied to it determine its rate of vaporization
Puddle of water evaporates slower in sun than same amount of water evaporates on a stove because more thermal energy is applied
Volatility or ease with which liquid gives off vapor influences how easily it can ignite
Size of liquid’s surface area influences extent to which liquid will give off vapor
In many open containers, surface area of liquid exposed to atmosphere is limited

slides.title: Flash Point vs Fire Point (1 of 2)
content: Flash Point vs Fire Point (1 of 2)

slides.title: Flash Point vs Fire Point (2 of 2)
content: Flash Point vs Fire Point (2 of 2)

Flash point is commonly used to indicate the flammability hazard of liquid fuels

Liquid fuels that vaporize sufficiently to burn at temperatures under 100°F (38°C) present significant flammability hazard

slides.title: Solids
content:
Solids have definite size and shape
Each type of solid reacts differently when exposed to heat
Some solids, such as plastics and metal, will change their state and melt
Others such as wood will not
When solid fuels are heated
Begin to decompose (pyrolyze or off-gas)
Release combustible fuel gases and vapors
If there is enough fuel and heat, process of pyrolysis generates sufficient flammable vapors to ignite in the presence of sufficient oxygen or another oxidizer

content: Pyrolysis of Wood and Polyurethane Foam

slides.title: Solid Fuels
content:
Have a definite shape and size which significantly affects how easily they ignite
Primary consideration in ignition of solid fuels is surface area of fuel in proportion to its mass, which is called the surface-to-mass ratio
As surface-to-mass ratio increases, fuel particles become more finely divided and their ability to ignite increases tremendously
As surface area increases, more of the material is exposed to heat and generates combustible pyrolysis products more quickly

slides.title:
Section IV:
Oxygen
content: Objective 4 – Explain the function of oxygen within the combustion process.

slides.title: Oxygen (2 of 3)
content:
At normal ambient temperatures (68°F [20°C]), materials can ignite and burn at oxygen concentration as low as 15 percent

When oxygen concentration is limited, the flaming combustion will diminish, causing combustion to continue in the nonflaming mode

Nonflaming or smoldering combustion can continue at extremely low oxygen concentrations, even when surrounding environment’s temperature is relatively low

However, at high ambient temperatures, flaming combustion may continue at considerably lower oxygen concentrations

slides.title: Safety Alert
content: Oxygen concentration in the atmosphere has a significant effect on both fire behavior and our ability to survive. Typically, an atmosphere having less than 19.5 percent oxygen is considered oxygen deficient and presents a hazard to persons not wearing respiratory protection, such as self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA), to provide fresh air. When the oxygen concentration in the atmosphere exceeds 23.5 percent, the atmosphere is considered oxygen enriched and presents an increased fire risk.

slides.title: Lower Flammable and Explosive Limit
content:
For combustion to occur after fuel converts to gaseous state, fuel must be mixed with an oxidizer in the proper ratio
Flammable range – range of concentrations of fuel vapor and air
Lower limits of this range are called the lower flammable limit (LFL) or lower explosive limit (LEL)
LFL/LEL is minimum concentration of fuel vapor and air that supports combustion; concentrations below LFL/LEL are too lean to burn

slides.title: Upper Flammable and Explosive Limit
content:
Upper limits of the range are called upper flammable limit (UFL) or upper explosive limit (UEL)
Combustion cannot take place at concentration above UFL/UEL
Concentrations above UFL/UEL are too rich to burn
There is an ideal concentration with exactly correct amount of oxygen and fuel for combustion

slides.title: Flammable vs Explosive Hazard
content:
When confinement of the fuel vapors and air is not a concern, measurement is expressed as a flammable limit and a flash fire may occur
When fuel vapors and air are confined, measurement is expressed as an explosive limit, and an explosion may occur

slides.title: NOTE 1
content: Variations in temperature and pressure can cause the flammable range to vary considerably.

slides.title:
Section V:
Self-Sustained Chemical Reaction
content: Objective 5 – Explain the self-sustained chemical reaction involved in flaming combustion.

slides.title: Self-Sustained Chemical Reaction (1 of 2)
content:
As flaming combustion occurs, molecules of fuel gas and oxygen break apart to form free radicals (electrically charged, highly reactive parts of molecules)
Free radicals combine with oxygen from fuel gas to form new substances and more free radicals
This process increases speed of oxidation reaction

slides.title:
Flaming Combustion as a 
Chemical Chain Reaction
content:
Flaming Combustion as a 
Chemical Chain Reaction

Sufficient heat will cause fuel and oxygen to form free radicals and initiate a self-sustained chemical reaction
Fire will continue to burn until it consumes the fuel or oxygen, or an extinguishing agent is applied in sufficient quantity
Chemical flame inhibition occurs when an extinguishing agent, such as a dry chemical or clean agent
Interferes with chemical reaction
Forms a stable product
Terminates the combustion reaction

Section VI: 
Stages of Fire Development
content:
Section VI: 
Stages of Fire Development
Objective 6 – Differentiate among the stages of fire development

slides.title: Stages of Fire Development (1 of 2)
content: Compartment fire development depends on whether fire is fuel-limited or ventilation-limited

slides.title: Stages of Fire Development: Incipient and Growth Stages
content: Stages of Fire Development: Incipient and Growth Stages

slides.title: Stages of Fire Development: Fully Developed Stage
content: Stages of Fire Development: Fully Developed Stage

Occurs when all combustible materials in the compartment are burning at peak heat release rate based on the available oxygen
Fire is consuming the maximum amount of oxygen that it can
If the fire is limited to one fuel package, the fully developed stage occurs when the entire fuel package is on fire, and the fire has reached peak heat release rate

slides.title: Stages of Fire Development: Decay Stage
content: Stages of Fire Development: Decay Stage

Begins as fire consumes available fuel or oxygen and heat release rate begins to decline
Fuel-limited fires may self-extinguish in this stage or reduce to a smoldering phase
Ventilation-limited fires may also self-extinguish
If oxygen becomes available during decay stage before complete extinguishment, these fires are likely to reenter the growth stage and rapidly become fully developed

slides.title: Flashover
content:
Rapid transition from growth stage to fully developed stage
When flashover occurs, combustible materials and fuel gases in compartment ignite almost simultaneously; the result is full-room fire 
Typically occurs during the fire’s growth stage, but may occur during fully developed stage as result of change in ventilation

slides.title:

content:

slides.title:
Reaction of Building Construction to Fire
(2 of 4)
content:
Reaction of Building Construction to Fire
(2 of 4)

In a structure fire, the method by which fire receives the needed oxygen to sustain the combustion reaction occurs through flow paths
Flow path is composed of two regions
Ambient air flow in
Hot exhaust flow out

slides.title:
Reaction of Building Construction to Fire
(3 of 4)
content:
Reaction of Building Construction to Fire
(3 of 4)

Flow, as opposed to flow path, is always unidirectional due to pressure differences
In intake flow, the ambient air (higher pressure) flows toward the seat of the fire (lower pressure) and reacts with fuel
In exhaust flow, products of combustion (higher pressure) flow away from fire toward low-pressure outlet

slides.title:
Reaction of Building Construction to Fire 
(4 of 4)
content:
Reaction of Building Construction to Fire 
(4 of 4)

In a structure fire, the floor plan and openings within the structure determine available flow path
For example, hot gases from fire in bedroom will travel out of the doorway and into the hallway if door is open

slides.title: Contents of a Structure (1 of 2)
content:
Interior finishes and furnishings
Often the most readily available fuel source
When contents release a large amount of heat rapidly, both intensity of fire and speed of development will increase
Synthetic furnishings begin to pyrolyze rapidly even when located far from fire’s origin

slides.title: Structural Elements in a Fire
content:
Structure itself provides a new source of fuel
Fire may be burning in hidden cavities throughout the building
Hidden spaces make finding and extinguishing fire more difficult and increase the potential risk of building collapse
Higher the fuel load, more likely fire will behave in following ways
If structural members are part of fuel load, building will deteriorate faster
Longer the fire burns, the more fire spread accelerates
Fire may have higher HRR
Structure may self-ventilate, introducing more oxygen and accelerating fire development

slides.title: Building Compartmentation (1 of 3)
content:
Arrangement of compartments in a building directly affects fire development, severity, possible duration, and intensity
Open floor plans have fewer fire barriers than compartmentalized floor plans

slides.title: Building Compartmentation (3 of 3)
content:
Any open space without a complete fire barrier dividing it is considered a compartment
Two rooms that a doorway connects are considered two compartments only if the door between them is closed
When door is open, a fire in either room can access oxygen from adjoining room
Rooms will affect one another more slowly than if intervening wall were not there at all
Closed door will slow the effect of a fire in one room on the adjoining room even further
Given enough available fuel, fire will follow oxygen through a building along any available flow path

slides.title: Learning Objectives 1-3
content:
Identify construction materials.

Describe construction types.

Identify structural system types.

slides.title: Construction Materials (1 of 3)
content:
Inspectors must be able to recognize different types of construction materials in order to
Identify construction and occupancy classifications
Apply building code requirements
Determine fire rating
Construction materials also influence which protection systems and structural separations are required by an occupancy

slides.title: Construction Materials (3 of 3)
content:
Chemical and mechanical properties and characteristics of different building materials determine their usefulness in architectural applications
Fire inspector should be familiar with physical properties, such as
Combustibility
Thermal conductivity
Rate of thermal expansion
Variation of strength with temperature
In order to identify and understand construction materials, the fire inspector needs to recognize how construction-related terminology differs in meaning

slides.title: Non-Interchangeable Terms (2 of 3)
content:
Fire-resistant materials and assemblies —Rating established through laboratory testing to determine a material or assembly’s ability to withstand fire conditions over a set time period
Fire-retardant coatings
Materials applied to the surface of combustible materials to suppress, reduce, or delay flame spread
Typically applied to reduce a material’s flame-spread rating
Behavior depends on their chemical makeup and application

slides.title: Non-Interchangeable Terms (3 of 3)
content:
Ignition-resistant construction
Materials used to decrease vulnerability of structures to hazards, such as wildland fires
Features include use of fire-resistant roof coverings and approved vents to prevent fire brands and embers from entering attic spaces

slides.title: Review Question 1
content: What is the difference between fire-resistant materials and fire-retardant coatings?

slides.title: Solid Lumber
content:
Lumber is milled from a log that has been sawed or planed
Has three primary size classifications
Dimensional lumber
Boards
Timbers
Member size of solid sawn wood is given as a nominal size
Its final dressed size is smaller and depends on both nominal size and size classification

slides.title: Scarf and Finger Joints
content:
To obtain the necessary length from shorter pieces, scarf joints or finger joints are used to create longer laminated members
These joints provide additional surface area for the glue, which allows the transmission of a greater amount of force than a typical butt joint
Inspector should know that scarf and finger joints hold laminated members together

slides.title: Cross-Laminated Timber (CLT) (1 of 2)
content:
Engineered lumber panel product similar to plywood
Consists of multiple laminations that are assembled using solid-sawn lumber material, either boards or dimension lumber
Lamination thicknesses currently range between 5/8 and 2 inches (16 to 51 mm)
Direction of the wood grain in CLT is alternated 90 degrees between the laminations — Increasing the panel strength and stability

slides.title: Cross-Laminated Timber (CLT) (2 of 2)
content:
CLT panels can be used for both floor and wall systems
In floor systems, they behave like a flat plate spanning in two directions
In wall systems, CLT panels act as load bearing walls
CLT panels are typically used as a system in buildings constructed using mass-timber, but they may also be used as individual elements in other construction methods

slides.title: Wood Panel Products (2 of 2)
content:
In stressed skin panels, a skin of plywood or oriented strand board (OSB) is attached to an interior frame or plastic foam core
Manufactured panels are commonly used in modular buildings
Has replaced plywood and planking in many construction applications, including roof decks, walls, and subfloors

slides.title:
Fire-Retardant-Treated Wood (FTRW) 
(2 of 3)
content:
Two main methods of fire-retardant treatment for wood are surface coating and pressure impregnation
Surface coating is used primarily to reduce the surface burning and flame spread rating of wood
Pressure impregnation of wood affects the whole component, and is permanent when used under proper conditions
Fire-retardant treatments most commonly used are combinations of inorganic or organic salts
Fire-retardant chemicals used in the pressurization process are proprietary products, so their exact formulations are rarely available

slides.title:
Fire-Retardant-Treated Wood (FTRW)
(3 of 3)
content:
Disadvantages and limitations
Especially with regard to water solubility and structural integrity
In high humidity and/or elevated temperatures, some fire-retardant chemicals may adversely affect the structural strength of this wood
Intumescent coatings can be applied to wood to make its surface fire resistant
Must be applied per the manufacturer’s specification(s) and listing for the surface/material to be protected
In accordance with the applicable building code, a special inspection may be required

slides.title: Exterior Wall Materials
content:
Exterior walls of a wood-frame building include materials that resist damage from weather and pests
Sidings are often chosen for aesthetic reasons, and underlayer components may be chosen for compatibility with sidings

slides.title: Building Wrap
content:
Layer of building wrap material acts as a vapor barrier between the sheathing and the siding
Reduces the infiltration of moisture and air
Modern synthetic building wraps are much more fire-resistant than the asphalt impregnated felt or tar paper used in older installations

slides.title: Insulation (1 of 2)
content:
Use of combustible insulation may increase the possibility of a fire starting within a wall
For example, an electrical malfunction may ignite the insulation within a wood-framed wall
Extent to which combustible insulation increases fire spread depends on the existence of air space
Any void between the insulation and the wall surface contributes to rapid fire development within the wall space
If insulation completely fills the void, the fire has to burn upward through the material and will progress much more slowly

slides.title: Insulation (2 of 2)
content:
Solid-fill foam insulations are applied as soft foam and harden after application
Foam is treated with flame retardants before application
Two types of solid-fill foam insulations are 
Polyurethane foam
Urea formaldehyde foam
Noncombustible materials used for insulation include glass/rock wool and fiberglass
Can also take the form of loose-fill material, including granulated rock wool, mineral/glass wool, cellulose fiber, treated-shredded wools

slides.title: NOTE2
content: Some older vermiculite and batt insulation also contain asbestos. See the Safety Alert, “Asbestos Components,” for more information on the dangers of asbestos in building materials.

content:
Aluminum
Asphalt siding/shingles
Cement board
Plywood

Stucco
Wood boards/shingles

slides.title: Safety Alert — Asbestos Components (1 of 2)
content:
Asbestos can be found in a wide variety of building products
Siding
Adhesives
Electrical/Heating Equipment
Floor/Ceiling Tiles 
Drywall Compound
Insulation

slides.title: Safety Alert — Asbestos Components (2 of 2)2
content: Asbestos is a carcinogen linked with causing chronic lung disease and cancer. While use of asbestos has decreased significantly since the 1970’s, exposure concerns are still present in older structures. When decomposing, asbestos fibers can become airborne, requiring inspectors to wear proper PPE and to follow decontamination procedures, such as discarding contaminated resources after use.

slides.title: Concrete (4 of 4)
content:
There are many different types of concrete, including ordinary and lightweight
Used for the following
Pavement
Foundations
Columns
Floors
Walls
Masonry units

slides.title: Masonry
content:
In masonry wall construction, individual units are laid on top of one another and bound with mortar
Although masonry units are inherently fire-resistive, mortar joints may deteriorate over time
Exposure to fire may also weaken the structure
Masonry units can be 
Brick and concrete block
Stone
Clay tile block and gypsum block

slides.title: Stone (1 of 2)
content:
Stonemasonry consists of pieces of rock that have been removed from the earth and assembled to form a structural element
Stone may be cut to a specific size and shape
In construction, stone can be used in two ways
It can be laid with mortar to form walls (similar to brick or concrete block)
Used as an exterior veneer when attached by supports to a building’s structural frame

slides.title: Stone (2 of 2)
content:
Principal types of stone used in construction are
Granite
Limestone
Sandstone
Slate
Marble

slides.title: Clay Tile and Gypsum Block
content:
Where clay is readily available, clay tile blocks are used for foundations and walls
Hollow blocks provide a space for fill material
Deteriorate over time and susceptible to damage from water and freezing temperatures
Both clay tile and gypsum blocks were once widely used in the construction of interior partitions
Gypsum blocks can still be found in some existing structures
Not used in exterior construction because they absorb water
Structural glazed tile (SGT) provides a smooth, durable surface and is often found in shower rooms, schools, and correctional facilities

slides.title: Steel (2 of 4)
content:
As a structural material, steel has two main disadvantages
When exposed to air and moisture, steel tends to corrode (rust)
When exposed to high temperatures, steel loses strength and elongates

slides.title: Steel (4 of 4)
content:
When subjected to fire, steel loses strength and elongates depending on orientation
Steel connected to exterior walls can fail, leading to collapse
Can melt when exposed to extreme levels of heat common in compartment fires
Rate at which unprotected steel fails when exposed to fire depends on several factors
Mass of the steel members and surface area exposed
Intensity of the fire 
Load supported by the steel
Type of structural connections used to join the steel members

slides.title: Fire Protection (2 of 2)
content:
Lighter-weight insulating materials are 
More fragile than heavier materials
More susceptible to damage or dislodgement
May reduce or negate the member’s fire rating
Intumescent coatings also provide fire protection for steel

slides.title: Membrane Ceilings (1 of 2)
content:
Steel floor support systems are frequently protected using a noncombustible ceiling system or a special insulating ceiling tile that is part of a fire-rated membrane ceiling
Provide an attractive, finished surface that hides ductwork and electrical conduit

slides.title: Membrane Ceilings (2 of 2)
content:
Rated ceiling acts as a thermal barrier between the fire below it and the floor or roof assembly overhead
When workers penetrate a membrane ceiling to install light fixtures or ventilation ducts, increased insulation or fire dampers may be required to maintain the ceiling’s integrity

slides.title: Glazing
content:
Used as a building material to transmit light
In addition to windows, architectural applications of glass include
Skylights
Storefronts
Church windows
Partition walls 
Exterior curtain walls

slides.title: Glazing Hazards
content:
Inspector must be aware that when glazing is broken, it is often replaced with the wrong and/or inferior glass
When glass is heated, internal thermal stresses cause it to shatter and fall out of its frame
Fire-rated glass may be used in fire-rated assemblies and as a structural component
Fire-rated glass and frames are required to be labeled
Inspectors should check for the appropriate markings

slides.title: Wired Glass
content:
Wired glass
Used in both interior and exterior applications, fire doors, windows adjacent to fire escapes, and corridor separations
Used to protect against exterior exposures
When the glass breaks, wires hold glass in place, permitting it to act as a barrier to a fire
Not all wired glass is fire-rated

slides.title: Fire-Rated Glass
content:
Fire-rated glass
Panels are constructed from a combination of glass and plastic and do not require interior wires
Fire-rated glazing must be installed in a fire-rated framing that is rated as an assembly

slides.title: Gypsum Board
content:
Also known as drywall or Sheetrock®, gypsum is a mineral-based product from which plaster and wallboards are constructed
High water content gives it excellent heat-resistant/fire-retardant properties
Commonly used in the fire protection of individual beams and girders because it breaks down gradually under fire conditions through a process called calcination
Used for fire-resistive assemblies 
Produced for different purposes
Research a building’s original plans to verify that the correct gypsum board has been used

slides.title: Types of Gypsum
content:
Regular gypsum board — Used for most applications
Water-resistant gypsum board — Produced with water-repellent paper facing 
Exterior gypsum board — Used in commercial exterior applications 
Impact-resistant gypsum board — Used in high impact areas
Types X and C gypsum board — Used in fire-rated assemblies
Foil-backed gypsum board — Used to replace the vapor barrier in outside walls
Gypsum backing board — Used as a backing layer in multilayer assemblies
Coreboard — Used for shaft walls and solid partitions

slides.title: Type X and Type C Gypsum Boards
content: Type X and Type C Gypsum Boards

slides.title: Plastics
content:
Strength of plastic materials is close to that of wood, although carbon-reinforced plastic may approach the strength of steel
In building constructions, plastic materials are used in both interior and exterior applications

slides.title: Exterior Insulation and Finish Systems (EIFS) (1 of 2)
content: Exterior Insulation and Finish Systems (EIFS) (1 of 2)

slides.title: Exterior Insulation and Finish Systems (EIFS) (2 of 2)
content: Exterior Insulation and Finish Systems (EIFS) (2 of 2)

Highly combustible, so inspectors must be able to recognize its use in building construction
Can be ignited from an exterior source or from the radiant heat of an exposed fire

slides.title: Flammability
content:
Varies widely
Plastics like cellulose nitrate burn so rapidly that they constitute a unique fire hazard
Other plastics may burn slowly and stop burning when the ignition source is removed
Fire retardants can be added to some plastics to reduce their flammability and ignition sensitivity
Even plastics with low flammability are subject to deterioration and may give off toxic gases at temperatures above 500°F (260°C)
Plastic materials frequently exhibit burning properties different from other materials

slides.title: Fire Hazards
content:
Plastics used in building construction increase the fire hazard because they add to the amount of fuel in a building and increase the toxicity of products of combustion
Where large amounts of plastic are used, such as foam plastic in wall insulation, the fire hazard is greatly increased
Special treatment, such as covering the surface of the insulation with a noncombustible material or installing automatic sprinklers, is required in these instances
Of special importance to the inspector are plastics used in buildings that are classified as either noncombustible or fire-resistive under the provisions of a building code

slides.title: Review Question 2
content: What are the hazards associated with plastics?

slides.title: U.S. Construction
content:
Construction materials and their performance under fire conditions determine the construction type of a structure
Both the IBC® and NFPA 5000® recognize five types of construction
Type I through Type V
Each construction type is further divided into subcategories
Inspector should refer to locally adopted codes and standards for specific information on each construction type
Every structure is composed of structural frame, load bearing walls, non-load bearing walls and partitions, floor and roof construction

slides.title: Type I (2 of 5)
content: Small quantities of specific combustible materials are occasionally allowed in Type I construction
Courtesy of Ron Moore, McKinney (TX) Fire Department

slides.title: Type I (5 of 5)
content:
Type I construction provides structural stability during a fire and limits fire spread by virtue of fire barriers
By itself this construction type may not offer greater life safety or loss reduction

Amount of combustible materials in the structure (furniture, merchandise, wall or window coverings) may compromise the structure’s fire resistance and structural integrity

slides.title: Type II (2 of 3)
content:
Common Examples
Structures with metal framing members
Metal cladding
Concrete block walls with metal deck roofs supported by unprotected open-web steel joists

slides.title: Type III (1 of 3)
content:
Exterior walls must be constructed of noncombustible materials

Interior elements can be constructed of any material permitted by the adopted code

Brick, concrete, and reinforced concrete are typically used in exterior walls and interior nonbearing walls

Floors, roofs, and interior nonbearing framing and partitions are constructed of small-dimension wood or metal stud systems

slides.title: Type III (2 of 3)
content: Common in churches, schools, apartments and mercantiles

slides.title: Type III (3 of 3)
content:
Inspectors must be aware of the following Type III construction factors

Voids inside the wooden channels created by roof and truss systems will allow fire spread unless proper firestopping is applied

Renovations in older Type III structures may result in greater fire risk

New construction materials used during renovations may reduce the load-carrying capacity of the supporting structural member

Original use of the structure may have changed to one that requires a greater load-carrying capacity

slides.title: NOTE3
content: Firestopping is required for all construction with vertical or horizontal penetrations.

slides.title: Type IV (2 of 4)
content:
Interior building elements are of solid or laminated wood with no concealed spaces

Structures are stable and more resistant to collapse from the effects of fire

slides.title: Type V (2 of 5)
content: Normally consists of framing materials that include wooden 2 × 4-inch (50 mm by 100 mm) studs or wood sill plates

slides.title: Type V (4 of 5)
content:
Modern Type V construction includes use of more lightweight engineered lumber systems to support roof and floor loads 
Lightweight wood truss can be assembled in many configurations to support large loads over relatively long spans
Trusses typically use a triangular configuration to provide stability and efficiently transfer the applied loads
Trusses are an efficient use of lumber materials and provide many open areas to install mechanical, plumbing, electrical systems throughout a structure
Disadvantage to truss construction is that structural redundancy is reduced- all truss members critical

slides.title: Canadian Construction (1 of 2)
content:
National Building Code of Canada (NBC) types of building construction
Combustible construction — Construction that does not meet the acceptance criteria for noncombustible construction
Noncombustible construction — Construction in which a degree of fire safety is attained by using noncombustible materials for structural members and other building assemblies
Heavy timber construction — Combustible construction in which a degree of fire safety is attained by placing limitations on the sizes of wood structural members and thickness/composition of wood floors and roofs and avoiding concealed spaces

slides.title: Review Question 3
content: Name and describe the five U.S. construction types.

slides.title:
Section III:
Structural Systems
content: Learning Objective 3 — Identify structural system types.

slides.title: Structural Systems (4 of 4)
content:
When evaluating a particular structure, inspector may need to refer to the building department/permit office files for construction documents that were submitted with the original building permit application
Fire department’s inspection file may also contain a description of the construction system used
Courtesy of Ron Moore, McKinney (TX) Fire Department

slides.title: Bearing Wall Structures (1 of 2)
content:
Use the walls of a building to support spanning elements, such as beams, trusses, and precast concrete slabs
Load walls support vertical loads from floors and roofs in addition to their own weight
Exterior walls normally serve as the bearing walls, with the interior support system consisting of columns and beams
Interior walls may also be used for structural support

slides.title: Bearing Wall Structures (2 of 2)
content:
In a bearing wall structure, the walls are subjected to compressive loads
Walls may be continuous or interrupted for door and window openings

slides.title: Dead Loads (2 of 2)
content:
Dead loads usually remain the same throughout the life of a structure
Air conditioning installed on the roof of a building is considered a dead load, but moving the unit to a different position on the roof may substantially change the load on an individual roof support member

slides.title: Live Load
content:
Live load is any non-fixed or non-permanent load, such as building contents and occupants
Actual weight and distribution of a building’s contents are not known exactly and have to be estimated based on historical information
Since live loads can be characterized by occupancy, building codes specify minimum live loads in the design process for different occupancies
Building codes also specify that, when the live load for a given occupancy is known and exceeds the values contained in the code, the actual load must be used in design calculations

slides.title: Lateral Load (2 of 2)
content:
Fundamentally, the building wants to stay in motion as the movement of the earth suddenly changes direction
It must be emphasized that minimum live loads are uniformly distributed and applied over a large area

slides.title: Shell and Membrane Structures (1 of 5)
content:
Shell and membrane structures consist primarily of an enclosing, waterproof surface
Applied loads create tensile stresses in the membrane
These stresses are transferred to the anchorage of the structure
Tents and membrane structures can be distinguished by their construction methods 
Tents are supported in any manner other than by air or their contents
Membrane structures vary from cable-supported to air-supported

slides.title: Shell and Membrane Structures (3 of 5)
content:
Because fabrics cannot support compressive forces, membrane structures must be supported by cables, masts, framework, or pneumatic pressure
Support system must provide sufficient rigidity to avoid shaking or flapping

slides.title: Shell and Membrane Structures (5 of 5)
content:
Fabrics used in membrane structures are considerably thinner than other roof system assemblies
Two layers of material, separated by several inches (millimeters) of air space, can be used to provide adequate thermal insulation
Intervening air space acts as a thermal barrier
Materials in membrane structures must be noncombustible or meet the fire propagation performance requirements in the locally adopted code
Membrane structures can also be used in fire-resistive construction when the building code requires only a noncombustible roof for a fire-resistive building

slides.title: Frame Structural Systems
content:
A frame supports a building like a skeleton supports the human body
Walls act like skin to enclose the frame
In the fire service, frame construction often refers to a light wood-frame building, but frame structural systems are also built using other materials

slides.title: Braced Frames (2 of 2)
content:
When lateral loads are exerted onto the frame, it tries to deform
Bracing resists the loads, transferring them down through the building and eventually to the ground	
Efficient and cost effective 
Can significantly impact the architectural layout of the building

slides.title: Slab and Column Frames (2 of 2)
content:
The intersection between the slab and column is usually reinforced by a column capital or a drop panel
Wood decks and metal decks, supported by beams and columns, can be used to support floor loads

slides.title: Rigid Frames (2 of 2)
content:
Also used in other types of structures, such as multistory and multi-span designs
Typically, the joints are the last portion of the assembly to fail under fire conditions

slides.title: Wood Structural Systems
content:
Most common structural system for low-rise and mid-rise residential and commercial buildings
Interior and exterior wood framing is common in Type IV and Type V structures, including one- and two-family dwellings and apartment buildings or hotels of less than four stories
Two most frequently encountered wood framing systems 
Light wood framing (Type V)
Heavy-timber framing (Type IV)

slides.title: Light Wood Framing (2 of 2)
content: Two most common methods of wood framing are balloon and platform framing

slides.title: Balloon Framing
content:
Closely spaced studs are continuous from the sill to the top plate of the roof line
Joists that support the second floor are nailed directly to the studs
Vertical combustible spaces between the studs provide a channel for the rapid spread of fire from floor to floor
Fire that originates in the stud space, or spreads into it, can spread from the vertical cavity into the horizontal joists and into the attic space
Firestopping must be provided to stop this movement

slides.title: Platform Framing (2 of 2)
content: Plate installed on top of the studs provides a firestop that tends to block fire spread from floor to floor within the walls

slides.title: Heavy Timber Framing (2 of 2)
content:
Post and beam construction uses a series of vertical elements (posts) to support the horizontal elements (beams) that are subject to transverse loads
This system is historically associated with wood beams and columns, but masonry, steel, and precast concrete are also used for posts and beams

slides.title: Distinctive Characteristics of Post and Beam Framing (1 of 2)
content: Distinctive Characteristics of Post and Beam Framing (1 of 2)

Spacing of the vertical posts and the cross-sectional dimension of the members
Vertical posts may be spaced much farther apart than stud wall construction where distance between the studs is 12 to 24 inches (300 to 600 mm)
Minimum dimensions used for the wood posts and beams are larger than the studs in stud wall construction
Typical dimensions for the posts are 6 x 8 inches (150 mm x 200 mm) when supporting roofs only
Post and beam construction may require the addition of other members, such as diagonal braces, to withstand lateral loads

slides.title: Distinctive Characteristics of Post and Beam Framing (2 of 2)
content: Distinctive Characteristics of Post and Beam Framing (2 of 2)

The interior wood surface is usually left exposed in both post and beam and heavy timber framing
Exposed wood framing eliminates combustible voids
Architecturally, the exposed surface of the wood creates an attractive, rustic finish

slides.title: Masonry Walls (1 of 3)
content:
To construct, brick units are laid side by side in a horizontal layer known as a course
Horizontal courses of brick are laid on top of each other in a vertical layer known as a wythe
Simplest brick wall consists of a single wythe
Multiple wythes are used to supply the necessary strength and stability

slides.title: Masonry Walls (2 of 3)
content:
Other placements are made for appearance or strength
Soldier course — Has bricks placed vertically on end
Header course — Has bricks placed with the end facing out
Stretcher course — Bricks placed end-to-end
Courtesy of Ron Jeffers, Union City, NJ

slides.title: Masonry Walls (3 of 3)
content:
In an unreinforced masonry wall, the strength and stability of the wall are derived from
Weight of the masonry 
Horizontal bonding between adjacent wythes 
Vertical compressive strength of the masonry units
Different types of corrosion-resistant metal ties can be used to provide horizontal bonding
Metal ties are commonly used when the wall is constructed of brick and concrete block

slides.title: Brick Veneer Systems
content:
Exterior non-load bearing brick wythe is usually constructed with a vertical cavity between the exterior and interior wythes
Vertical cavity prevents water from seeping through the mortar joints to the building’s interior and helps to increase the thermal insulating value of the wall
Rigid insulation board in this cavity may further increase the insulating value of the wall system
Placement of metal ties connecting the veneer to the backup wall is important in all cases because
Brick header course is not practical
Wall has little to no structural stability on its own

slides.title: Structural Stability (2 of 4)
content: One method of reinforcing a masonry structure and tying the structure to the floor system is to extend tension rods through the masonry walls and attach them to thrust plates on the outside

slides.title: Structural Stability (3 of 4)
content: Thrust plates are usually visible and may indicate that the building has undergone repairs

slides.title: Structural Stability (4 of 4)
content:
The higher the masonry wall, the thicker and wider the base must be to support the increased load from above 
Due to reduced floor area and increased cost compared with frame structures, very tall masonry structures are impractical

slides.title: Steel Structural Systems (2 of 4)
content:
Rigid frames and arches can be constructed from steel, and steel cables or rods are used to support roofs
Cold-rolled steel studs are used in the construction of exterior walls
Courtesy of Ron Moore, McKinney (TX) Fire Department

slides.title: Steel Structural Systems (4 of 4)
content:
Steel trusses, which can be fabricated in various shapes, are frequently used in three-dimensional space frames
Trusses can also be constructed of a combination of steel and wood
Courtesy of Ron Moore, McKinney (TX) Fire Department

slides.title: Cast-in-Place Concrete (2 of 2)
content:
Does not develop its design strength until after it has been placed in the location it will be cured and used
May result in longer construction times
Curing of concrete is sensitive to the surrounding conditions

slides.title: Precast Concrete (2 of 2)
content: Precast concrete structures have more in common with steel-framed buildings than with cast-in-place concrete buildings

slides.title: Ordinary Reinforcing (2 of 2)
content:
Concrete must be properly consolidated (vibrated) as it is placed in the forms to completely surround the rebar and to avoid cavities in the cured concrete
As the concrete cures, it bonds to the reinforcing bars because of textural shaping on the surface of the bars

slides.title: Posttensioned Reinforcement (3 of 3)
content:
Pulled end of the reinforcing strand is anchored to the concrete
Reinforcing cables are trimmed to the edge of the concrete and grouted

content:

slides.title: Learning Objectives 6-11
content:
