slides.title:
Section I:
Walls
content: Objective 1 – Describe wall types and components

slides.title: Walls (1 of 2)
content:
All types of walls affect development of fire in a building
Can be used for fire protection by creating smaller compartments
Can limit fire travel to allow for building egress

slides.title: Fire Wall Construction Types (1 of 3)
content:
Required to be of noncombustible materials in all construction types except Type V

IBC® permits Type V to use wood-framed fire walls

Required fire-resistance ratings for fire walls are 2 to 4 hours

slides.title: Fire Wall Construction Types (2 of 3)
content:
Building codes may allow reduction in fire wall’s fire-resistance rating if building is equipped throughout with an approved automatic sprinkler system

Automatic sprinkler systems typically allow an increase in the building area and may reduce the need for fire walls

May be required to extend beyond walls and roofs to prevent radiant heat of flames from adjacent surfaces

slides.title: Fire Wall Construction Types (3 of 3)
content:
Fire wall continues through roof in form of parapet

Building codes determine parapet height above combustible roof

Alternative, equivalent method of protection is to require that specific materials be used as part of assembly on either side of wall

slides.title: NOTE 1
content: A building code may require a parapet to provide a barrier to the communication of fire between closely spaced buildings.

slides.title: Discussion Question 1
content: Why are fire walls important in buildings?

slides.title: Party Walls (1 of 2)
content:
Fire wall located on a lot line between two buildings; common to both buildings

Creates separate buildings and must be constructed without openings

Almost always load bearing

Normally against regulations to breach party wall
Courtesy of Ron Jeffers, Union City, NJ.

slides.title: Fire Barriers (1 of 2)
content:
Interior walls that subdivide a floor or area of a building to resist and restrict fire travel, but are not constructed to same requirements as fire walls

Material chosen for fire barriers depends on fire resistance required and construction type of building

Fire barriers are used to
Protect exits
Function as shaft enclosures
Create or subdivide fire areas into smaller control areas
Separate different occupancy types as required by building code

slides.title: Review Question 2
content: What are the purposes of fire barriers?

slides.title: Smoke Barriers
content:
Required to resist passage of both smoke and fire
These vertical or horizontal assemblies are designed to restrict travel of smoke by creating a continuous membrane within the building
Required to have minimum fire-resistance rating of 1 hour
All joints, voids, openings, penetrations, and intersections must be addressed according to building code requirements
Material for smoke barriers depends on required fire resistance and construction type of the building

slides.title: Smoke Partitions
content:
Joints, voids, openings, penetrations, and intersections for all fire and smoke barriers and partitions must be addressed
Material chosen for these barriers and partitions depends on the required fire resistance and building’s construction type

slides.title: Enclosure and Shaft Walls (1 of 2)
content:
Enclosure walls, designed to block vertical spread of fire through a building, are placed around vertical openings that extend from floor to floor
Required to have fire-resistance rating and are usually non-load bearing
Most common construction materials can be used
Gypsum board
Lath and plaster
Concrete block

slides.title: Enclosure and Shaft Walls (2 of 2)
content:
In stairways, enclosure walls are designed to protect a means of egress
Hollow, clay-tile enclosure walls still exist in old, fire-resistive structures
Inspectors may also find load bearing, masonry stair enclosures in older buildings
Fire-rated glazing (glass)
Can be used in conjunction with stair enclosures
In addition to providing a fire barrier, fire-rated glazing can enhance security by permitting observation of stair enclosure

slides.title: Curtain Walls (1 of 3)
content:
Exterior wall that encloses building
Designed to separate interior environment from exterior environment
Often conceals building’s structural details
Installation commonly results in gap between edge of floor and curtain wall
Gap provides path for fire to move up inside of curtain wall
Firestopping needed to maintain continuity of floor as fire-resistive barrier

slides.title: Curtain Walls (3 of 3)
content: Some curtain wall assemblies, such as those made of aluminum and glass, have little to no fire resistance

slides.title: Review Question 4
content: What is the function of a curtain wall?

slides.title: Firestopping
content:
System used to close small gaps that are left when a joint is created
These small voids have potential to accelerate fire travel
Maintains or restores continuity and integrity of fire-rated assemblies when they intersect or when they are penetrated by building services
To address small voids, building industry works with intumescent materials that expand when exposed to heat
Can be used in joint system as premanufactured collars, wraps, pillows, or caulk
Intumescent caulk is typically installed as part of assembly incorporating mineral wool as backing material

slides.title: Discussion Question 2
content: What are some buildings in your area that use the different types of walls?

slides.title:
Section II:
Doors
content: Objective 2 – Distinguish among types of doors.

slides.title: Sliding Doors
content:
Suspended from overhead track and may use steel or nylon rollers
Floor guides or tracks prevent door from swinging laterally
Can be designed as surface sliding, pocket sliding, or bypass sliding
Main advantage - Eliminate door swing that might interfere with use of interior space
Used for 
Elevators
Power-operated doors in storefront entrances
Fire doors to protect openings that are not a part of means of egress

slides.title: Vertical Doors
content:
Often used in industrial occupancies
Can be a single leaf that is raised in vertical guides along the edge of the doorway, or it can consist of two or more horizontal panels
Many vertical rolling doors consist of interlocking metal slats
Normally have counterbalance mechanism designed to help overcome the weight of the door using weights or springs
Can be power-operated, raised manually, or raised mechanically
When swinging door is installed in a large overhead door to provide means of egress, swinging door must meet code requirements

slides.title: Revolving Doors (1 of 2)
content:
Constructed with three or four sections or wings that rotate in circular frame
Designed to reduce heat or cooling losses by minimizing flow of air through a door opening
Prevents movement of hose or equipment into building, which can present a problem for firefighters
A crowd attempting to flee an emergency cannot move through revolving door as quickly as they can through swinging door
To overcome these restrictions, wings of door must be collapsible to provide unobstructed opening

slides.title: Revolving Doors (2 of 2)
content:
Side-hinged swinging door must be located within 10 feet of revolving door
Several types of mechanisms hold wings in place
Most models employ collapsing mechanism that allows wings to open to book-fold position when pushed in opposite directions

slides.title: Styles and Construction Materials (1 of 3)
content:
Fire-rated door assemblies are manufactured, assembled, and installed in accordance with specific requirements that have been tested and listed by independent testing laboratory
These doors are commonly constructed of wood, glass, and/or metal

slides.title: Style and Construction Materials (2 of 3)
content:
Solid-core doors have solid interior of wood or wood composite
Hollow-core doors have wooden frame with interior of cardboard honeycomb wrapped with veneer or fiberboard

slides.title: Style and Construction Materials (3 of 3)
content:
Glass doors are used for both exterior and interior applications, most commonly in office and mercantile buildings
Can be either frameless or framed
Codes require that glass doors be made of tempered glass that resists breakage
Various non-glass components are often used in framed door to provide additional security
Metal doors are hollow and made of steel or aluminum
Hollow metal door can be either panel or flush
Vertical sheet metal ribs within the door separate face panels of steel door from one another

slides.title: Review Question 6
content: List the five types of doors commonly used in construction.

slides.title: Discussion Question 3
content: What are some examples of the different door types in your local area?

slides.title:
Section III:
Fire Doors
content: Objective 3 — Describe the operation and construction of fire doors.

slides.title: Fire Door Operation
content:
May be open during normal operations or are easy to open to allow for ordinary occupant movement 
Must be closed in order to properly perform their function during fire
Can be automatic or self-closing
Automatic door normally held open closes when an operating device is activated
To activate closing device and shut a fire door, a smoke or fire detection device must be installed

slides.title: Fire Doors with Non-Approved Hold-Open Devices
content: Fire Doors with Non-Approved Hold-Open Devices
Only approved devices, such as magnetic hold-open devices that release on fire alarm activation, are permitted

Require removal of non-approved devices
Educate building owner or occupant about importance of fire doors remaining closed

slides.title: Fusible Links and Smoke Detector Releases
content: Fusible Links and Smoke Detector Releases

Oldest and simplest detection device is fusible link that detects heat from approaching fire
When it melts, door closes
Inexpensive, relatively rugged, and easy to maintain
Fusible link is slower to operate than detection devices that react to smoke or temperature rise
To close quickly, smoke detector may be used to activate door release
Permit easy testing of fire door but require periodic cleaning and may cost more than fusible link
Ensure all smoke detectors are properly installed

slides.title: Classifications (1 of 2)
content: Fire doors are classified by one of three systems

slides.title: Review Question 8
content: What are the classification systems for fire doors?

slides.title: Frames and Hardware (1 of 4)
content:
For fire door to block spread of fire, it must remain closed and attached to fire-rated wall under fire conditions
Testing of fire doors includes frames and hardware
Door hardware and frame must withstand stresses and pressures of fire exposure

slides.title: Frames and Hardware (2 of 4)
content:
Fire door is one part of tested assembly that must be rated, assembly is certified as single unit for specified time
To qualify as rated fire door, third party must test
Door and door seal
Hardware (hinges, latches, and locks)
Frame

slides.title: Frames and Hardware (3 of 4)
content:
Glass panels in fire doors must achieve same test results as rest of assembly
Fire door hardware is used on both sliding and swinging fire doors and normally ships with fire doors; hardware includes
Hinges
Locks
Latches
Bolts
Closers

slides.title: Rolling Steel Fire Doors (1 of 2)
content:
Used in industrial occupancies to protect an opening in a fire wall
May be used on one or both sides of wall opening, but cannot be used on any opening required to be part of means of egress

slides.title: Rolling Steel Fire Doors (2 of 2)
content:
Rolling fire doors close under force of gravity when fusible link is melted by heat from fire
In some cases, overhead doors are controlled by motors activated by smoke or heat detectors
Without swinging door at location, overhead rolling fire door may create dangerous dead-end when it closes

slides.title: NOTE 2
content: In some schools, the inspector will encounter security rolling doors that are tied to the fire detection and alarm systems. These doors roll up on activation of the system and need to be tested during an inspection.

slides.title: Horizontal Sliding Fire Doors (1 of 2)
content:
Found in old industrial buildings and usually held open by fusible link
Slide into position along a track by gravity or by force of counterweight
Metals used to cover wood core include steel and galvanized sheet metal

slides.title: Horizontal Sliding Fire Doors (2 of 2)
content:
Some are certified to protect openings in walls that are required parts of means of egress
Used to separate large areas and connected to fire detection and alarm system
When system activated, doors automatically close

slides.title: Review Question 9
content: Describe the operation of rolling steel fire doors and horizontal sliding fire doors.

slides.title: Swinging Fire Doors
content:
Operation of swinging fire doors may impede exit path when used in certain configurations
When fire doors are on both sides of fire wall, inspector should verify that both doors swing in direction of egress
Fire-resistive-rated vestibule between doors provides space needed for doors to swing in same direction

slides.title: Special Types
content:
Available for following
Freight and passenger elevators
Service counter openings
Security (bullet-resisting) doors
Dumbwaiters
Chute openings
Fire-rated partition is required and fixed wall is not desirable, horizontal-folding fire door system may be used to meet fire separation requirements
Signal from smoke or fire detector activates door closer
Battery powers motor if regular power supply is interrupted

slides.title: Glass Panels and Louvers
content:
Fire door often contains glass vision panels
There are restrictions on allowable area of glass in fire doors
Glazing material used in fire doors must be fire-rated
In some enclosures, louvers may be installed in a fire door to permit ventilation while the door is closed
Louvers must close to protect opening during fire
In fusible link louvers, fusible link melts at high temperatures and allows blades of louver to close
Only fire doors listed for installation of louvers can have louvers installed

Frame includes members that form perimeter of a window and is fixed to surrounding wall or other supports

content:
Metal bars and screens are commonly used on windows to provide additional security
Metal bars may be
Fastened to building
Embedded in masonry
Mounted on hinges and locked with padlocks or other devices

Section V:
Stairs
content: Objective 5 — Describe the use of stairs in buildings.

slides.title: Stairs (1 of 2)
content:
Provide access to different levels of structure and serve as means of egress
Recognize fire and life safety requirements for stairs designated as means of egress
Building codes govern geometric configurations of stairs

slides.title: Review Question 12
content: What governs the geometric configurations of stairs?

slides.title: Section VI: Interior Finishes
content: Objective 6 — Describe interior finishes in buildings.

slides.title: Interior Finishes (1 of 4)
content:
Materials used for exposed surfaces of walls and ceilings
May also be part of building’s structural materials
For example, a masonry wall left exposed as part of restaurant’s décor

slides.title: Interior Finishes (4 of 4)
content:
Building codes may define doors, door and window frames, chair railings, and wainscotings as interior finishes
Hanging fabrics are not treated as interior finishes unless they are applied to a ceiling or wall
Building codes usually exclude paint and other surface treatments
Inspectors should be alert to carpeting on walls and other materials used as interior finishes that may not be approved for that application

slides.title:
Section VII:
Floors
content: Objective 7 — Describe floor construction and the effects of penetrations and openings in floor assemblies.

slides.title: Review Question 15
content: List construction materials used for floors.

slides.title: Supports and Coverings (1 of 3)
content:
Floors installed over crawl space or above grade level must have underlying support such as masonry, wood, or steel
Exact type of floor system may not be readily apparent

slides.title: Penetrations and Openings (1 of 3)
content:
Fire resistance of floor assembly plays key role in preventing vertical spread of fire and products of combustion
Often desirable to have communicating openings between floors
For this reason, building codes require vertical penetrations of floors be provided with fire-resistive enclosure
Examples of vertical floor penetrations
Atriums
Escalator openings
Elevator shafts
Stairwells

slides.title: Penetrations and Openings (2 of 3)
content:
Ideally, all vertical openings should be enclosed
Architect can specify that doors be held open by automatic devices that release upon activation of smoke detector
Fire-rated glazing can also be used to enclose a vertical opening
In open areas, building codes may require automatic sprinkler and smoke management systems

slides.title: Penetrations and Openings (3 of 3)
content:
Small vertical openings can allow fire and smoke to spread
Annular space around pipes that pass through floor and ceiling is often left unprotected
Under increased pressure of fire, small opening can act as nozzle, pushing fire and byproducts farther than they would go otherwise

slides.title: Review Question 16
content: What are some types of vertical floor penetrations and openings?

slides.title:
Section VIII:
Ceilings
content: Objective 8 — Identify the functions of ceilings.

slides.title: Ceilings (2 of 2)
content:
Materials, such as gypsum board or mineral tiles, are often required fire-resistance component for floor/ceiling system
As a distinct building component, ceilings rarely play a structural role

slides.title: Review Question 17
content: What are the functions of ceilings?

slides.title:
Section IX:
Roofs
content: Objective 9 — Describe roofs as a building component.

slides.title: Roofs
content:
Normally consist of a supporting structure and an outer layer
Timber and steel beams are typically used to build supporting structure
Outer layer provides water-resistant barrier for roof system
Choice of roof covering materials depends on several factors, such as
Climate
Home design
Roof slope

slides.title: NOTE 3
content: Inspectors should be aware of emerging technology and energy efficiency systems that affect rooftop systems, such as green spaces, solar panels, and skylights.

slides.title: Fire Resistance of Roof Coverings
content:
Wood shingles and shakes are highly combustible, but can be pressure-impregnated with fire-retardant chemical to reduce combustibility and meet building code requirements
Asphalt shingles are combustible and tend to drip, run, and produce heavy black smoke
Typically produced with grit surface that reduces ease of ignition 
Clay, slate, and cement-based tiles are noncombustible and produce fire-resistant roof coverings
Flying embers may still ignite roof deck if they blow under tiles
Metal roof coverings are noncombustible, provide resistance

slides.title: Evaluation of Building Components
content:
A passive fire protection system is a type of fire and safety system that often goes unnoticed after a building is constructed
These systems consist of noncombustible components and assemblies designed to resist the passage of fire
Passive fire protection system components are rated by amount of time they can pass standardized fire exposure tests without failure

slides.title: Evaluating Fire Walls (1 of 3)
content:
Fire walls subdivide a building into smaller areas so that fire in one portion of a building is likely to be contained to that area
Can also separate functions within a single structure
Fire walls can be constructed as freestanding walls or tied walls
Freestanding fire walls are self-supporting and independent of building frame
Tied wall requires support from surrounding structure
Tied walls may be used as part of double-wall system to meet code requirements

slides.title: Review Question 20
content: What is meant when a building is compartmentalized?

slides.title:
Evaluating Wall Integrity and 
Overall Stability
content:
Evaluating Wall Integrity and 
Overall Stability

Fire-resistance ratings identify the amount of time a material or assembly will resist a typical fire
Fire-rated assemblies are central to how the building codes passively deal with fire travel in buildings and how buildings behave under fire conditions
ASTM E119, Standard Test Methods for Fire Tests of Building Construction and Materials, and ANSI/UL 263, Standard for Fire Tests of Building Construction and Materials, are the only standardized test methods universally accepted by the building codes

slides.title: Limitations of Fire-Resistive Assemblies
content:
When continuity of assembly is destroyed, it cannot function as a fire-rated assembly
Over time, fire resistive assemblies may be penetrated
Penetration of fire-resistive assemblies, such as those made for ductwork, plumbing, electrical, and communication purposes, may not be adequately firestopped

slides.title: NOTE 4
content: Joint systems for floor-to-wall and wall-to-wall connections are tested in accordance with UL Standard 4079, UL 4079 Standard for Test for Fire Resistance of Building Joint Systems.

slides.title: Review Question 21
content: Which two standardized test methods for fire-resistance ratings are universally accepted by the model building codes?

slides.title: NOTE 5
content: The reason for a difference between the rating of a fire door and a fire-rated wall is that the test criteria for the two are different.

slides.title: Evaluating Interior Components
content:
Inspectors must evaluate whether finishes and materials used on interior components comply with locally adopted fire and safety codes
Interior finishes pose a fire danger because they typically cover a large area and are relatively thin compared to structural components
Substandard interior finishes have contributed to many loss-of-life fires
Inspector must evaluate if interior components comply with locally adopted fire and safety codes

slides.title: Ceiling Materials
content:
In a multistory building, ceiling materials can be attached directly to the underside of floor joists or trusses or installed at a distance below floor supports
If they are installed below floor supports, ceiling materials create a large concealed space
Old buildings commonly have a new ceiling installed below an existing ceiling
Ceiling materials can conceal the type of floor or roof structure above them

slides.title: Interstitial Space
content:
Space above ceiling can be used to conceal air conditioning ducts, electrical and communications wiring, and plumbing and sprinkler piping
When the interstitial space is used as return-air plenum, fire inspector must verify that materials are noncombustible or rated for plenum use

slides.title: Review Question 22
content: What must the inspector evaluate when inspecting interior components?

slides.title: Evaluating Interior Finishes
content:
UL and other organizations have created smoke development ratings to establish and evaluate flame spread ratings for interior finish materials
Fire-retardant coatings have also been developed, tested, and approved
Inspectors should be aware that modifications to building construction components, such as interior finishes, can affect component’s fire rating
Modifications or repairs to a component should conform to same rating that was originally approved
Inspectors may need to research original building plans to determine these fire ratings

slides.title: Steiner Tunnel Test
content:
Also known as the tunnel test, it is widely used method for evaluating surface burning characteristics of materials
Produces numerical evaluation of flammability of interior materials, known as Flame Spread Index and Smoke Developed Index 
Flame spread rating is means of comparing surface flammability of material to standard materials under controlled test conditions
Building codes use flame spread and smoke developed ratings to establish control over interior finishes
Only materials with low flame spread ratings are permitted in vertical exits and exit corridors

slides.title: NOTE 6
content: In the U.S., the Steiner Tunnel test is typically designated as ASTM E84, Standard Test Method for Surface Burning Characteristics of Building Materials or ANSI/UL 743, Standard for Test for Surface Burning Characteristics of Building Materials. In Canada, CAN/ULC-S104, Standard Method of Test for Surface Burning Characteristics of Building Materials and Assemblies, utilizes the tunnel apparatus.

slides.title: Smoke Developed Index (SDI)
content:
Measured by means of a photoelectric cell and light source located at end of tunnel furnace
Based on a scale where red oak wood has a value of 100
Under test conditions, material that has SDI of 200 produces smoke that is twice as visually obscuring as red oak
Not an indication of toxicity of combustible products in interior finish materials
Tunnel test does not
Detect or measure completely transparent product of combustion such as carbon monoxide
Measure combined effects of heat, irritation, and toxicity

slides.title: Review Question 23
content: Describe the Steiner Tunnel Test, Flame Spread Index, and Smoke-Developed Index.

slides.title: Fire-Retardant Coatings (1 of 3)
content:
Can affect both smoke-developed and flame spread ratings
Properly applied fire-retardant coatings can reduce flame spread rating of some interior finishes, most notably wood materials

slides.title: Fire-Retardant Coatings (2 of 3)
content:
Respond to heat in different ways; for example
Intumescent paints expand when exposed to heat and create a thick, puffy coating that insulates surface beneath the wood
Mastic coatings form a thick, noncombustible membrane over the surface of the wood

slides.title: Safety Alert
content: Fire-retardant coatings only affect the surface of a material. A fire-retardant coating does not increase the fire resistance of structural components or assemblies unless it has also been tested and listed for use in a fire-resistive assembly. However, because fire-retardant coatings can be field-applied, contractors and design professionals may use them as an inexpensive remedy for other fire protection shortcomings.

slides.title: Evaluating HVAC Systems (1 of 2)
content:
Designed primarily to maintain comfortable environment
Regulate intake of outdoor air and recirculation of indoor air
Components vary based on size and use of structure
Have potential to significantly affect any fire event
Inspector should verify that HVAC equipment is properly maintained by reviewing maintenance records and conducting field observations

slides.title: Evaluating HVAC Systems (2 of 2)
content:
Verify documentation of regular maintenance of
Air ducts
Air filtration devices
Air heating and cooling equipment
Exhaust (properly sealed into chimneys)
Fans
Outside air intakes
Smoke and/or fire dampers

slides.title: Review Question 25
content: How can the inspector verify that HVAC equipment is properly maintained?

slides.title: Smoke and Fire Dampers (1 of 3)
content:
Codes may require the installation to protect duct penetrations through fire-rated assemblies
Smoke damper usually activated by a smoke detector, and closes by active mechanical action
Fire damper usually a spring-loaded shutter held open by a fusible link
May also be activated by signal from fire alarm system

slides.title: Smoke and Fire Dampers (2 of 3)
content:
Ductwork for HVAC systems can provide a ready means for the products of combustion to travel through the entire area served by the system
Provisions must be made to control flow of smoke within building through HVAC systems
Most HVAC systems are designed to turn off immediately upon detection of fire
Most codes require HVAC systems above certain capacity to have internal duct smoke detection device
Automatic shut-off designed to prevent spread of smoke
Duct smoke detection devices should never be a substitute for area smoke detection devices

slides.title: Review Question 26
content: What is the purpose of fire and smoke dampers?

slides.title: Smoke Control Systems (2 of 2)
content:
Smoke detectors within the HVAC system may be located in main supply ducts, downstream of air filters and cleaners, or in the return air ducts
Locations depend on mechanical building code under which they were installed
When HVAC system is used for active smoke control, system operates in special mode that no longer delivers supply air to fire area
Air is drawn from fire area and discharged to outside without recirculating or contaminating air intake
At same time, the return air supply to the building ceases
Fire dampers usually omitted from this type of active smoke control system

slides.title: Refrigerants
content:
International Mechanical Code® (IMC®) and the American Society of Heating, Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE) classify refrigerants by flammability and toxicity
Inspectors need a basic understanding of the ASHRAE standard because a refrigerant’s classification and amount of refrigerant in the system dictate when jurisdiction’s fire code requirements apply

slides.title: Electrical Service Panels
content:
All structures with electrical power systems have service panels where incoming electricity is distributed into individual circuits
Circuits designed to deliver electricity in proper proportion
Prevents wiring from becoming overloaded

slides.title: Review Question 30
content: What is the function of an electrical service panel?

slides.title: Switchgears
content:
Used to control, protect, and isolate electrical equipment
Located in
Electrical power stations
Industrial complexes
Electrical equipment rooms
Contain multiple disconnect switches or circuit breakers that prevent short circuits, can also reset a system after short has occurred

slides.title: Review Question 31
content: What is the function of switchgears?

slides.title: Generators
content:
Supply backup power to buildings during emergencies
May be limited to operating fire protection and emergency lighting systems
Usually located outside or in basement
Natural gas and diesel
Automatic transfer switch starts and stops generator when needed

slides.title: Transformers
content:
Convert high-voltage electricity supplied by electric utility service to an appropriate voltage for use in a building
Some transformers supply special systems and equipment in industrial and commercial buildings
Generate heat as they change voltage

slides.title: Caution 1
content: Transformers present the same dangerous hazards as any other energized electrical equipment — especially electrocution and fires caused by shorts, arcs, and sparks.

slides.title:
Evaluating Elevator Hoistways and Doors 
(1 of 5)
content:
Evaluating Elevator Hoistways and Doors 
(1 of 5)

Elevator hoistway is vertical shaft where elevator car travels
Constructed of fire-resistive materials and equipped with fire-rated door
Any penetrations must be done with appropriately rated assembly
No wiring, ductwork, or piping should be run in hoistway unless for elevator itself

slides.title:
Evaluating Elevator Hoistways and Doors
(2 of 5)
content:
Evaluating Elevator Hoistways and Doors
(2 of 5)

Elevator hoistway has potential to act as vertical chimney and spread fire and smoke through a building
If not vented at top, hot gases and smoke may accumulate and spread horizontally to upper floors
Building codes require venting at top
Elevator hoistway enclosures are usually required to be fire-rated assemblies
Any penetrations through the hoistway walls must be done with installation of appropriately rated assembly
No wiring, ductwork, or piping should be run within hoistway unless required for elevator itself

Provide additional barrier for smoke travel out of the hoistway
Work like regular doors
Hinged at one side and swing outward from the hoistway
Equipped with handle for manual operation

Vertical Shafts (1 of 2)

Utility chase – Vertical pathway in a building that contains building services
Can be used for variety of purposes including
Plumbing
Electrical raceways
Telecommunications
Data cables
Ductwork for HVAC and grease
Vertical shaft is also vertical pathway in building used for other building services like trash chutes and linen chutes

slides.title: Refuse and Linen Chutes (1 of 2)
content:
Large vertical chute that extends through a building and has openings on each floor for depositing trash or soiled linens
Chute terminates at grade level or in basement where material is collected
Required to be constructed of fire-resistive materials and may require sprinkler protection
Must be constructed of noncombustible material with rated doors and surrounded by fire-rated enclosure
Automatic sprinklers may be required at top of chute and in its termination room
Common for some smoke to leak out of waste chutes through the doors

slides.title: Refuse and Linen Chutes (2 of 2)
content:
Smoke is transferred throughout floors, and there may be heavy smoke in upper floors
Inspectors should be aware of these weak points and evaluate that components of these vertical shafts are intact
Fire in a properly designed, installed, and maintained waste chute should be contained within the chute

slides.title: Grease Ducts (1 of 5)
content:
Installed over cooking appliances that produce grease-laden vapors
Carry grease vapors to outside of building
Has no areas where grease may become trapped
Application, design, and protection required for grease ducts are specified in codes
Inspector should examine duct to see that it is clean and free from grease buildup

slides.title: Grease Ducts (2 of 5)
content:
Kitchen grease exhaust ducts always require 1-hour fire-resistive separation
Can be achieved with conventional duct construction, but a fire-resistive-rated duct wrap system is normally used
Single-exhaust duct is one that serves only one exhaust hood
It typically has one fire suppression system to cover appliance, hood, and all ductwork
Grease duct designed to withstand fire inside duct
Commercial cooking venting system may require automatic fire suppression equipment

slides.title: Grease Ducts (3 of 5)
content:
Inspectors may encounter manifold exhaust ducts while evaluating grease ducts 
Manifold ducts serve more than one exhaust hood
Duct is smallest as it leaves each single exhaust hood and increases in cross-section as it joins with another branch duct
Typically have separate fire suppression systems for each hood, but each duct operates simultaneously
If system is not properly maintained, common ductwork may allow fire to spread through large areas of building

slides.title: Grease Ducts (4 of 5)
content:
Some exhaust systems have additional grease-removal devices, known as extractors, in the duct system
May be located in false ceiling spaces, in a mezzanine, or on the roof
May contain the following

slides.title: Grease Ducts (5 of 5)
content:
Grease extraction and control equipment may be installed to remove odors from exhaust stream
Most installed on roof but may also be located in ceiling spaces
Some designed with water or odor-control chemical spray systems
Extractors can present additional fire hazards due to accumulation of grease on filters and fusible links that activate fire suppression system
Some design applications include horizontal ducts, which must slope to vertical section and cannot have a trap or dam

slides.title: Occupancy Classification
content: AHJ’s adopted building codes establish occupancy classifications based on the anticipated use of the space

slides.title: Applicable Codes and Standards (4 of 4)
content:
If the intended use of the space is specifically listed in the code, the determination of a building’s occupancy classification can be relatively straightforward
If not, the inspector may need to make a judgment call as to the occupancy classification that most closely fits the intended use	
Inspectors who need to interpret a code should consult with other inspectors in the agency to determine what may have been done previously in similar situations
It is very important that the inspector and the enforcement agency be as consistent as possible in their interpretation and application of the code

slides.title: NOTE1
content: The occupancy classification is based on the building code and is set by the building code official. If there are questions regarding an occupancy classification, the fire inspector should contact the building code official for clarification.

content: List model codes that deal with occupancy classifications.

Single-Use Occupancy Classifications
content: Learning Objective 2 — Distinguish among single-use occupancy classifications.

slides.title:
Single-Use Occupancy Classifications
(2 of 3)
content:
Self-preservation is the ability to evacuate or leave the structure without assistance
Critical to determining the overall hazard to a building’s occupants
Using occupancy classifications and construction types, building officials and code enforcement personnel can gain a reasonable expectation of the hazard level in a particular building

slides.title:
Single-Use Occupancy Classifications
(3 of 3)
content:
Building conditions rarely remain the same throughout the life of the structure
Building renovations and changes in building tenants often result in uses for which a building was not initially intended
Due to ongoing research and advances in knowledge of the built environment, code requirements for a given occupancy may change over time
Prior to proposing a change to the occupancy classification of a space, building systems must be evaluated
Some owners or developers may neglect to make necessary updates because they believe the original structure was approved for occupancy regardless of how the space is used

slides.title: Reviewing Renovation Plans
content:
Inspectors reviewing plans for a renovation, issuing a new occupancy permit, or making a field inspection, must answer the following questions
Have the building’s construction materials changed since the last inspection?
Has the building’s purpose (occupancy classification) changed since the last inspection?
Have the building’s stored contents changed since the last inspection? 
What effect will the observed changes in materials and occupancy changes have on the fire and life safety provisions for the structure?

content: ICC® codes divide assembly occupancies into five groups, based on the intended use of the space and the perceived hazard associated with that use

slides.title: Ambulatory Care Classification Differences
content:
IBC® Business occupancy classification includes ambulatory care facilities and outpatient clinics where patients are not rendered incapable of self-preservation by the services provided
NFPA codes classify outpatient clinics as separate-use, ambulatory health care (AHC) occupancies

slides.title:
Inspecting Educational Occupancies
(3 of 4)
content: In the wake of active shooter incidents, inspectors are also challenged to find a balance between fire safety and the public perception that security, not fire, is the greater potential hazard in educational settings

slides.title:
Inspecting Educational Occupancies
(4 of 4)
content:
Day-care facilities that provide supervision or personal care service to more than five children above 2½ years of age for less than 24 hours per day are also classified as educational occupancies
Facilities that provide care exceeding 24 hours a day are classified as institutional occupancies
Although educational facilities are not intended for 24-hour operations or boarding, maintenance staff and other building personnel may be in the buildings at any hour

slides.title: Review Question 6
content: What determines the classifications for industrial occupancies?

slides.title: Group B Institutional Occupancies
content: Group B Institutional occupancies in the Canadian code include most of the individual uses listed as Group I in the IBC®

slides.title: Health Care and Ambulatory Health Care Occupancies (1 of 2)
content: Health Care and Ambulatory Health Care Occupancies (1 of 2)

Health care occupancies provide health or medical services to four or more individuals who cannot evacuate themselves during an emergency without assistance from staff or emergency responders
Patients may be unable to escape or respond due to 
Age
Mental and physical limitations
Security provisions
Health Care occupancy classification is identified only in NFPA 1 and NFPA 101®

slides.title: Health Care and Ambulatory Health Care Occupancies (2 of 2)
content: Health Care and Ambulatory Health Care Occupancies (2 of 2)

slides.title: Outpatient Care Facilities
content: ICC® Codes classify outpatient care facilities as Group B Business occupancies

slides.title:
Detention and Correctional Occupancies
(1 of 2)
content: Detention/correctional occupancies are used to confine/house one or more persons under different degrees of security

slides.title:
Detention and Correctional Occupancies
(2 of 2)
content: In emergency situations, residents of these occupancies are normally prevented from taking anything but limited life-preservation actions without direct assistance from staff personnel

slides.title: Day-Care Occupancies (2 of 3)
content:
Inspection of a day-care facility must be tailored to meet the specific needs of its clients
Inspectors need to understand the capabilities of the occupant groups being served

slides.title: Review Question 8
content: Describe health care and ambulatory health care occupancies, residential board and care occupancies, and day-care occupancies.

slides.title: Mercantile Occupancies (2 of 2)
content:
May contain large quantities of combustible and hazardous materials – have the potential for a large loss of life
Arrangement of merchandise, both on display and in storage, can result in high fuel loads and restrict exit access for customers

slides.title: Review Question 9
content: Why do mercantile occupancies have the potential for a large loss of life?

slides.title: Residential Occupancies (1 of 4)
content:
ICC® divides the requirements for residential occupancies between the IRC® and the IBC®
IRC® contains the requirements for the design and construction of one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses that are three stories or less above grade plane
No specific provisions in the IRC® determine the number of occupants legally permitted to occupy a building constructed and/or used under these requirements
IBC® separates residential occupancies into four subgroups, based partially on the number of occupants, the duration of stay, and the conditions of use

slides.title: Residential Occupancies (4 of 4)
content: According to the NFPA, a residential occupancy provides sleeping accommodations for purposes other than detention and correctional or health care

slides.title: One- and Two-Family Dwellings (2 of 2)
content:
One- and two-family dwellings are not subject to periodic inspections in most jurisdictions
Units used as rental properties are an exception

slides.title: Lodging or Rooming House
content:
Defined as a building or part of a building that does not qualify as a one- or two-family dwelling
Guest houses, foster homes, bed and breakfasts, motels
Provide sleeping accommodations for 16 or fewer people on a transient or permanent basis
Separate cooking facilities are not included for individual occupants
Boarding or rooming house is usually a separate, distinct occupancy
When a building shares space, services, and/or operations with a lodging or rooming house, the most restrictive code provisions for these occupancies are applied

slides.title: Dormitories
content:
A dormitory is any building or portion of a building that provides sleeping accommodations to more than 16 persons who are not related
Sleeping accommodations may be in one room or in a series of smaller rooms 
Cafeteria or dining hall may be part of the facility
Fires in college, university, and boarding school dormitories, as well as fraternity and sorority houses, have increased awareness of the need to improve fire and life safety in these occupancies

slides.title: Apartment Buildings (3 of 3)
content: Inspection division should keep official records as part of the building’s permanent file and use them as a reference for all inspection activities

slides.title: Inspector Considerations (1 of 2)
content:
New rooms or dwelling units are often created in areas that were not designed to serve in that capacity
Inspector will find that exit halls have been converted into sleeping or living areas- eliminating exit passageways
Inspector must verify that the maximum number of residents does not exceed the number of residents that are permitted to reside in the unit

slides.title: Inspector Considerations (2 of 2)
content: With any occupancy designed for transient use, the inspector must remember that occupants are unfamiliar with their surroundings

slides.title: Converted Structure Concerns
content:
Some structures that were originally intended for one use have been converted into another use
These conversions usually result in multiple apartments or individually owned condominiums in structures that were not intended for residential use
Increased fire and life safety requirements are usually established during the plan review stage of the conversion project
Inspector should become familiar with these requirements and verify they are present during inspections

slides.title: Review Question 10
content: Describe a lodging or rooming house, hotel, dormitory, and apartment building.

slides.title: Materials Classification
content:
Storage Group S occupancies are used to store materials that are not classified as hazardous
High-Hazard Group H classification is used for the storage of hazardous goods in excess of maximum allowable quantities
The IBC® divides the Storage Group S occupancy classification into the following two subgroups
Moderate-hazard storage, Group S-1 —  Contains materials such as clothing, furniture, sugar, and lumber
Low-hazard storage, Group S-2 — Contains materials such as beverages up to and including 16-percent alcohol content, dry cell batteries, and metal parts

slides.title: Review Question 11
content: What usually determines a storage occupancy’s overall classification?

slides.title: Utility/Miscellaneous Occupancies
content:
Only the ICC® codes recognize the Utility/Miscellaneous Group U occupancy classification
This classification is used for buildings or structures that do not fit any other classification or are accessory to the primary occupancy

Learning Objective 3 — Explain mixed- and multiple-use occupancy classifications.

slides.title:
Mixed- and Multiple-Use Occupancies 
(1 of 2)
content: Buildings often contain more than one occupancy

slides.title:
Mixed- and Multiple-Use Occupancies
(2 of 2)
content:
Occupancy classification process can become complex when additional uses are introduced
Person charged with determining the building occupancy must first establish how the building is being used
Determine if any uses are considered accessory/incidental to primary use
If use is accessory/incidental and all code requirements are met, accessory/incidental use reverts back to the primary
Once individual spaces have been classified, requirements of governing code are applied
Methodology varies from code to code

slides.title: Inspector Considerations in Mixed- and Multiple-Use Occupancies
content: Inspector Considerations in Mixed- and Multiple-Use Occupancies

slides.title:
ICC® Codes for Mixed-Use Occupancy
(1 of 2)
content:
ICC® Codes for Mixed-Use Occupancy
(1 of 2)

Critical for inspectors to understand how a mixed-use occupancy is determined because maintaining the required separations is paramount to the safety of the building occupants
Automatic sprinkler system and alarm system requirements are applied individually to each of the spaces separated by a fire barrier
Building owners and/or building tenants frequently do not understand or appreciate the complexity and importance of these systems and may inadvertently compromise them during even minor construction projects

slides.title:
ICC® Codes for Mixed-Use Occupancy
(2 of 2)
content:
ICC® Codes for Mixed-Use Occupancy
(2 of 2)

slides.title: Nonseparated Mixed-Use
content:
Individual uses are not segregated from each other
Spaces must meet the minimum code requirements for their individual occupancy classifications
Most restrictive provisions that apply to the nonseparated occupancies also apply to the total nonseparated occupancy area
Additional requirements typically add additional cost, but may be less expensive than creating the separations that would be required to qualify for a separated mixed-use occupancy

slides.title: Review Question 12
content: How are mixed-use buildings designated in the ICC® codes?

slides.title: NOTE 2
content: Due to the cost and complexity associated with creating a separated mixed-use building, design professionals will often choose to construct the building as a nonseparated mixed-use structure.

slides.title: NFPA Codes
content:
Similar to the ICC codes, NFPA 101® defines both nonseparated and separated mixed occupancies
According to the NFPA, a multiple occupancy is a building or structure in which there are two or more classes of occupancy
NFPA defines a separated occupancy as a multiple occupancy in which fire resistance-rated assemblies separate the occupancies
If the occupancies are not separated, the most restrictive requirements of the occupancies involved must be used
If the occupancies within the structure are completely separated by fire barriers, as specified in the code, the individual occupancies are treated as separate and distinct occupancies

slides.title: Particular Importance for Inspection
content:
Two types of multiple occupancies are of particular importance to inspection personnel
Buildings that have different uses in distinctly different portions of the building
Buildings that have different uses in an intermingled manner that makes it impractical to separate portions of the building for different classifications

slides.title: NFPA 101® Recommendations
content:
Occupancies that feature intermingled uses represent a significant challenge in determining occupancy classification
NFPA 101® recommends that the most restrictive fire and life safety requirements be enforced in this situation
To follow this recommendation, either all requirements for one type of occupancy will take precedence or various requirements from each of the two occupancies will be used

In addition to floor area requirements, the ICC® codes require that a fire barrier or horizontal assembly be used to separate certain occupancies
In some situations, an automatic sprinkler system may be installed as an alternative

slides.title: Elements of a Means of Egress
content: Elements of a Means of Egress

Three basic elements
Exit access
Exit(s)
Exit discharge

slides.title: Inspecting Means of Egress (1 of 4)
content:
Most effective way to reduce risk to building occupants is removing them from dangerous environment
Inspector evaluates building’s means of egress to determine whether structure is safe
Components of means of egress must work together so occupants can safely exit from anywhere at any time

slides.title: Inspecting Means of Egress (3 of 4)
content:
Verify occupancy conditions and use of space have not been changed or modified
Determine if building permit is required for work and if egress requirements for structure are affected if changes are made

slides.title: Means of Egress
content:
Starts at any occupied point in structure
Continues through the exit
Terminates at public way or area of safe dispersal
Public way is
Street
Alley
Parcel of land open to outside air and leads to a street

slides.title: Public Way or Area of Safe Dispersal
content: Public Way or Area of Safe Dispersal

When access to public way is not available, area of safe dispersal can be used

Must be minimum area of 5 square feet per occupant attributed, located minimum of 50 feet from building

Must have a clear width & height of not less than 10 feet

Path must remain unobstructed at all times

slides.title: Exit Access (1 of 4)
content:
Leads from any occupied portion of building to exit
Corridors leading to exit
Aisles within assembly occupancy that guide people to exit
Common paths of egress travel leading to exit
Unenclosed ramps or stairways
Occupied rooms or spaces

slides.title: Areas of Refuge (1 of 2)
content:
Must provide protection to occupants who cannot evacuate without assistance
Must be accessible from area it serves by accessible means of egress
Must have direct access to stairway

slides.title: Exit (2 of 3)
content:
Examples of exits 
Doors at ground level that lead to outside of building
Exit passageways to outside
Horizontal exits
Smoke-proof enclosures

slides.title: Interior Exit Stairways and Ramps
content:
Interior configuration of building often requires change in elevation as part of the exit
When part of means of egress, stairways and ramps are required to be enclosed and separated from rest of building by fire barriers
If stairway or ramp connects four or more stories, enclosure must be fire-resistance rated for minimum of 2 hours
If stairway or ramp connects fewer than four stories, enclosure requires minimum 1-hour fire-resistance rating
Building code requires exit stairways and ramps to lead directly to exterior

slides.title: Exit Passageways (1 of 2)
content:
Similar to exit stairway enclosure, but is constructed in a horizontal plane
Connect interior exit stairway or ramp, or a corridor without stairs on same level, to exit door on structure’s exterior
Must be constructed of same fire-resistance-rated material as egress stairway; never less than a 1-hour rating
In large area buildings, exit passageways can be used to shorten the required travel distance to the exterior

slides.title: Horizontal Exits (1 of 4)
content:
Not well understood, therefore not widely utilized as element of means of egress
Often used in large buildings or buildings with large occupant loads
Can help resolve issues like means of egress capacity and travel distance
Horizontal exits provide an area of refuge for building occupants
Separates two fire compartments in a structure
Required to be protected from primary building area or refuge area by compliant fire wall or fire barrier

slides.title: Horizontal Exits (2 of 4)
content:
May be substituted for other exits if they do not compose more than 50 percent of total exit capacity of building
Provide means of egress from one building to area of refuge in another building on same level, or means of egress through fire barrier

slides.title: Exit Discharge (1 of 2)
content:
Element of means of egress system located between exit and a public way

Examples of an exit discharge include
Exterior walkway along side of structure

Private drive or alley that connect a building’s exit with public way

slides.title: Egress Courts
content:
Provides access to public way from one or more exits at ground level
May be a yard, a court, or a combination of the two
According to IBC®, configuration of an egress court depends on occupant load of exits being served
Egress courts, except those in Group R-3 and U occupancies, must be at least 44 inches wide
Egress courts serving Group R-3 and U occupancies must be at 36 inches wide
Minimum unobstructed height of all egress courts is 7 feet

Section II:
Accessory Components
content: Learning Objective 2 — Identify the different types of accessory components that make up fire-resistance-rated egress assemblies.

slides.title: Accessory Components
content:
Components that make up fire-resistance-rated assemblies separate occupants from products of combustion for a calculated time period
Panic hardware helps occupants open and secure doors
Handrails and guardrails provide protection on stairways and ramps
Recognize and evaluate these accessory components
Verify that components, such as doors, stairways, and walls, comply with adopted codes and function properly
Be aware of any exemptions or modifications in means of egress requirements for structures protected by automatic sprinkler systems

slides.title: Doors (2 of 5)
content:
Model codes require egress doors be pivoted or side-hinged swinging type
Exit doors must open in direction of travel toward primary exit
Opening must be wide enough to accommodate number of people expected to travel through door in emergency
Means of egress doors are normally required to provide minimum of 32 inches of clear unobstructed width, but there are exceptions
Refer to applicable building code for more information on these exceptions

slides.title: Doors Opening into Means of Egress
content: Doors Opening into Means of Egress

slides.title: Hardware (1 of 5)
content:
Building and fire codes allow various security options for entrance and egress doors
Inspectors should familiarize themselves with application and acceptance of different locking devices, as well as minimum code requirements for operation
Locking hardware permits unrestricted egress while exit doors remain locked from outside
Other security devices cause exit doors to remain locked until activated by fire detection, water flow, or other alarm devices
In occupancies where security concerns are present, delayed egress locking systems are permitted when used with detection or suppression systems

slides.title: Hardware (4 of 5)
content:
Model building codes define types of door locks permitted for installation in buildings that do not require panic hardware on exit doors
Exit doors normally feature locks with latches that do not require keys, special tools, or special knowledge to operate
Key-operated locking devices located on the egress side of door are permitted in some occupancies
May be wanted for security reasons
Use of egress-side key locks require signage that states: THIS DOOR TO REMAIN UNLOCKED WHEN THIS SPACE IS OCCUPIED

slides.title: Panic and Fire Exit Hardware (1 of 2)
content: Panic and Fire Exit Hardware (1 of 2)

Most recognizable egress latching system
Designed to open easily when subjected to thrusting force
Prevents crowd from building up behind door, especially in emergency situation

slides.title: Panic and Fire Exit Hardware (2 of 2)
content: Panic and Fire Exit Hardware (2 of 2)

In some occupancies, operation of panic hardware to open exit doors activates alarm
Code requires use of panic hardware on swinging doors in H occupancies
Panic hardware is required in A and E occupancies when occupant load is greater than 50
Panic and fire exit hardware may be installed where not required

slides.title: NOTE 1
content: A thumb-turn bolt that operates independently of the door latch is one example of an unacceptable locking device on the egress side of an exit door.

slides.title: Access-Controlled Egress (1 of 2)
content:
Locking hardware on access-controlled egress doors provides free egress to occupants while securing entry from outside
Occupant must use security card or enter code to gain entrance
According to the IBC®, sensor release of electrically locked egress doors is permitted in all occupancy classifications except H occupancies

slides.title: Delayed Egress (1 of 3)
content:
Used on doors in occupancies with security concerns, such as in a hospital maternity ward to deter abductions
Unlocks after door latching hardware is depressed for a specific period of time, reducing chance that person can leave unnoticed
Buildings with delayed egress locking systems must be equipped throughout with an automatic sprinkler system or approved automatic smoke or heat detection system
Actuation of automatic smoke detection, fire detection, or sprinkler system disables locking system and allows immediate egress
Loss of power to the lock or lock mechanism disables locking system

slides.title: Delayed Egress (2 of 3)
content:
Additional requirements for installation and operation include the following
Force of no more than 15 pounds must initiate release mechanism and permit door to open within 15 seconds
Opening door must activate audible signal
For doors that swing in direction of egress, signage must state
PUSH UNTIL ALARM SOUNDS
DOOR CAN BE OPENED IN 15 SECONDS

slides.title: Delayed Egress (3 of 3)
content:
For doors that swing in opposite direction of egress, signage must state
PULL UNTIL ALARM SOUNDS
DOOR CAN BE OPENED IN 15 SECONDS
For doors with a 30-second delay, signage will state 30 seconds instead of 15 seconds
Egress path must not pass through more than one egress locking system

slides.title: Self-Closing Doors (1 of 2)
content:
Be familiar with self-closing doors and latching doors activated by fire detection, water flow, and other alarm devices
Usually held open by magnetic devices that allow doors to close automatically upon activation
Hold-open devices are installed as part of convenience system in building
May be located in areas where occupants tend to block open doors that are required to self-close

slides.title: Security Devices (1 of 2)
content:
May be installed in buildings to prevent unauthorized entry
Include security bars, grilles, or doors over or behind exit doors
Slow access by emergency services personnel
Responsible for many fatalities

slides.title: Security Devices (2 of 2)
content:
Requirements include
Operation of locks on egress side of security bars must conform to requirements for exit doors
During periods of occupancy,
Horizontal sliding or vertical security grilles at main exit must be operable from inside, without use of key, special knowledge, or special effort
Grilles must remain secured in full-open position
Where two or more exits required, no more than half of exits can be equipped with security grilles

slides.title: Review Question 2
content: What is a disadvantage of security devices?

slides.title: Walls (2 of 5)
content:
Become familiar with building codes in effect when structure was built
Modifications to structure or changes in occupancy classification may require changes in fire-resistance rating requirements of egress elements
Inspector should look for penetrations in fire-resistance-rated walls 
Penetrations are often made during addition or modification of building services
If not sealed properly, penetration can compromise wall rating and allow smoke or fire to pass through

slides.title: Corridors (1 of 2)
content:
Used to provide a path of egress travel to an exit
Width requirement based on occupant load to be served
Unless code states otherwise, corridors that form part of a means of egress system must be at least 44 inches wide
According to the IBC®, the minimum width of corridors that serve spaces with an occupant load of less than 50 is required to be 36 inches

slides.title: Dead-End Corridor
content:
Has no outlet to means of egress
Length of a dead-end corridor is limited so occupants can realize there is no outlet and can change direction quickly
Code states length is limited to 20 feet, but there are exceptions
Maximum length is 50 feet in occupancies with automatic sprinkler systems
Construction and fire-resistance rating of ceiling system determines use of interstitial space between corridor ceiling and underside of structure above

slides.title: Stairways (2 of 6)
content:
Occupant load is total occupant load for all floors served by stairway
According to the IBC®, stairways serving an occupant load of 50 people or more must be at least 44 inches wide
Stairways serving occupant load of less than 50 people must be at least 36 inches wide

slides.title: Stairways (4 of 6)
content:
To provide protected path of travel and qualify as an exit, fire-resistance-rated construction must separate interior stairs from other parts of the building
This construction must lead directly to the exterior of the building or be extended to the exterior by conforming exit passageway
Construction that encloses exit must have at least one-hour fire-resistance rating when exit connects three stories or fewer
One-hour fire rating is required whether the stories connected are above or below story at which exit discharge begins

slides.title: Stairways (5 of 6)
content:
When exit connects four or more stories, separating construction must have fire-resistance rating of at least two hours
May be exceptions to requirements, so always consult locally adopted code
Self-closing and latching fire-resistance-rated exit door must protect any opening in exit stairways
Must be rated according to required fire-resistance rating of wall system
Only permissible openings in exit stairways are those that provide access to stairway from inside building and those that empty to exit discharge

slides.title: NOTE 2
content: Exit doors must have a 1-hour rating when used in a 1-hour-rated enclosure and at least a 1 1/2-hour rating when used in a 2-hour-rated enclosure.

slides.title: Fire Escape Stairways and Ladders (1 of 5)
content: Fire Escape Stairways and Ladders (1 of 5)

Provide a means of egress under emergency conditions, but should not be used for any other purpose
Lower level of fall protection safety is permitted in the construction of these stairways
Openings between rails and treads on fire escape stairways are not required to meet the same regulations as normally occupied spaces

slides.title: Fire Escape Stairways and Ladders (4 of 5)

To avoid trapping occupants, fire escape stairs must be exposed to smallest number of door or window openings possible
Each model code provides detailed guidelines for the protection of openings that may expose fire escape stairs
Openings within 10 feet of fire escape stairways must have 3/4 hour fire-resistance-rated opening protectives
If opening size meets certain criteria, windows may be used as access to fire escapes in existing buildings
Windows used for this purpose must open with a minimum of effort or open outward in manner that does not obstruct exit path

Occupant Loads
content: Learning Objective 3 — Explain how to calculate occupant loads.

slides.title: Occupant Loads (2 of 7)
content:
Occupant load for building or room is established during plan review process
In assembly occupancies, maximum occupant load must be visible, legible, and clearly posted near main exit
Inspectors must be able to verify occupant load of existing occupancies during field inspections

slides.title: Occupant Loads (4 of 7)
content:
If inspector suspects or observes a change in occupancy of space, the inspector should notify building code official
Change in occupancy classification should initiate building permit application and plan review
New certificate of occupancy is issued upon completion of required building modifications
Determining occupant load of structure requires more information than floor area and number of exits

slides.title: Occupant Loads (6 of 7)
content:
Occupant load factor – maximum floor area allowed per person based on function of space, stated in square feet
Gross square footage is entire square footage of space measured wall to wall with no deductions for furniture or movable items
Net square footage is gross square footage minus any space taken up by equipment, furniture, and corridors
To determine maximum occupant load, divide floor area by occupant load factor
Occupant Load = Floor Area / Occupant Load Factor

content: Learning Objective 5 — Describe how to determine occupancy egress requirements.

slides.title: Review Question 7

slides.title: Capacity (2 of 2)
content:
To determine exit capacity, use mathematical calculations based on established minimum exit widths outlined in model building codes
Capacities of each individual means of egress are added to determine total exit capacity 
Total exit capacity determines number of required exits
To determine required width of means of egress, inspector must apply an egress capacity factor expressed in inches per occupant
Most common egress capacity factors are 0.3 inches per occupant for stairways and 0.2 inches per occupant for ramps and level means of egress components such as doors and corridors

slides.title: Exit Capacity
content:
Measure each element in clear width at narrowest point
Element with smallest capacity determines total capacity for means of egress system

slides.title: Total Exit Capacity (1 of 3)
content:
To calculate, determine capacity of each exit and find sum of these numbers
Determining total exit capacity when exit is at grade level differs from procedure when an exit is not at grade level
Means of egress stairway is not sized to handle sum total of all occupants from all floors it serves
Occupant load of each floor considered individually
Occupants do not enter stairway or pass same point at same time
By the time occupants of third floor reach second floor, occupants of second floor should have exited building

slides.title: Total Exit Capacity (2 of 3)
content:
IBC® states that means of egress cannot narrow in direction of egress travel or beyond any point where two or more exits converge
Total of exit capacities cannot be less than sum of all capacities

slides.title: Total Exit Capacity (3 of 3)
content:
In multistory structures with emergency notification systems, personnel can instruct occupants to exit in order of proximity to fire floor
Three floors closest to fire floor exit first, then next three, and so on
Egress continues until structure is evacuated
In some jurisdictions, high-rise structures must have designated fire wardens on each floor to supervise and/or monitor evacuations

slides.title: Arrangement (1 of 2)
content:
During an emergency, multiple means of egress enable occupants to quickly locate an exit and evacuate the building
Inspectors should be able to
Determine location of multiple exits for new construction
Evaluate if maximum travel distance to existing exits is acceptable
If exits are insufficient, inspector should
Verify that building permit was issued for modifications
Recommend alternatives for meeting means of egress requirements

slides.title: Location of Exits (1 of 4)
content:
Multiple exits are often required and provide occupants with an alternative means of egress
The one-half diagonal rule is usually applied to determine placement of two or more exits
Rule states that exits must be separated by distance equal to or more than one half of longest diagonal distance of the building or area to be served
Distance must be measured in a straight line between the exits

slides.title: Location of Exits (2 of 4)
content:
Measurement can be made from following locations
Any point along width of the doorway
Closest riser if an exit access stairway is used
Start of ramp run if an exit access ramp is used

slides.title: Location of Exits (3 of 4)
content:
If space is equipped throughout with automatic sprinkler system, required separation distance may be reduced to one third of longest diagonal distance of building or area being served
If exit stairway or ramp is connected by a 1-hour fire-resistance-rated corridor, measurement follows shortest direct line of travel in corridor
In spaces that require more than two exits or exit access doors, at least two doors must meet minimum separation requirements

slides.title: Location of Exits (4 of 4)
content:
Other exits should be located where they are accessible to occupants if primary exits become blocked or unavailable
Regardless of configuration, each room, space, or building must have adequate exiting capabilities
Verify that designed exit plans follow fire and life safety code requirements, even if changes have been made to the occupancy

slides.title:
Maximum Travel Distance to an Exit 
(1 of 2)
content:
Maximum Travel Distance to an Exit 
(1 of 2)

Each model code establishes maximum allowable travel distance to nearest exit and limits length of dead-end corridors
Travel distance – total length of travel necessary to reach protection of exit
Measurement starts from most remote portion of occupancy, curves around corners or obstructions with 1-foot clearance, and ends at center of exit doorway or point at which exit begins

slides.title: Fire Apparatus Access Roads & Fire Lanes (2 of 2)
content: Fire Apparatus Access Roads & Fire Lanes (2 of 2)

Firefighters use fire apparatus access roads & fire lanes responding to & working on an emergency scene

Path from fire station to incident may include streets, highway, roadways, cartways, & fire lanes

Fire lanes provide means of access, parking area for apparatus, area for deployment of equipment
Courtesy of Ron Jeffers, Union City, NJ

slides.title: Requirements
content:
Fire apparatus access roads & fire lanes must be appropriately sized to allow emergency apparatus unimpeded passage to & around a facility
Most model fire codes contain minimum requirements for

slides.title: Width
content:
Width requirements allow a vehicle to pass parked apparatus deployed for fire fighting operations

Fire lanes & fire apparatus access roads must be at least 20 feet wide, exclusive of shoulders

If hydrant is located on fire lane or access road, width of lane must be at least 26 ft. wide in front of hydrant for a minimum of 10 ft. in either direction of hydrant

These measurements exclude parking widths

slides.title: Angles of Approach & Departure
content:
The municipality must establish the maximum angle of approach & departure based on fire department apparatus

Generally, an angle not exceeding 8 degrees allows apparatus to drive on or off a roadway without the tailboard or front bumper striking the ground

slides.title: Road Markings & Signs
content:
Local jurisdiction generally establishes marking requirements for fire lanes & fire apparatus access roads

Inspectors may 
Make recommendations about the location of road signs 
Offer guidance on parking restrictions based on the need for site access

Fire lane & access road markings & signs indicate 
Areas designed to support weight of apparatus to emergency responders & provide most effective access 
Areas that must remain clear at all times to the public

slides.title: Painted Curbs
content:
Curbs are generally painted red or red with white lettering

In some locations, large, painted letters on the road surface designate fire lanes

slides.title: Posted Signs
content:
Must conform to the local or state design for information signs

Normally have a reflective white background with the words "NO PARKING — FIRE LANE" or "NO STOPPING — FIRE LANE" in red lettering

slides.title: NOTE1
content:
In climates where seasonal snow is common, exclusive use of curb markings is not effective. 

Drivers may disobey fire lane regulations because snow is blocking or obscuring curb markings. 

The use of elevated signs can avoid violations often overturned in court for failure to give notice.

slides.title: Considerations for Alternative Construction
content:
AHJ should post signs at entry & exit points of fire lanes or access roads constructed with subsurface support materials
To keep apparatus on paved or supported surface, responders need to see edge of roadway

Apparatus that leaves access road or lane can get stuck in adjacent soil or even overturn

Reflective markings or other indicators placed along edge of subsurface construction indicate area designed to support weight of an apparatus

Inspector should verify that markings are in correct location & unobscured by vegetation
