content:
Unless otherwise indicated by the AHJ, a single gate provided across a fire apparatus access road must be at least 20 ft. (6 096 mm) wide.

The gate must be at least 12 ft. (3 658 mm) wide when the access road consists of a divided roadway.

slides.title: Impediments to Exterior Access & Delayed Response
content: Impediments to Exterior Access & Delayed Response

slides.title: Roadway Maintenance
content:
Road maintenance & repairs are often delayed until a roadway becomes impassable due to funding

Prior to point where passenger vehicles cannot make passage, access for emergency vehicles will be impaired

Notify emergency services of any problem with an access roadway

Even if inspectors cannot require that condition be corrected, inform those responsible about associated hazards

slides.title: Addressing Illegal Parking
content:
Work with local law enforcement agencies & property owners to address illegal parking issues

Ensure that unobstructed emergency access is available at all times
Courtesy of Ron Jeffers, Union City, NJ

slides.title: Overhead Obstructions
content:
Look for overhead obstructions

Blocking apparatus access

Obstructing aerial device operations

Hindering use of ground ladders

May also impede 13-ft., 6-in. (4 115 mm) minimum unobstructed height requirement above fire lanes or fire apparatus access roads

slides.title: Examples of Overhead Obstructions
content:
Electrical lines or utility poles
Trees, vines, other vegetation
Parking lot lights or street-lights
Building canopies, marquees, overhangs
Flagpoles
Signs
Satellite dishes
Overhead pipes in industrial complexes & facilities

slides.title:
Overhead Obstructions & Plan Review 
(1 of 2)
content:
Proper application of locally adopted codes during plan review, construction, & initial inspection process should limit number of overhead obstructions

Eliminating overhead obstructions during plan review is most cost-effective option, followed by early observation during initial construction

Mitigating obstructions can be expensive once construction is complete

slides.title:
Overhead Obstructions & Plan Review 
(2 of 2)
content:
Document any overhead obstructions observed during annual inspections so fire department can be notified & corrections can be made

If new overhead obstructions indicate construction without a permit, building official must be notified, a permit obtained, & subsequent reviews & inspections conducted

slides.title: Inspector Actions
content:
Evaluate/mitigate all landscape situations that are or have potential to be exterior barriers to emergency access

Note changes in landscape design that may require further evaluation

slides.title: Topographic Features
content:
Features can be exterior barriers to emergency access 
Railroad tracks

Drainage ditches, streams, rivers, canals, ponds, or lakes

Steep slopes, cliffs, or variations in topographical grades

Unstable terrain 

Narrow alleys or passageways between structures

Retaining walls
Courtesy of Ron Jeffers, Union City, NJ

slides.title: Climatic Conditions
content:
Climatic conditions can obstruct or prevent emergency access to buildings & facilities

Responsibility for mitigating weather-related barriers may belong to owner/occupant or AHJ

AHJ's street department or private contractor may be responsible for snow removal

On private property, owner/occupant must keep free of snow & ice all exterior exit doors, pathways, & areas of refuge

slides.title: Heavy Rain
content:
Periods of heavy rain can overwhelm systems designed to control surface runoff

Excess water on fire lanes & access roads, parking lots, & detention ponds can create access problems for emergency responders

slides.title: Drought Conditions
content:
Drought conditions also create exterior barriers obstructing site access

Travel on dirt & loose gravel roadways in extremely dry conditions can be hazardous

Dust produced by wind conditions or traffic on unpaved fire apparatus access roads may produce enough dust to limit or obstruct visibility of buildings, vehicles, or people

Increase risk of grass fires around facilities

Building owners/occupants may be required to clear all dead or dry vegetation away from structures & fences near fire lanes & access roads

slides.title: Review Question 3
content: What topographic features could be exterior barriers to emergency access?

slides.title: Force Protection Systems
content:
Designed to secure buildings against intrusion & hostile action

Robust design keeps vehicles from breaching location perimeter at high speed

Deploy quickly, placing formidable barrier between vehicle & building

Some can be opened or moved to allow vehicle passage, but become effectively impenetrable when deployed

slides.title: Bollards
content:
Vertical posts widely used for safety & security

Normally made of steel & may extend 3 to 4 ft. (0.9 m to 1.2 m) in height

Stationary bollards can provide pedestrian or traffic control

Other types block vehicles by rising from the ground when activated

slides.title: Wedge or Plate Barriers
content:
Consist of heavy gauge steel plates, hinged at trailing edge, pop up from ground when deployed

Because plate functions as part of the driving surface, it escapes notice

When deployed, mechanical or hydraulic actuators raise leading edge of steel plate to a height of 3 to 4 ft. (0.9 to 1.2 m), creating a formidable barrier

slides.title: NOTE3
content: As the size of bollard systems may vary, the measurements provided above are estimates, inspectors should consult the adopted codes & policies of their AHJ for specific measurement requirements.

slides.title: Disarming
content:
Most systems can be disarmed by a remote arming/disarming control or a key access system

If the system does not perform properly, it should be disabled

Alternative security measures must be put in place until the system can be restored to normal operation

slides.title: Interior Access Barriers
content:
Inspectors

Need to ensure that alternative means of entry are provided & maintained

Should also inform the fire department of interior barriers they discover

Firefighters normally access a building through doors & windows

If local ordinances require lock boxes containing keys to the facility or structure, these boxes may be located near the entry doors

Security fences & gates may also have lock boxes located near an entry point

slides.title: Inspector Actions Regarding Access Issues
content:
Inspectors must 
Verify proper location of key boxes

Ensure boxes contain the minimum number of required keys or access cards

Confirm the location, key, & access information has been provided to other agencies in accordance with locally adopted regulations

Some structures with on-site, 24-hour security may not be required to have a lock box

AHJ will evaluate the need for a key box in those locations

slides.title: Utilizing Building Features for Access
content:
Responders may utilize building features, such as fire escapes, roof access doors, when doors & windows fail to provide full access to a building

Remember that first responders gain access through these openings while wearing turnout gear & SCBA

When examining interior access features, consider feature’s structural condition, location, operation

slides.title: Construction Prior to Code
content:
Buildings constructed prior to building code adoption or under a previously adopted code may have insufficient interior access based on current standards

Unless code specifically allows for retroactive enforcement, these preexisting, nonconforming conditions will always exist

slides.title: Special Issues with Windowless Buildings & Underground Buildings
content: Special Issues with Windowless Buildings & Underground Buildings

slides.title: Internal Building Security Systems
content:
Facilities are often segregated based on the need for security

One part of a building may be open to public

Other areas are employees only

Building segregation may be accomplished through traditional locking mechanisms or more complex access systems such as biometric scanning

Security systems may be important to the function of a building, but they should not create life-threatening conditions for its occupants

slides.title: Inspector Expectations During Inspection
content:
Visualize how to exit a space in an emergency 
Determine if multiple means of egress are required
Watch for systems installed without proper permitting
Evaluate measures in place to allow emerg. responders quick & efficient access
Report their findings to the appropriate parties
Deficiencies impeding emergency egress must be corrected immediately or system must be disabled until corrections are made

slides.title: Security Grilles on Doors & Windows
content:
Some owners, tenants install security devices over or behind windows & doors
Help prevent vandalism & robberies
Although not designed to delay or impede access of emergency responders, they often do

Typically installed over windows & stationary

Gates
Installed over doors & sometimes over windows, hinged at one side to allow access
Locking mechanism for windows, typically on inside of gate, cannot be accessed from exterior

slides.title: Hazardous Conditions Involving Equipment (1 of 2)
content:
Building equipment is a common cause of building fires

Equipment requires ongoing maintenance and upkeep

Improper maintenance creates hazardous conditions such as 
Mechanical wear
Buildup of heat
Degradation of protective coatings

slides.title: Hazardous Conditions Involving Equipment (2 of 2)
content:
Equipment user greatly impacts equipment safety
While the equipment may have been manufactured and supplied with safety devices, the end user may disable  these devices of ignorance to make a job easier
Removal or modification of any equipment's safety features can and often will create a hazardous condition

slides.title: Cooking Equipment
content:
Cooking is leading cause of non-residential fires
Fires ignite easily, spread rapidly in presence of high heat and fuel sources, such as combustible liquids and fine granular materials
Evaluate condition of cooking environment as well as equipment used

slides.title: Hood and Ventilation Systems
content: Inspections of commercial cooking establishments are focused on the ventilation hood, exhaust, and fire protection systems installed above the cooking area

slides.title: Hazard Reduction Requirements of Solid Fuel Cooking Equipment
content: Hazard Reduction Requirements of Solid Fuel Cooking Equipment

slides.title: Verify During Inspections (1 of 3)
content:
Cooking appliances protected by system have not been changed or replaced 
 If wrong appliances are in place, systems may not be adequate for hazard
Instruction sign for manual system operation is present, and employees have been trained to perform manual operations
Suppression system has been maintained per standards
Suppression nozzles are properly oriented toward hazard to be protected
Suppression system parts are properly positioned and connected

slides.title: Verify During Inspections (2 of 3)
content:
Manual actuators are free of obstructions
Tamper indicators and seals are intact
System maintenance tag or certificate are properly placed
Qualified technician has inspected suppression system within code-specified time parameters
Pressure gauges read within their operable ranges

slides.title: Review Question 1
content: What type of fire suppression is most effective for fires involving vegetable oils?

slides.title: Industrial Furnaces and Ovens
content:
Found in industrial applications that require melting, tempering, or drying of materials or products
Explosions and fires in fuel-fired and electric-heat-utilization equipment constitute a potential loss of 
Life
Loss
Production
Most failures can be traced to 
Inadequately trained operators
Lack of proper maintenance
Improper application of equipment

slides.title: Interlock Systems
content:
Critical to interlock the entire system
In the event of a malfunction
Safety interlocks shut down equipment
Remaining fuel is removed 
Once a safety feature or device has deactivated system, operator must manually intervene to reestablish normal operation
Testing of interlock feature should be verified and specifically noted as part of scheduled inspection procedure

slides.title: NOTE1
content:
During inspections, the inspector must verify that inspection, testing, and maintenance programs meet or exceed the minimum code requirements. 
Often, owners/tenants only inspect equipment to prepare for a scheduled code inspection. To minimize costs, they may not perform required inspection, testing, and maintenance at other required times.

slides.title: Review Question 2
content: Name and describe the four classifications for industrial ovens.

slides.title: Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) Equipment
content: Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) Equipment

Recognize types and operating conditions of various heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems
Can be used to temper (heat/cool) air, filter and/or clean air, or modify moisture level of air in a compartment
Major components within an HVAC system

slides.title: NOTE2
content: The HVAC information in this section is generic. An inspector needs to consult the adopted codes for jurisdiction-specific information. Additional requirements for HVAC systems are contained in the International Building Code® (IBC®), International Fire Code® (IFC®), and several NFPA standards.

slides.title: Inspecting HVAC System/Mechanical Equipment Rooms
content:
Qualified personnel inspect and maintain HVAC system
Unit clearances are properly maintained
Operating instructions are available for use on-site
Only authorized personnel should have access
Type and size of equipment will determine fire separation requirements
Fire-resistive construction and appropriate protective openings should be used to meet requirements
Be vigilant for combustible storage inside 
Consult appropriate codes for housekeeping requirements within mechanical and electrical rooms

slides.title: Furnaces
content:
Most common type of central heating appliance
Most use forced-air principles to move air, some gravity furnaces remain in use
Gravity furnaces, located in basements of buildings, circulate air without fans
As heated air rises through building, colder air settles and enters return-air ducts to become makeup air for furnace

slides.title: Forced-Air Furnaces
content:
Forced-air furnaces rely on a fan to move heated air through building
Because they can become hot enough to ignite adjacent, unprotected woodwork, plenums and ductwork in these units require appropriate clearances and insulation
Automatic controls turn off furnace when temperature within ductwork or plenum reaches a set level

slides.title: Floor Furnace
content: Most common in single-family dwellings built pre-1960, some commercial occupancies still use them

Designed and approved for installation underneath combustible floors
Require temperature-limit controls and proper clearances from combustibles
Must have safety controls that shut off fuel source if pilot light goes out
Properly vented so carbon monoxide (CO) does not accumulate

slides.title: Wall Furnace Units
content:
Self-contained heating units are installed within or on a wall
Some wall furnaces are indirect-fired heaters with propane or gas heating units
Other units are electric or heated by fuel oil
Gas and oil heaters may vent directly to the exterior or be equipped with an indirect vent or chimney

slides.title: Boilers
content:
A pressure vessel that can generate steam to power machinery and provide heat required by industrial processes
HVAC applications, boilers can provide both steam heat and hot water

Heat is transferred to compartment through radiators
Boilers are more prevalent in older structures
More efficient boiler-based heating systems are available 
Large boilers also serve multiple buildings

slides.title: Boiler Design
content:
American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel Codes (BPVC) governs boiler design, construction, and operation
When building boilers, manufacturers must strictly adhere to all applicable codes
All boilers should meet fire and explosion prevention requirements
Entire boiler system should include interlocks, detectors, alarms, and sensors to turn off fuel sources when a problem occurs

slides.title: Two Common Types of Steam-Generating Boilers (1 of 2)
content: Two Common Types of Steam-Generating Boilers (1 of 2)

slides.title: Two Common Types of Steam-Generating Boilers (2 of 2)
content: Two Common Types of Steam-Generating Boilers (2 of 2)
Combustion process in a boiler results from a continual introduction of fuel and air in a flammable mixture

slides.title: Hazardous Conditions Associated with Boiler Systems
content: Hazardous Conditions Associated with Boiler Systems

Include size, age, level of maintenance
Operating at elevated pressures, vessel failure can be catastrophic and send pieces of the boiler material airborne over a long distance at a high rate of speed
Others directly relate to system’s fuel type
In natural gas system, gas buildup can ignite during mechanical failure
Gas leaks in natural gas-fired boilers can cause a buildup of fuel-rich mixtures if a burner fails
Deterioration or modification of unit exhaust systems may cause a dangerous buildup of CO in the structure

slides.title: NOTE3
content: As with many other systems, if an inspector observes signs of deterioration or indications that modifications have been made to a boiler system, additional investigation is required.

slides.title: Unit Heaters
content:
Self-contained heating devices 
Thermostatically controlled
Fueled by oil, gas, electricity, steam, hot water
Mounted on floor or suspended from a wall or ceiling

slides.title: Unit Heaters Code and Testing
content:
For specific information, consult building code, NFPA 1, IFC®
Model fire codes also regulate type and amount of fuel used to operate unit heaters
All heating appliances must be listed by an accredited testing agency and meet safety and design requirements for specific applications
Field modifications can compromise and/or void a heater's listing
If modification poses significant life safety hazard, use of unit should be discontinued immediately

slides.title: NOTE4
content: The heating element and fan are enclosed in a common operating unit. Inspectors should verify that unit heaters are installed with appropriate clearances from combustibles. An inspector should also confirm proper storage and handling of the fuel source.

slides.title: Room Heaters
content:
Appliances designed for installation in space being heated
Use circulation of radiant heat as heating medium
Manual- or thermostat-controlled drafts
Solid-fuel room heaters — Free-standing appliances that burn coal or wood and vent to building exterior
Include wood/coal stoves, electric/gas logs, electric baseboard heaters, open-front heaters

slides.title: Avoiding Combustible/Toxic Gas Accumulation
content:
Confirm room heating equipment is vented in accordance with manufacturer instructions
Verify
Storage of solid fuels is a safe distance from stoves
Provisions are made for the safe storage and removal of ashes and cinders
Chimneys and flues are kept clear of excessive creosote
Combustibles are stored a safe distance from heating units
All heating appliances are industry-approved and labeled accordingly
Proper clearances are maintained

slides.title: Verify for Portable Heating Equipment
content:
Well maintained and in safe working condition
Safety switches turn off heating element if unit tips over
Do not block an egress route
Located a safe distance from flammable/combustible materials
Electric heaters plug directly into electrical receptacle that is circuit listed/approved to carry required current
Liquid-fueled heaters use only approved fuel— fueling is done according to manufacturer specifications
Fuel for kerosene heaters is stored outside structure and refilled outside 
Portable natural gas or propane heaters are not used in normally occupied structures due to potential fuel leaks

slides.title: NOTE5
content: Portable heaters or wood-burning fireplaces located near awnings or other combustible materials can create an exposure hazard through radiant heat or burning embers.

content: Requirements for Installation of CO Detection

slides.title: Air Conditioning Systems
content:
Uses a refrigeration cycle
Working principle of an air conditioner is to
Remove hot air from a given space 
Evaporate and absorb the heat 
Send cool air back into the space

slides.title: Ventilation Systems
content:
Move and distribute air mechanically
Do not heat or cool air
Air quality and characteristics remain unchanged
Primary fire safety concern is potential for transmission of fire, smoke, and products of combustion

slides.title: NOTE6
content: An inspector must recognize the difference between an air conditioning system and a ventilation system.

content:
Caused by 
Age
Improper installation
Improper maintenance 
If not replaced, worn equipment creates hazardous conditions
Dust/water/foreign materials can be drawn into motor causing
Short circuit
Increased load
Jammed armature that overheats
Arcing caused by loose or worn electrical connections can also ignite combustibles

slides.title: Improper Use of Electrical Equipment
content:
Improper use of electrical equipment, such as overloading a circuit, also creates hazardous conditions
As a circuit is overloaded, resistance increases, resulting in exponential growth of heat
Nearby combustibles exposed to the heat may ignite

content:

Motors may need to be non-sparking and intrinsically safe
Equipment used in areas that may contain explosive concentrations of dusts or vapors must
Comply with NFPA 70®
Be listed for both environment and use

slides.title: NOTE7
content: The Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) can recall even properly installed equipment if the equipment becomes obsolete, if it is unrepairable, or if a manufacturing defect is identified.

slides.title: Photovoltaic Power Systems
content:
Provide electrical power to residential and commercial buildings
During peak times, may also send electricity into public utilities grid
To produce higher amounts of energy, panels can be linked in a solar array

slides.title: Electrocution
content: At a current of 10 amps, death is likely.

slides.title: Electrocution Hazard
content:
A 39-inch (991 mm) x 65-inch (1 651 mm) solar panel can produce 320 watts of DC electricity. At 12 volts, the panel would be producing more than 26 amps of current. 

OSHA defines the freezing current “let go” range as 9-30 milliamperes. Beyond this point, a person does not have the ability to let go or break contact without intervention. Possible consequences include severe burns and cardiac arrest.

slides.title: System Labeling
content:
Labeling on electrical panel, utility meter, other electrical disconnect alerts occupants and responders that alternative energy generation is present
Verify that system labeling is legible and properly positioned

slides.title: Use, Storage, and Handling of Flammable and Combustible Liquids
content: Use, Storage, and Handling of Flammable and Combustible Liquids

Liquids are classified as either flammable or combustible based on flashpoint and boiling point temperatures
Flammable and combustible liquids are often handled and stored improperly due to ignorance or complacency
Unsafe practices include
Improperly dispensing, mixing, or transferring flammable and combustible liquids
Using flammable liquids for cleaning
Storing flammable or combustible liquids in unapproved containers or locations 
Using a flammable liquid to ignite a solid fuel

slides.title: Storage Guidelines
content:
NFPA, ICC®, OSHA develop standards and regulations for safe storage and use of flammable and combustible liquids
Provide specific requirements for storage options, such as safety cans, flammable storage cabinets, and fire areas

slides.title: Guidelines for Safe Storage and Handling
content: Guidelines for Safe Storage and Handling

slides.title: Grounding and Bonding
content: Appropriate electrical bonding and grounding procedures must always be followed

slides.title: Dispensing and Handling Procedures
content:
Spills, releases, or leaks frequently occur while transferring liquids from one container to another
Dispensing liquids of any amount can be hazardous, but loading and unloading procedures at bulk-handling operations are particularly dangerous

slides.title: Requirements for Dispensing and Handling
content:
Loading and unloading stations for Classes IA through IC liquids no closer than 25 feet (7 620 mm) from storage tanks, property lines, or adjacent buildings
Loading and unloading stations for Class II and Classes IIIA and IIIB liquids no closer than 15 feet (4 572 mm) from storage tanks, property lines, or adjacent buildings
Loading and unloading stations constructed on level ground
Curbs, drains, natural ground slope, or other methods of fluid containment to keep spills in the containment area
Adequate ventilation (natural or mechanical) in loading and unloading stations

slides.title: Static Discharge
content:
Static electricity is a potential ignition source. Dry air and low humidity increase the buildup of static electric charge.

Flowing liquid or gas contaminated with metallic oxides, scale or liquid particles may develop a static electrical charge. If an electrically charged gas comes into contact with an ungrounded conductive material, the charge transfers to that body. To prevent static discharge, bond the two receptacles with a metal chain or cord and ground them.

slides.title: Safe Procedures for Handling Flammable or Combustible Liquid
content: Safe Procedures for Handling Flammable or Combustible Liquid

slides.title: Storing and Labeling Loading Hoses
content:
All cylinders on loading stations must be clearly labeled with name of gas being used 
Do not rely solely on color coding
Loading hose furnished by receiver 
Must be properly maintained
Replaced at least every 5 years
When not in use, hoses must be stored away from direct sunlight
Bonding is generally not required if hose has vapor-tight connections

slides.title: Storage Guidelines for Cylinders
content:
Cover cylinder valves with safety caps when cylinders are not in use to protect valves and male threads
Anchor cylinders to a wall or other secure object with chains around the tanks so they cannot fall over
Nest bulk cylinders (instead of anchoring and chaining them)
Store and/or use cylinders at ground (grade) level in areas with adequate ventilation to prevent accumulation of flammable gas vapors that are clean and free of combustibles

slides.title: Handling Procedures
content:
To evaluate handling procedures for these cylinders, verify that workers are 
Properly trained
Under competent supervision
Company’s administrative and engineering control policies/guidelines also assist inspectors in identifying unsafe behaviors

slides.title: Potential for Explosion
content:
Given correct mixture of oxygen and ignition source, sufficient quantity of combustible dust suspended in air can fuel fire, deflagration, or explosion
Many processes produce potential for dust explosion, but five elements must be present for dust explosion

slides.title: Dust Explosion Series
content:
First explosion
Not usually as severe as subsequent explosions
Stirs dust settled on ledges, walls, equipment, or in areas of low travel
Second explosion
Generally results in larger and stronger explosions
Can be severe enough to destroy an entire facility

slides.title: NOTE9
content: As part of the Combustible Dust Document Consolidation Plan, NFPA 654 is being combined into NFPA 660, Standard for Combustible Dusts.

slides.title: Dust Controls
content:
Passive dust controls include providing enclosures for conveyor belts and reducing speeds at which materials move through on conveyor belts or through chutes
Active dust controls (air material separators) —usually mechanical dust-collection systems capable of collecting 99.5 percent of dust and storing it in bins outside the facility

slides.title: Requirements and Safety Measures for Dust Collection and Reduction (1 of 2)
content: Requirements and Safety Measures for Dust Collection and Reduction (1 of 2)

Cleaning programs must be performed daily or as needed
Continually remove dust by manual sweeping, vacuuming, or other means and placed in appropriate storage bins or containers

slides.title: Pallet Storage
content:
Hazardous conditions include flammability and rapid spread
Multiple stacked pallets and pallet racks can obstruct sprinklers, making a fire difficult to reach, wet, and control
Encapsulated storage creates additional fire hazards
Because plastic encapsulation covers the top, water from fire suppression system cannot penetrate surface

slides.title: Pallet Stacking and Fuel Load
content:
Materials stacked 3 to 4 feet (1 m to 1.2 m) high on each pallet, pallets may be stacked up to 30 feet (10 m) in height
Stacking can prevent sprinkler water from reaching bottom layers
Air space between top and bottom layers of pallets (approximately 4 inches [100 mm]) provides a natural path for fire spread
Packing and wrapping materials add to fuel load and may be regulated for type and amount used
Plastic pallets change commodity class if sprinkler system is not designed for Group A plastics

slides.title: Rack Storage Suppression Requirements
content:
Warehouses and retail outlets with rack storage may have sprinklers located within racks themselves
NFPA 13 contains specific requirements for fire suppression systems in rack storage

slides.title: Solid Piled Storage
content:
Materials are stacked directly on top of one another
Gives a fire the least chance to develop
Limits air space between fuel units
Used for a variety of commodities
Storage of certain commodities in solid piles or on pallets at a specific height above finished floor is considered high-piled combustible storage and must meet locally adopted fire code requirements

content:

May require changes in storage systems, in-rack sprinkler arrangements, width of access aisles

slides.title: Responsibility and Review
content: Store owners are responsible for design, installation, and maintenance of fire protection systems

slides.title: Lumberyards
content:
Primary hazard is high fuel load created by large quantities of combustible materials stored on-site
Fires can quickly overwhelm local fire suppression resources
Large, undivided stacks of lumber or other materials can obstruct access, increase fire spread, cause early collapse
Congested storage conditions can delay fire detection
Other conditions include inadequate fire protection and Class A, B combinations

content:
Burning is not the only method of waste disposal used

content:
Most waste is sent to landfills, burning is a also an effective means
Reduces bulk of waste by as much as 95 percent
Used to destroying medical, chemical, and biological wastes that can create hazardous conditions 
Many areas allow residents to burn domestic garbage if they 
Remove metals and glass
Follow environmental controls
Local authorities may require burn permit

Fuel-fired incinerators preheat for 30 minutes before use

Feed door closes fully after loading for entire cycle
Waste material ash compartment is cleaned regularly
Waste disposal follows approved guidelines

Facility's emergency response plan placed in appropriate location for use during an incident

slides.title: Flammable Compressed Gas Installation
content:
Comply with general provisions for compressed gas systems & material-specific provisions for flammable gases

Categorized in two ways 
Physical state in containers under certain temperatures & pressures
Range of boiling 

Three groups of flammable gases are
Liquefied compressed gases
Nonliquefied compressed gases
Dissolved gases

slides.title: Liquefied Compressed Gases
content: Become liquids at ordinary temperatures & pressures from 25 to 600 psig

Elements or compounds with boiling points relatively near atmospheric temperatures ranging from −130°F to 30°F (-90°C to -1°C)

Become solid at the low temperatures used for cryogenic fluid

Since liquefied gases expand as ambient temperatures rise, container-filling limits account for that potential expansion

Include anhydrous ammonia, propane, carbon dioxide

slides.title: Organic Peroxides, Solids or Liquids (1 of 2)
content: Organic Peroxides, Solids or Liquids (1 of 2)

Only exist as solids or liquids

Degree of hazard depends on classification

Release energy as heat & introduce energy into chemical reactions so more useful compounds can be created

As they react, all organic peroxides may present
Sensitivity to heat
Heat release upon decomposition
Formation of free radicals upon decomposition
Introduction of contaminant that initiates uncontrolled reaction
Decomposition products that can be flammable or toxic

slides.title: Organic Peroxides, Solids or Liquids (2 of 2)
content: Organic Peroxides, Solids or Liquids (2 of 2)

Have limited shelf life, usually one year or less
Shortened if temperature limits not maintained
Disposal should comply with manufacturer recommendation
Expired organic peroxides can become unstable

Model fire codes divide organic peroxides into four classes based on  decomposition rate, reactivity hazard, burning rate

Organic peroxides with lowest numerical ratings present greatest overall hazards

Peroxides present fire & reactivity hazards

slides.title: Oxidizers, Solids or Liquids
content:
Yields oxygen or other chemical compounds that promote or initiate combustion

Accelerate burn rate

Fire code-compliant storage & use of oxidizers separate them from incompatible hazardous materials

Produce very flammable or explosive mixtures when combined with combustible organic materials

slides.title: Contact Reactions
content: If oxidizers come into contact with petroleum-based materials, an immediate & violent reaction will occur.

NFPA 1, Fire Code, & IFC® prohibit storage or use of any pyrophoric material in an unsprinklered building

NFPA 55 & NFPA 318 contain additional requirements for pyrophoric gases

Model fire codes also reference ANSI/CGA G-13, Storage & Handling of Silane & Silane Mixtures, published by CGA

slides.title: NFPA Hazard Diamond Organization
content:
Top three quadrants represent three hazard categories & are color-coded as 
Health — blue (left quadrant) 
Flammability — red (top quadrant) 
Instability — yellow (right quadrant)

Hazard ratings are based on a scale from 0 to 4
0 represents minimal presence of hazardous material, the least severe hazard
4 represents highest presence/most severe hazard

Rating numbers 
Appear in black when backgrounds are blue, red, yellow
May be color-coded

slides.title: Special Hazard Symbols
content:

No specified background color, white is most commonly used

Only 3 special hazard symbols authorized by NFPA
W — Unusual reactivity with water
OX — Oxidizer
SA — Simple asphyxiant

Inspectors may see other symbols in white quadrant on old placards, including trefoil radiation symbol

If more than one special hazard, multiple symbols may appear

slides.title: NFPA 704 Limitations
content:
NFPA 704 markings on a building do not identify the presence of exact location of specific chemicals. 

Examine container markings, employee information, company records, or preincident surveys to positively identify the materials. 

The NFPA 704 marking system is only as good as the system maintenance. 

Ensure the marking system is current & accurate.

slides.title: Shop-Fabricated Aboveground Storage Tanks
content:

content:
UL 142 requires permanent nameplate on any shop-fabricated AST storing flammable or combustible liquids

Nameplate is important to fire officials because it provides 
Application for which tank is designed

Special installation requirements

Standard to which tank is constructed

Required flow rate for tanks equipped with emergency vents

slides.title: Vent Openings
content:
ASTs are constructed with normal vent & emergency vent
Vents protect tank from excessive vacuum or positive pressure
Normal vent required for all underground storage tanks
Protects tank from collapse or overpressurization
All photos courtesy of Austin (TX) Fire Department

slides.title: NOTE55
content: An emergency vent is not required for underground storage tanks because they have no fire risk.

slides.title: Field-Erected Aboveground Storage Tanks
content:
Fabricated from plate carbon steel & stainless steel

Steel sheets used to erect structurally safe tank on-site

Model codes do not limit diameter or height of field-erected ASTs

Often designed to store millions of gallons of flammable & combustible liquids

slides.title: Field-Erected Aboveground Storage Tank  Standards
content:
Conform to American Petroleum Institute (API) standards
Operate at atmospheric pressure to meet API 650
Tanks operating at pressure between 2-15 psig or store liquids at temperatures above 200°F (93°C) are classified as low-pressure, field-erected ASTs
Constructed in compliance with API 620

API Standard 653 requires major modifications or repairs to field-erected ASTs be noted on repair nameplate permanently affixed to tank

Review manufacturer’s nameplate affixed to storage tank to determine construction standard for tank's design

slides.title: Underground Storage Tank Construction
content:
Constructed of carbon steel or fiberglass reinforced plastic
Carbon steel USTs are constructed to UL 58
Fiberglass-reinforced USTs are constructed to ANSI/CAN/UL/ULC 1316 

Underground installation of aboveground tank violates model fire codes

Listed USTs are designed to store
Gasoline
Diesel
Bio-Fuels
Alcohol-blended fuels

slides.title: UST Openings
content:
UST openings located on top of tank & prohibited below tank’s liquid level

Additional to normal vents, USTs require openings to fill tank with liquid & accommodate pumps to supply dispensers

Model fire codes require electronic monitoring of tank’s liquid level for product reconciliation & to prevent overfill

slides.title: Types of Fire Protection
content:
NFPA 400 & IFC® require fire protection for many hazardous materials classes

Types of fire protection include fire-resistant enclosures & fire-resistive construction

Fire-resistant enclosures include gas cabinets & hazardous materials storage cabinets

Fire-resistive construction separates rooms/areas for hazardous material use or storage from other areas of a building

Both codes require an automatic sprinkler system protect the building or area

slides.title: Fire Protection Codes
content:
Goal is to protect the stored material from fire & limit risk of involvement

Refer to appropriate NFPA standard for a given class of hazardous materials to determine if sprinkler discharge density & design area are correct for stored materials

slides.title: Spill Control & Secondary Containment
content:
Hazardous occupancies storing hazardous liquids or solids require spill control or secondary containment
Accidental spill must be contained & kept within occupancy
Secondary containment prescribed when outdoor MAQ is exceeded
Not required for compressed or liquefied compressed gases

Using floor surface of hazardous occupancy satisfies requirements for spill control if container's volume is
Less than 55 gallons (220 L) of liquids 
Less than 550 pounds (275 kg) of solids

slides.title: Model Fire Code Requirement for Secondary Containment
content: Model Fire Code Requirement for Secondary Containment

Liquids — When container volume is greater than 55 gals. (208 L) or aggregate volume of multiple vessels or containers is greater than 1,000 gals. (3 785 L)

Solids — When individual container weight is greater than 550 pounds (250 kg) or aggregate weight of hazardous materials is more than 10,000 pounds (4 540 kg)
All photos courtesy of Austin (TX) Fire Department

slides.title: Mechanical Ventilation Systems
content:
High-Hazard occupancies must have mechanical ventilation systems

Provide adequate air movement to exhaust fumes, vapors, or gases created by leaks in a container, piping, valve, or component

Not required for flammable solids

Hazardous exhaust systems are designed & constructed in accordance with

International Mechanical Code® (IMC®) 

NFPA 91, Standard for Exhaust Systems for Air Conveying of Vapors, Gases, Mists, & Particulate Solids

slides.title: Hazardous Mechanical Exhaust Systems & Vent Flow Rate
content: Hazardous Mechanical Exhaust Systems & Vent Flow Rate

slides.title: Automatic Sprinkler Protection
content:
Group H occupancies require automatic sprinkler protection

Sprinkler protection varies according to occupancy classification & locally adopted codes
Automatic sprinkler protection may be required throughout a building or only within hazardous occupancy
Model fire codes require system comply with NFPA 13

NFPA 13 requires specialized automatic sprinkler designs be installed for certain classes of physical hazard materials
Flammable & combustible liquids
Compressed gases
Solid & liquid oxidizers & organic peroxides

slides.title: NFPA 30 Compliance
content:
NFPA 30 provides specific guidance for design of automatic sprinkler systems for combustible & flammable liquids

Compliance for these sprinkler systems is based on class of liquid, container type, & storage configuration

slides.title: Electrical Installations
content:
Because electricity is a readily available ignition source in high-hazard occupancies, additional care must be taken to limit fire potential

NFPA 70®, National Electrical Code® (NEC®), provides additional provisions for high hazard occupancies

NEC® divides requirements for electrical installations into classes & divisions

Inspectors should be aware of need for special equipment, connections, & provisions in inspection area 

Inspectors should be vigilant when it appears modifications have been made

Learning Objective 1 — Describe water supply systems.

slides.title: Private Water Supply Systems
content:
Provide water under contract to customers in a municipality, a multi-municipal region, or a single property
Some specifically service an industrial facility or complex
Others systems may supply water to residential subdivisions
Facility owner/occupant is typically responsible for
Inspection
Testing
Maintenance
Inspector determines system has been properly tested, inspected, maintained

slides.title: Processing and Receiving
content:
Water must be processed to remove impurities that can be harmful to humans, animals, and plants
Water purveyors are owners or operators of potable water systems
Most operate water treatment plants 
Those using ocean water operate desalination plants and treatment plants
Private water supply distribution systems receive water from 
Municipal water supply distribution system separated from private system by water meter and check valve
On-site water supply
Independent source similar to a municipal system

slides.title: Water Sources
content:
Obtain water from groundwater, surface water, oceans, etc.
Some are independent of public water systems and supply water for other uses
Others may be a water system's sole provider
Divided into following groups

slides.title: Moving Water Sources (2 of 2)
content:
Water is pumped from water source into pretreatment storage or directly to treatment plant
Care must be taken to avoid contamination or impairment
Environmental regulations set limits on water withdrawals

slides.title: Static Water Sources
content:
Oceans, lakes, and ponds supply water
Water purveyors must evaluate static water sources to ensure even in drought conditions, smaller bodies of water can support demand
Open water sources do not become impaired or polluted
Causes of impairment may be manmade or natural
If adequate hydraulic head between static water source and treatment facility, water may be moved by gravity
If adequate hydraulic head is not present, pumps must move the water

slides.title: Drilling and Pumping
content:
When a well is drilled, a pump brings groundwater to the surface mechanically
For shallow wells, pumps may be mounted at or above ground
More commonly, pumps are suspended in the aquifer
Water is pumped to the surface and stored in pretreatment tanks or piped directly to treatment plants

slides.title: Water Storage Tanks
content:
Used before and after the treatment process
Some contain a system's only water source
Others augment systems or balance/regulate system pressure
Typically characterized by use
Tanks may be constructed of

slides.title: Gravity Tanks
content:
Elevate water supply above end user and provide head pressure to move water through system when needed
Elevated above point of demand, on a tower, atop a structure, or at high terrain
Reliable when full
Minimize need for system pumps and can provide primary storage in a water system
Courtesy of Sand Springs (OK) Fire Department

slides.title: Demand on Gravity Tanks
content:
Also used to stabilize or balance pressures on distribution systems in peak demand
Once demand on a system becomes so great that pumps cannot keep up, system pressure begins to drop
When pressure drops to a point where it cannot keep tank full, tank begins adding water to system
Elevated storage tanks become important fire protection feature during peak demand periods
Only necessary to keep tanks full and valves open so water will flow when needed

slides.title: Pumping Systems
content:
Pumps are required when differential in elevation cannot develop required pressure in water system
Two types of pumps used in water distribution are 
Positive displacement pumps
Centrifugal pumps
Positive displacement pumps utilize a rotating or piston motion to move fluid and air in measured amounts
Centrifugal pumps use an impeller to move large amounts of fluid
Both pump types are found in public and private water systems

Section II:
Distribution System Components
content: Learning Objective 2 — Describe water distribution system components.

slides.title: Grid System Advantages
content:
High demand in one area does not reduce water flow in other areas
Even with grid systems, some areas have dead-end lines served by a single water main
Areas with dead-end lines typically have reduced water flows
Users on a dead-end line are susceptible to service interruption when there is excess water use between their location and supply main
Connections provide access to water supply system 
Through fire hydrants or through water flow control valves
Flowmeters at point where customers gain water from system

slides.title: Piping System
content:
May encounter several types of distribution piping due to
Age of many water systems in North America
Lack of municipal funding to upgrade/replace infrastructure
First water distribution pipes were made of hollowed-out logs or pieced-together wood segments joined with iron staves
May still appear in older, original system construction
Piping must resist both internal and external forces
Best piping materials are durable, such as ductile iron or PVC
Piping materials must have an inner surface or liner system that can be sanitized

slides.title: Common Types of Indicating Control Valves
content: Common Types of Indicating Control Valves

Gate valve 
Usually non-rising stem type
As operator turns valve nut, gate either rises or lowers to control water flow
Butterfly valve 
Usually has a rubber or rubber-composition seat bonded to the valve body
Disk within the valve rotates 90 degrees to open or close the valve
Located above ground in treatment plants and pump stations

slides.title: Underground Nonindicating Valves
content:
Cast iron covers located in or near the street indicate access to underground control valves
Where properly installed, a buried valve is operated through a valve box using a special key
Water purveyors typically keep the key, but valve keys may also be carried on fire apparatus

slides.title: Pressure Reducing Valves (PRVs)
content:
Common causes of high system pressure include
Elevation differences in mountainous regions
High pump discharge pressures required to reach remote sections of a water system
PRVs reduce high water pressure and maintain it at a safe level for use within a building
Control water pressure by reducing size of opening (orifice) through which water flows into a building
Reduced orifice slows water flow and lowers pressure 
Two basic types of PRVs
Fixed pressure drop valves 
Adjustable valves

slides.title: Adjustable Valves
content:
More common
Allow device to be set in the field
Controlled in one of two ways
First way is through an adjustable spring manually set in the field
Second way is through a pilot line that constantly adjusts the pressure drop based on the difference between upstream and downstream pressures and flows
Reducing pressure to more precise levels also saves significant amounts of water for the end user
PRV use has increased as communities focus on the benefits of water conservation

slides.title: Fire Hydrants
content:
Types and locations are based on a municipality's geographic features and fire protection needs
Specifications are conveyed to the end user through the locally adopted building code
In North America, the two main types of fire hydrants are dry and wet barrel hydrants

slides.title: Dry-Barrel Hydrants (1 of 2)
content:
Designed for use in climates with freezing temperatures

Control valve 
On the distribution line of the water main
Located below the frost line

Stem nut used to open and close the control valve is located on top of the hydrant

When firefighter operates stem nut, water flows into hydrant
Any water remaining in a closed dry-barrel hydrant drains through a small valve (foot valve)

slides.title: Dry-Barrel Hydrants (2 of 2)
content:
Small valve opens at the bottom of the hydrant when the main valve approaches a closed position
Hydrant wrench is used to turn the stem nut and the attached stem, which opens and closes the valve
In areas where dry-barrel hydrants do not properly drain after use, compressed air must be used to pump or blow out the hydrant barrel

slides.title: Wet-Barrel Hydrants
content:
Designed for use in mild climates where temperatures remain above freezing
Water remains at all times
Compression valves are usually located at each outlet
In some cases, another control valve in the top of the hydrant controls the water flow to all outlets

slides.title: Hose Connection
content:
Must be provided to convey water from hydrant into fire hose
Number and configuration are dictated by
Local fire department
Stated in locally adopted building code
Included in water purveyor’s hydrant specifications
Standard fire hydrant has 
Two 2½-inch (65 mm) hose connection outlets 
One 4½-inch (115 mm) pumper connection outlet

slides.title: Coupling Systems
content:
Threaded or sexless coupling systems
Traditional threaded connection uses 
Nationally accepted hose diameter and thread pitch, also known as national standard thread
Locally dictated connection size and thread pitch
Most commonly used sexless coupling system is the Storz connection

slides.title: Annual Inspections
content:
In some jurisdictions, fire companies perform inspections
In other municipalities, inspections are responsibility of water purveyor
In all cases, hydrant inspection, testing, and maintenance records must be maintained and available for review
Inspectors need accurate reporting of observations and tests to evaluate operational readiness 
Qualified individuals should conduct the inspections
Records must be kept in accordance with NFPA 25 and ISO guidelines
Annex B of NFPA 25 provides more information about inspection, testing, and maintenance forms

content: Learning Objective 5 — Explain how to use the fire flow formulas.

slides.title: Calculations (2 of 2)
content:
Constant 29.83 (0.0667766) is derived from physical laws relating to water velocity, pressure, and conversion factors
Resulting answer will be in gallons per minute (gpm) or liters per minute (L/min)
Correction from input to output units is resolved by the constant during the derivation
This formula assigns a coefficient of 1.0 for an ideal frictionless discharge orifice

slides.title: Common Hydrant Outlet Types and Discharge Coefficients
content: Common Hydrant Outlet Types and Discharge Coefficients

If actual orifice or nozzle does not match the three common types, consult hydrant manufacturer for appropriate coefficient
Feel inside contour to determine outlet type used
To determine the coefficient of discharge for a specific nozzle, refer to the manufacturer’s recommendations
Flow formulas depend on actual internal diameter of outlet or nozzle opening

slides.title: Alternative Method and Correction Factors
content:
If the pressure from a single outlet is too great to accurately measure hydrant flow, use two small outlets and measure flow from both of them at the same time
To test using large outlet, use a correction factor to give more accurate results
Multiply fire flow by the correction factor that corresponds to the velocity pressure measured by the pitot tube and gauge

content: Learning Objective 6 — Describe fire flow testing.

slides.title: NOTE2
content: Water is never discharged from a test hydrant. A pressure gauge cap is placed on the discharge, and the hydrant is fully opened.

slides.title: Available Water Flow on Test Hydrants
content: Available Water Flow on Test Hydrants

Remove hydrant cap from test hydrant
Attach pressure gauge cap with petcock in open position
After checking other caps for tightness, slowly open hydrant by turning operating nut several turns
Once air has escaped and steady stream of water is flowing, close petcock and fully open hydrant
Read and record static pressure as seen on pressure gauge

slides.title: Available Water Flow on Flow Hydrants
content: Available Water Flow on Flow Hydrants

slides.title: NOTE3
content: The residual pressure should not drop below 20 psi (138 kPa) during the test. If it does, reduce the number of flow hydrants.

slides.title: Ending Test Procedures
content:
Slowly close flow hydrant to prevent water hammer
After checking for proper drainage, replace and secure all hydrant caps
Report any hydrant defects
Check pressure gauge on test hydrant for a return to normal operating pressure
Then close hydrant
Open petcock valve to prevent a vacuum on pressure gauge
Remove pressure gauge cap
After checking for proper drainage, replace and secure cap
Report any hydrant defects

slides.title: Water Main Testing
content:
Water mains may contain flow pressures too low to read on the pitot gauge
Reduce flow orifice by using a straight stream nozzle with tips smaller than 2½ inches (65 mm)
Place nozzle on hydrant outlet to increase flow velocity until velocity pressure can be measured with the pitot gauge
When using straight stream nozzles, adjust calculation to include smaller nozzle diameter and correct coefficient of friction

slides.title: Warning
content: Do not stand in front of closed caps or lean over the top of a hydrant when operating it. Do not flow water during freezing weather.

slides.title: Hazards During Flow Testing
content:
Water flowing from a hydrant can 
Erode soil
Ruin landscaping
Flood buildings
To minimize property damage during flow testing
Open and close hydrants slowly to avoid water hammer
Only flow hydrants where drainage is adequate
Check downstream to see where water will flow

slides.title: Public Safety Concerns during Hydrant Testing
content: Public Safety Concerns during Hydrant Testing

Do not leave deep standing water from a hydrant test unattended in retention basins in locations where children are playing. Wait until the water has been absorbed or drained before leaving the area. Do not allow children to play in runoff water.

slides.title: Other Causes of Reduced Water Flow
content: Other Causes of Reduced Water Flow

Encrustations, growths, crusts, tubercular lump corrosion, or rust around inside wall of water main
Can narrow actual diameter of pipe and impair capacity

Found chiefly in the bottom of a water main, especially in a system's large, low-velocity portions and dead-end, idle flow parts

slides.title: Water Flow Control Valves
content:
Prevent sprinkler water from flowing back into water supply
Isolate or shut off water supply to system when it is necessary to perform maintenance, change sprinklers, interrupt operation
Located between water supply and sprinkler system
Located throughout system to isolate specific zones/floors
Must visually indicate whether open or closed
Courtesy of Richard Boisvert, Fire Marshal, Brighton (MI) Area Fire Authority

slides.title: Outside Stem and Yoke
content:
Outside Stem and Yoke (OS&Y) Valve
Gate valve that has a yoke on the outside with a threaded stem or screw
When open, threaded portion of stem is out of the yoke
Sits inside the yoke when the valve is closed

slides.title: Post Indicator Valve
content:
Post indicator valve (PIV) 
Underground gate valve with a hollow metal post attached to valve housing
Words OPEN or SHUT appear on the target of the valve stem inside the post

slides.title: Wall Post Indicator Valve and Assembly
content: Wall Post Indicator Valve and Assembly

slides.title: Branch Lines
content:
Risers supply cross main that serves a number of branch lines
Sprinklers can be installed on branch lines in multiple configurations
Hangers and clamps support entire system, may be pitched to facilitate drainage
Requirements for spacing of supports can be found in applicable design specification
Compare design to installation and approved plans to determine compliance
Additional bracing is required to support system in areas with seismic activity

slides.title: Hydraulic Calculation Method
content:
Design is based on the greatest demand at the greatest distance from the base of the system riser
Due to complexity, properly performing hydraulic calculation method requires additional knowledge and training
Can provide a cost-effective design
Not limited by restrictions placed on pipe schedule design

slides.title: Sprinklers
content:
Sprinkler is actual discharge device that applies water (or foam) to fire or other hazard
Emit a stream of water and break it into droplets
Typical sprinkler has six parts

slides.title: NFPA 13 and Sprinklers
content:
Defines sprinklers according to orientation and application
Orientation refers to sprinkler installation
Orientation types include
Recessed
Concealed
Flush
Pendent
Sidewall
Upright

slides.title: Variations in Sprinkler Types
content:
Multiple variations may exist within each sprinkler type, depending on
Manufacturer
Hazard requirements
All sprinklers must 
Meet the design criteria set forth by NFPA 13
Be tested for the specific application for which they are intended and listed
Inspectors may encounter other sprinkler types during plan review or field inspections

slides.title: Corrosion-Resistant
content:
Constructed of stainless steel or factory-coated with a corrosion-resistant material
Wax
Asphalt
Lead
Enamel
Polyester
Teflon®
Installed in corrosive atmospheres
Pool enclosures
Chemical storage or areas containing acids/caustic materials

slides.title: Intermediate-Level/Rack Storage
content:
Used in high-rack storage spaces
Shields protect the operating elements of these sprinklers from the discharge of sprinklers at a higher level
