slides.title: Sprinkler Activation
content:
Occurs when thermocouples reach a preset temperature, releasing sprinkler plug
Commonly used release mechanisms include fusible links, glass bulbs, and chemical pellets
Sprinklers are rated by activation temperatures, which may be stamped on the sprinkler

slides.title: Electronic Detector
content:
Activates preaction and deluge systems by smoke, heat, flame or rate-of-rise detectors in the protected area
May also activate notification or alarm systems to warn occupants
When the detector senses an abnormal situation, it sends an electronic impulse to the fire control panel and the sprinkler waterflow control valve
Valve opens, permitting water to enter the system

slides.title: Manually Activated System
content:
Relies on human intervention to operate the sprinkler system
In this case, a worker may activate the system before a fire occurs, such as in the case of a hazardous gas or liquid release
Some locations have manual systems for fire brigades to activate
Manual systems are also located in electrical rooms or data centers

slides.title: Review Question 2
content: Name and describe four types of sprinkler system activation devices.

slides.title:
Section II:
Automatic Sprinkler Systems
content: Learning Objective 2 — Identify the NFPA categories of automatic sprinkler systems.

slides.title: Automatic Sprinkler Systems
content:
Consists of a series of discharge devices (sprinklers) arranged to distribute enough water to either extinguish or control spread
Network of pipes supplies water to the sprinklers
Thermally sensitive devices keep most sprinklers closed
When heat from a fire affects these devices, sprinklers closest to the fire activate automatically
Deluge or preaction type sprinkler systems operate when an electronic detector or manual control device is activated
One or two operating sprinklers can control most fires in sprinkler-equipped structures

slides.title: Four Types of Automatic Sprinkler Systems (1 of 2)
content: Four Types of Automatic Sprinkler Systems (1 of 2)

slides.title: Four Types of Automatic Sprinkler Systems (2 of 2)
content: Four Types of Automatic Sprinkler Systems (2 of 2)

slides.title: Combined Dry Pipe and Preaction Sprinkler System
content: Combined Dry Pipe and Preaction Sprinkler System

Also known as double preaction system or double interlock system
Continually charged with air under pressure 
Combined with detection system that controls operation of waterflow control valve
Detection system activates 
Waterflow control valve
Release of pressurized air in the system
Facility fire alarm
Used in special circumstances and facilities that require additional level of protection against false activation

slides.title: NFPA 13R, 13D and IRC Section P2904 Systems
content: NFPA 13R, 13D and IRC Section P2904 Systems

slides.title: NFPA 13D and 13R
content:
NFPA 13D system 
Requires minimum 10-minute supply of stored water
Minimum amount of water necessary for single story structures with area of less than 2,000 square feet (180 m2) based on flow rate of two sprinklers operating for seven minutes
Structures equipped with NFPA 13R system require four sprinklers operate for 30 minutes
Sensitivity or speed of operation is a major difference between residential and standard sprinklers
Residential sprinklers respond more quickly than standard sprinklers

slides.title: Water Supply and Flow Rate Requirements for Residential Sprinklers
content: Water Supply and Flow Rate Requirements for Residential Sprinklers

Water supply requirements for residential sprinklers are less than standard sprinkler systems
Small domestic water supplies service many single-family dwellings and other residential buildings
10-minute water supply may not completely control fires, delays flashover and allows time for occupants to reach safety
Water supply for residential sprinklers may be taken from
Public connection
Onsite pressure tank
Storage tank with automatic pump

slides.title: Water Supply and Flow Rate Requirements
content: Water Supply and Flow Rate Requirements

slides.title: NFPA 13R and Sprinkler Valves
content: NFPA 13R permits sprinkler valves to be supervised or simply locked in open position where plumbing or water department requirements do not permit uninterrupted connection

slides.title: Review Question 3
content: Name three variations of the four basic designs of NFPA 13 sprinkler systems.

slides.title:
Section III:
Water Spray Fixed Systems
content:
Section III:
Water Spray Fixed Systems
Learning Objective 3 — Describe water spray fixed systems.

slides.title: Review Question 4
content: Name the hazard categories for which water spray fixed systems can be used.

slides.title:
Section IV:
Water Mist Systems
content: Learning Objective 4 — Describe water mist systems.

slides.title: Water Mist Systems
content:
Discharges a fine mist of water
Absorbs more heat than water-spray or automatic sprinklers
Raises humidity of the room enough to halt combustion
Very fine spray controls or extinguishes fire by 
Displacing oxygen
Blocking radiant heat production 
Protect lives and property by 
Extinguishing Class A and Class B fires
Controlling fire temperatures in compartments
Preventing flashover with subsequent extension to other compartments in a structure

slides.title: High Pressure Operations
content:
High-pressure systems may operate at or above 500 psi (3 500 kPa)
Compressed-air, nitrogen, or high-pressure water pumps create these higher pressures
Compressed air may be supplied from storage cylinders or air pumps
Air pressure may be applied to the water through 
Water tube (single-fluid system)
Second air tube to each spray nozzle (twin-fluid system)

slides.title: Water-Mist System Components
content:
Composed of small-diameter, pressure rated copper, or stainless-steel tubing
Small-diameter spray nozzles spaced evenly on tubing
Type depends on system design
Product-of-combustion detection system activates water mist system
Manual operation in case an individual discovers fire before system activates
Most common type is similar to deluge sprinkler system

slides.title: Review Question 5
content: What are some applications for water mist systems?

slides.title: Foam-Water Systems
content:
Discharge a foam-water solution onto a fire
Commonly employed to protect Class B fire hazards
Also used for Class A hazards
When properly designed, foam-water systems may be used to suppress vapors created by a flammable liquid spill
Can be wet-pipe, dry-pipe, preaction, or deluge systems
Designed to deliver foam-water solution at required design concentration over discharge density and design

slides.title: Proportioners
content:
All systems require a proportioner
In-line valve or pump designed to inject and mix foam with water to create correct concentration of foam-water solution
NFPA 25 requires annual testing for the proportioner 
In some designs
Pre-primed with foam solution
Ceiling sprinklers are used as the detection feature
In preaction and deluge systems —  fire alarm and detection system required to activate

slides.title: Review Question 6
content: What are some important design aspects of foam-water systems?

slides.title:
Section VI:
Standpipe and Hose Systems
content:
Section VI:
Standpipe and Hose Systems
Learning Objective 6 — Describe standpipe and hose systems.

slides.title: Standpipe and Hose Systems
content:
Provide means for rapidly deploying fire hose and operating fire streams in multistory structures and remote points in large-area structures
Different system types are designed for use by firefighters, trained occupants, or both
Most codes require standpipes be installed in all buildings where
Highest story sits more than thirty feet (9.1 m) above the lowest level of fire department vehicle access
Lowest level is more than thirty feet (9.1 m) below the highest level of fire department vehicle access

slides.title: Standpipe and Hose Systems during Construction
content: Standpipe and Hose Systems during Construction

Some building codes require operational standpipes during construction
As construction progresses, standpipe is extended to subsequent floors
System must have
Appropriate FDCs
Hose discharge connections
Fire pumps
Other necessary appliances

slides.title: Inspector Verifications for Standpipe and Hose Systems
content: Inspector Verifications for Standpipe and Hose Systems

Critical that inspectors verify connection threads on all hose connections and FDCs
Improper hose threads cost valuable time and may render standpipe unusable
Inspector should request documentation of the last test to verify system readiness
Courtesy of Sand Springs Fire Department

slides.title: Class I: Firefighters
content:
Primarily used by firefighters trained in handling large handlines 
Capable of supplying effective fire streams during more advanced stages of fire within a structure
2½-inch (65 mm) hose connections or hose stations attached

slides.title: Class II: Trained Building Occupants
content:
Primarily designed for use by trained building occupants
Provide a hose connection
Equipped with a 1½-inch (38 mm) hose, nozzle, and hose rack
Value is debatable
Presence of the small hose may give a false sense of security to occupants
Installation is declining in favor of Class I or Class III installations

slides.title: Class III: Combination
content:
Combine features of Class I and II systems
2½-inch (65 mm) hose connections for fire department personnel and 1½-inch (38 mm) hose and connections for use by trained building occupants
System design must allow for simultaneous use of both Class I and Class II services
Accomplished by using an adapter
More popular arrangement than equipping specific connection with their own valves

slides.title: Five Standpipe System Types (4 of 4)
content: Wet standpipe systems cannot be used in cold environments, so a dry system may be necessary

slides.title: NOTE1
content: Dry standpipes do not meet Canadian building and fire code requirements.

slides.title: Review Question 7
content: What should an inspector check for when assessing standpipe systems?

slides.title: Water Supplies and Residual Pressure
content:
Specific requirements are determined by the adopted code
Amount of water required for standpipe system depends on
Building's height and occupancy
Total number of standpipes in the building
Installation of an automatic sprinkler system may reduce water supply requirements
Some occupancies require secondary water supplies
Water supplied by automatic fire pumps that augment pressure from municipal water main
Be aware of multiple water supplies, verify operational readiness

slides.title: Pressure-Regulating Devices
content:
Prevents pressures that make fire hose difficult or dangerous to handle and enhances system reliability
Can improve system economy by eliminating need for additional fire pumps
Where hose outlet discharge pressure exceeds 175 psi (1 225 kPa), NFPA 14 requires a pressure-regulating device to limit pressure to 175 psi (1 225 kPa) 
Make system design more complex
NFPA 25 contains testing requirements 
Three basic categories — Pressure-restricting, pressure-control, pressure-reducing

slides.title: Pressure-Restricting Devices
content:
Consist of a simple restricting orifice inserted into the waterway
Residual pressure drop through orifice plate depends on orifice diameter and available flow and pressure 
Each standpipe discharge connection fitted with restricting orifice
Different sizes are required for each floor and application
Limited to systems with 1½-inch (38 mm) hose discharges, 175 psi (1 225 kPa) maximum pressure
Not preferred — Do not control or reduce system water pressure

slides.title: Pressure-Control Devices
content:
Preferred for managing excessive pressure
Considered the most reliable pressure control method
Use a pitot tube and gauge to read the pressure and automatically reduce the flow through the discharge
Some are field adjustable, and others are preset at the factory

slides.title: Pressure-Reducing Devices
content:
Preferred for managing excessive pressure
Use a spring mechanism that compensates for variations in pressure
Balance the available pressure within the system with the pressure required for hoseline use

slides.title: Pressure-Reducing Valves
content:
Standpipe systems equipped with pressure-regulating devices are designed for routine testing
Systems must have dedicated drainage pipes with connections on each floor and a means for determining water flow
Verify the required testing has been completed 
Verify required pressure-reducing valves (PRVs) are installed and tested as specified

slides.title: Review Question 8
content: Name and describe the three basic categories of pressure-regulating devices.

slides.title: Fire Department Connections (FDCs)
content:
Each standpipe system requires one or more FDCs through which a fire department engine can supply water into the system
Large buildings with two or more zones require an FDC for each zone
Raised-letter sign on a plate or fitting that reads STANDPIPE designates the FDC
Sign must indicate serviced floors

slides.title: FDCs and Standards and Codes
content:
Standard requirements do not permit shutoff valves between the FDC and the standpipe riser
In multiple riser systems, listed indicating valves are provided at base of individual risers
Included so entire system is not taken out of service during maintenance
Hose connections to the FDC 
Comply with the locally adopted code 
Have standard cap plugs or approved breakaway covers

slides.title:
Section VII:
Stationary Fire Pumps
content: Learning Objective 7 — Describe stationary fire pumps.

slides.title: Stationary Fire Pumps
content:
Inspectors should be familiar with stationary (fixed) fire pumps found in commercial, institutional, industrial facilities
Increases pressure of water that flows through it
Usually needed to supply a sprinkler or standpipe system because available water supply source lacks adequate pressure to meet fire suppression system demand
Size determined by most hydraulically demanding area
High-rise buildings or areas with low static pressure on the public or private water supply may require multiple pumps
All pumps and installations must comply with NFPA 20
NFPA standards on sprinkler, standpipes, water-spray, water-mist, foam-water systems contain references to fire pumps

slides.title: Centrifugal Pumps
content:
Centrifugal pumps are commonly used as stationary pumps in fire suppression systems
Impeller, mounted to the drive shaft, is a key component
When pump is activated, shaft rotates impeller at a high speed
Rapid motion draws water into impeller’s center or eye
As water moves through rotating impeller, centrifugal force increases pumps operating pressure

slides.title: Horizontal Split-Case Pump (1 of 3)
content:
Most common type of fire pump found in stationary fire suppression systems
Also referred to as a horizontal shaft pump
Drive shaft sits on a horizontal plane with pump on one end and driver (motor) on the other
Pumps boost pressure from an incoming, pressurized water source
Cannot draft water from a pond or other static supply source that has no positive head pressure

slides.title: Horizontal Split-Case Pump (3 of 3)
content:
Most common gallon rating for horizontal split-case pumps ranges from 500 to 1,500 gpm (2 000 L/min to 6 000 L/min)
Available for flows as low as 150 gpm (600 L/min) and as high as 4,500 gpm (18 000 L/min)
Unlike pumps on fire apparatus, stationary fire pumps are not rated at a particular pressure

slides.title: End Suction Pumps
content:
Variation of the horizontal split-case pump design
Have center line suction and discharge
Have pressure ratings 40-50 psi (280 kPa-1 050 kPa)
Flows range 50-750 gpm (200 L/min-3 000 L/min)
Advantages
Ease of installation
Simplified piping arrangement
Reduced pipe strain
Do not need an automatic air-release valve to prevent overheating

slides.title: Vertical Inline Pumps
content:
Single-stage pump designed to fit into intake/discharge line
Driver is located above inline impeller
Advantages
Compactness
Ease of installation as a replacement pump
Ease of pump and driver maintenance
Has a capacity as high as 1,500 gpm (6 000 L/min) and operating pressures up to 165 psi (1 155 kPa)

slides.title: Vertical Turbine Pumps
content:
Used to lift water from a source below the pump
Impellers are located within supply source
Water is drawn into the impeller and then discharged up through the impeller casing
Most of these pumps are multistage pumps
As water exits one impeller, enters the next
Process continues until water is discharged into the fire suppression system piping
Volume capabilities are consistent with those of horizontal and vertical split-case pumps
Discharge pressure ratings up to 500 psi (3 500 kPa)

slides.title: Pressure-Maintenance Pumps
content:
Automatic sprinkler systems may require a small-capacity pressure-maintenance pump
Known as jockey pumps or make-up pumps
Located in parallel with the primary fire pump
Prevent false starts at the fire pump by maintaining system pressure between present limits when the system is not flowing water

slides.title: Electric Motor Driver (1 of 2)
content:
Most common fire pump driver
Simple, reliable, and easily maintained
Not designed specifically for use on fire pumps
Must meet National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) requirements 
Must have adequate horsepower (hp) to drive fire pump
Capacity (gpm [L/min]), net pressure (discharge pressure minus the incoming pressure), and efficiency determine the required horsepower

slides.title: Electric Motor Driver (2 of 2)
content: Electric motors that power fire pumps use considerable electricity and may require a larger electrical service

slides.title: Review Question 9
content: Name and describe the three types of pump drivers.

slides.title: Controllers
content:
Stationary fire pump 
Starts automatically when the fire suppression system begins to flow
Frequently designed to stop automatically when no longer needed
Fire pump controller 
Govern the starting and stopping of fire pump drivers
Monitor and signal the status and condition of the fire pump unit

slides.title: NFPA 20
content:
Describes requirements for electric and diesel pump controllers
Additional requirements for testing and maintenance become considerations when pumps are connected to alternate supply
Most fire pumps are designed to start when a drop in water pressure occurs in the fire suppression system
Pressure-sensing switch detects drop in pressure resulting from water flow
Pressure switch energizes circuit, closes contacts for motor circuit, and starts fire pump motor
When water stops flowing, pressure switch detects resulting increase in pressure, interrupts motor circuit, turns pump off

slides.title: Operating Features of an Electric Motor Controller
content: Operating Features of an Electric Motor Controller

Circuit breaker
Power-available indicating lamp
Running period timer
Keeps fire pump motor operating for a minimum period of time once started
Eliminates rapid opening and closing of the main motor contacts from system pressure fluctuations
Contains provisions for manually starting and stopping the pump 
Basically opens and closes a motor’s electric circuit

slides.title: Review Question 10
content: What are the functions of a fire pump controller?

slides.title:
Section VIII:
Evaluating System Components and Equipment
content:
Section VIII:
Evaluating System Components and Equipment
Learning Objective 8 — Explain the methods of evaluating various system components and equipment.

slides.title: Evaluating System Components and Equipment
content:
NFPA 25 
Contains detailed lists of inspection, testing, maintenance requirements for all water-based suppression systems
Provides charts indicating how often to perform these tasks
Building owner or occupant
Responsible for ensuring that trained and experienced personnel perform these tasks
May contract the services of third-party testing and maintenance organizations
AHJ must verify that required testing and maintenance are complete and records are in order
Four opportunities to review, inspect, witness tests

slides.title: Opportunities for Inspection Occur During
content:
Plan review — Plan review and approval process is required for all fire suppression systems
Preacceptance inspections — Inspectors make periodic preacceptance inspections during the construction phase when the equipment is being installed
Acceptance testing — All systems must undergo this testing when installation is complete
Routine inspections and testing — Inspectors continue making periodic visual inspections for the life of the system, witnessing annual tests, and/or reviewing and updating inspection records

slides.title: Caution 3
content: Inspectors should only witness testing, inspection, and maintenance, or accept appropriate documentation that required inspection, testing, and maintenance has been conducted by the owner or owner’s representative.

slides.title: Caution 1
content: NEVER personally operate, adjust, manipulate, alter, or handle any fire suppression system devices or equipment during situations other than emergencies or planned training sessions.

slides.title: Caution 2
content: Always allow facility personnel to operate fire suppression system devices during the inspection and testing of these systems.

slides.title: Plans Review
content:
May be the first contact with a new fire suppression system
Inspector must verify that the proposed fire suppression system 
Is appropriate for the type of occupancy, hazard, and construction type
Is correctly designed
Complies with NFPA and adopted fire and building code requirements
Contains all necessary documentation to permit an accurate design assessment

slides.title: Review Question 11
content: What should inspectors look for during preacceptance inspections?

slides.title: Caution 4
content: Due to waterflow quantities and pressures, electric voltage required by fire pumps, and high noise levels, inspectors must wear appropriate protective equipment, including gloves, eye and hearing protection, and hard hat or helmet.

slides.title: Valves
content:
Every sprinkler system is equipped with 
Water-control valves
Operating valves
Shut off the water
Drain the system
Prevent recirculation of water
Serve other system needs

slides.title: Main Drains
content:
Each sprinkler system riser has a main drain to remove water from the system for maintenance purposes
NFPA 25 mandates quarterly main drain tests
Verify inspection of system and witness alarm test in conjunction with main drain test
System pressure gauge frequently indicates a higher pressure than supply pressure gauge due to pressure surges being trapped by a check valve 
Risers 4 inches (100 mm) or larger in diameter are equipped with a 2-inch (50 mm) main drain

slides.title: Main Drain Testing
content: Main drain test is useful for detecting impairments, such as closed valves, obstructions, or gradual deterioration

slides.title: Perform a Main Drain Test
content:
Observe and record the pressure on the system side gauge at the system riser 
Have a building representative fully open the main drain
Observe and record the pressure drop
Have the building representative slowly close the 2-inch (50 mm) main drain
Observe and record the final static pressure
If it differs from the initial static pressure, it is likely that pressure was trapped in the system

slides.title: NOTE2
content: On a system using an alarm check valve, inspectors should take the pressure readings from the lower gauge. Erroneously high static pressures can exist above the valve.

slides.title: Inspector Considerations for Main Drain Testing
content: Inspector Considerations for Main Drain Testing

Inspector should compare the new pressure readings to previously recorded readings
Significant differences may reveal a partially-closed supply valve or an obstruction in a supply line
Faulty backflow preventers can also cause a difference in pressure readings

slides.title: Verify During Dry-Pipe Sprinkler System Inspections (1 of 2)
content: Verify During Dry-Pipe Sprinkler System Inspections (1 of 2)

All indicating control valves are open and properly supervised in the open position
Air-pressure readings correspond to previously recorded readings
Ball drip valve moves freely and allows trapped water to seep out of the FDC
Velocity drip valve, located beneath the intermediate chamber, moves freely and allows trapped water to seep out
Check this valve by instructing the building representative to lift a push rod that extends through the drip valve opening
Can be checked by moving the push rod located in the valve opening

slides.title: Verify During Dry-Pipe Sprinkler System Inspections (2 of 2)
content: Verify During Dry-Pipe Sprinkler System Inspections (2 of 2)

Any drum drips are drained to eliminate trapped moisture in the low areas of the system
Priming water is at the correct level
If necessary, personnel can drain water by opening the priming water test level valve until air begins to escape
The system’s air pressure is maintained above the trip point, according to the manufacturer’s furnished instruction sheet or at least 20 psi (140 kPa)

slides.title: NOTE3
content: Similar steps to the list above apply to inspections of preaction and deluge systems. The main drain test for deluge and preaction sprinkler systems serves the same purpose as it does on wet- and dry-pipe systems. The test is also conducted in the same manner.

slides.title: Alarm Trip Test (1 of 2)
content:
Observe the alarm trip test performed by owner’s/occupant's sprinkler company representative
Inspector never performs this test due to liability issues
When planning an alarm trip test on a dry-pipe system, be aware that this procedure can take from two to four hours to complete
Time required depends on amount and size of piping in system and capacity of air compressor to pressurize the system

slides.title: Alarm Trip Test (2 of 2)
content:
Old valves may prove more difficult to reset because of leaking seats or worn parts and require more than one attempt
Inspector may want to have personnel notify the alarm-monitoring organization before they conduct any tests with electronically supervised equipment
Another method is to notify the monitoring company after the first portion of the test to verify that the company handles its responsibility
When testing is complete, the alarm-monitoring organization should confirm that the alarm equipment functions properly

slides.title: Sprinkler Cabinet
content:
Inspect the sprinkler cabinet to verify the required number of replacement sprinklers available
NFPA 13, 13R, and 13D sprinkler standards list the appropriate supply of extra sprinklers that the protected premises must keep on hand
Standards specify that these cabinets contain a minimum of one sprinkler for each type and temperature rating, as well as a sprinkler wrench

slides.title: Damaged Sprinkler
content:
Guards that protect against mechanical damage may need to be added or repaired 
Carefully examine sprinklers in buildings subject to high temperatures
May require the installation of different types of rated sprinklers
Any sprinkler showing evidence of weakness or damage needs to be replaced with a sprinkler of same type and temperature rating

slides.title: Weak Sprinklers
content:
Two indications of a weak sprinkler are leakage around sprinkler orifice and a creeping or sliding apart of fusible link (cold flow)
Cold flow is distortion caused by the repeated heating of a fusible link to near operating temperature
Using frangible bulb sprinklers or a higher temperature-rated sprinkler eliminates cold-flow problems

slides.title: Expectations for Inspections
content:
Determine that all sprinkler piping and hangers are in good condition
Check for corrosion and physical damage to verify there are no leaks in the pipes or fittings
Report loose sprinkler hangers
Note whether hangers are located at proper intervals and match the original installation plans
Must not permit occupants to use sprinkler piping as a support for ladders, stock, ceiling grids, other materials

slides.title: PIVs and FDCs
content: After an interior inspection of the sprinkler system, inspectors should examine PIVs and FDCs on the exterior of the facility

slides.title: PIVs and FDCs Considerations
content:
Check PIVs to ensure the operating wrench is in place
Verify the PIV’s target (open/shut sign) is properly adjusted and cover glass is in place and clean
Verify the PIV bolts are tightened and the barrel casing is intact
Confirm the FDC is unobstructed, swivels rotate freely, and locking caps are in place
Verify appropriate keys are provided 
Use a fire department male coupling to verify compatibility with FDC female threads

slides.title: Periodic Inspections of Water-Spray Fixed Systems
content: Periodic Inspections of Water-Spray Fixed Systems

slides.title: Inspector Considerations for Conducting Periodic Inspections of Water-Spray Fixed Systems (1 of 2)
content: Inspector Considerations for Conducting Periodic Inspections of Water-Spray Fixed Systems (1 of 2)

Review owner/occupant inspection reports to verify that frequency of inspections, tests, and maintenance meet the minimum requirements of NFPA 25
Piping and fittings are free of leaks, corrosion, and mechanical damage
Piping and fittings have no misaligned parts or missing components
Pipe hangers are not missing or damaged
Nozzles are operable; free from corrosion, paint, or accumulations of dirt; and properly aligned for the protected area

slides.title: Inspector Considerations for Conducting Periodic Inspections of Water-Spray Fixed Systems (2 of 2)
content: Inspector Considerations for Conducting Periodic Inspections of Water-Spray Fixed Systems (2 of 2)

Sprinkler cabinets contain replacement sprinklers and wrenches
All components are free of obstruction(s)
Water supplies are dependable
Waterflow control valves are in the locked and open position
Fire pumps, tanks, and connections to the public water supply comply with applicable codes and standards
Witness operational tests to determine that the system’s response time is less than forty seconds
Verify the discharge pattern is correct for the surface being covered

slides.title: Inspector Considerations for Water Mist Systems
content: Inspector Considerations for Water Mist Systems

slides.title: Standpipe and Hose System Inspections
content:
Require regular testing and inspections
Building management personnel should make a visual inspection at least once a month
Fire department must also inspect them at regular intervals because interior fire suppression operations depend on standpipe and hose systems 
Fire protection system contractor or owner’s/occupant’s employees should perform testing 
Employees must be trained and certified to perform tests

slides.title: Inspection Expectations for Standpipe and Hose Systems (1 of 3)
content: Inspection Expectations for Standpipe and Hose Systems (1 of 3)

All water supply valves are locked in open position
Fire pump, if present, is in operating condition with power available
Individual hose valves are free of paint, corrosion, and other impediments
Individual hose valves are operable and caps are in place
Hose valve threads are not damaged
Hose valve wheels are present and not damaged

slides.title: Inspection Expectations for Standpipe and Hose Systems (2 of 3)
content: Inspection Expectations for Standpipe and Hose Systems (2 of 3)

Hose cabinets/standpipes are accessible
Hose, if present, is dry, in good condition, and properly positioned on the rack or reel
Discharge outlets in dry systems are closed
Dry standpipe is drained of moisture
FDC is unobstructed
Swivels rotate freely, and caps are in place
Appropriate keys are provided for locking caps
Use a fire department male coupling to verify FDC female threads are compatible

slides.title: Inspection Expectations for Standpipe and Hose Systems (3 of 3)
content: Inspection Expectations for Standpipe and Hose Systems (3 of 3)

Water supply tanks are filled to the proper level
If the system is equipped with pressure-regulating devices, they are tested according to manufacturer requirements
Full flow testing is performed at intervals dictated by the applicable standard
Dry-pipe systems are hydrostatically tested every five years

content: Learning Objective 2 — Describe the different types of extinguishing agents.

slides.title: Extinguishing Agents
content:
Fire extinguishing agents are designed to protect specific hazards or locations
There are two basic groups of fire protection applications
First group allows the use of water-based suppression
Second group requires an alternative extinguishing agent, such as carbon dioxide (CO2), halon, halon replacements, dry chemicals, wet chemicals, or foams

Water-based suppression systems and fire extinguishers are designed for use on Class A fires

Fires involving other combustible materials, such as electrical equipment, require special-agent suppression systems

slides.title: Clean Agents
content:
Do not conduct electricity, evaporate without leaving a residue
Effective on Class A, Class B, Class C fires
Ozone safe and approved for production by EPA 
NFPA 2001 describes requirements for total flooding and local application 
Some are stored as liquefied compressed gas
When released and allowed to expand, gas extinguishes fire by displacing oxygen and disrupting the fire tetrahedron

slides.title: Carbon Dioxide (CO2)
content:
Asphyxiant that displaces and/or removes oxygen from environment

This colorless, noncombustible gas is heavier than oxygen

As an extinguishing agent, CO2 establishes a gaseous blanket between the fuel and the surrounding air
When discharged, it appears white and cloudy because of small, dry-ice crystals formed by the condensation of surrounding water vapor carried along in the gas stream
Once dissipated, CO2 leaves no residue 

Stored in a liquid state, which allows more agent to be stored in a given volume

slides.title: Limitations of CO2
content:
Limited cooling effect when applied directly to burning material
Example: Class A fires located deep within the burning material can rekindle after the CO2 dissipates into the atmosphere & normal oxygen returns

Another limitation to CO2 use as an extinguishing agent is its application method
Stored as liquefied compressed gas, CO2 converts to a gas when released from its container and allowed to expand
Difficult to project very far from discharge

slides.title: Warning
content: CO2 is an asphyxiant that can cause unconsciousness or death by suffocation.

slides.title: Dry Powder
content:
Extinguishing agents for combustible metals, also known as dry powders, extinguish Class D fires involving 
Aluminum
Magnesium
Sodium
Potassium
Metal fires produce extreme heat and require a long period for extinguishment
Extinguishing agent must be carefully chosen for the hazard metal being protected

slides.title: WARNING2
content: Do not confuse dry powder with dry chemical. Applying dry chemical agent to a Class D fire may result in an explosive reaction.

slides.title: Common Dry Powder Agents — NA-X®
content:
Sodium carbonate-based with flow-enhancing additives 
Used on most Class D fires involving potassium, sodium, and sodium-potassium alloy
NOT suitable for magnesium fires
Forms an encasing crust or cake on the burning material, causing an oxygen deficiency that interrupts the combustion process and extinguishes the fire
Application can be from fixed systems, by hand from pails, or from portable extinguishers
Listed by UL for use on burning materials at fuel temperatures up to 1,400°F (760°C)

slides.title: MET-L-X®
content:
Sodium chloride (salt)-based dry powder used in most Class D fires involving magnesium, sodium, and potassium
Contains additives to enhance its flow and prevent caking in the extinguisher 
Extinguishes metal fires by forming a crust on the burning metal
Applied from fire extinguisher, first to control fire and then to bury fuel in a powder layer
Stable when stored in sealed containers
Nonabrasive and has no known toxicity

slides.title: LITH-X®
content:
Graphite-based agent that extinguishes fires by conducting heat away from the fuel after a layer of the powder has been applied to the fuel
Can be used on several combustible metals
Was developed to control fires involving lithium, but it can also be used to extinguish magnesium, zirconium, and sodium fires
Unlike other dry powders, LITH-X® does not form a crust on the burning metal

slides.title: Potassium Bicarbonate
content:
Primary ingredient in Purple-K or PKP

Purple-K is purple in color to distinguish it from other dry chemicals

Has properties and applications similar to sodium bicarbonate and is most effective on Class B and Class C fires

Treated to be water-repellent and free flowing

When evaluated against an equal weight of sodium bicarbonate, potassium bicarbonate can extinguish a fire twice the size

slides.title: Monoammonium Phosphate
content:
Also known as multipurpose dry chemical or ABC dry chemical
Typically pale yellow in color
Effective on Class A, Class B, and Class C fires
Acts similarly to other dry chemicals on flammable liquid fires
Using a combination of extinguishing methods, this chemical quickly extinguishes flaming combustion
Melts on ordinary combustible materials, forming a solid coating that smothers the fire
Corrosion may form around extinguisher system nozzles, piping, and agent containers

slides.title: Wet Chemical
content:
Used on Class K fires involving vegetable-based oil & grease in commercial kitchens & food preparation facilities

Typically composed of water and either potassium carbonate, potassium citrate, or potassium acetate

Delivered to the hazard area in a spray

Saponification: wet chemical extinguishing agents convert burning substance into a noncombustible soap

Extinguishes oil fires by fuel removal, cooling, smothering, and flame inhibition

slides.title: Foam
content:
Suppresses fire by forming a chemical layer that is resistant to air on the liquid surface and absorbs heat
Water in foam solution absorbs additional heat, which suppresses further production of vapors and protects against re-ignition
Most fire extinguishing foam concentrates in use today are the mechanical type, which means they must be proportioned with water and mixed with air (aerated) before they can be used

slides.title: Foam Defined
content:
Foam (also known as finished foam) — Extinguishing agent produced by introducing air into the foam solution
Foam solution — Homogeneous mixture of foam concentrate and water before the introduction of air
Foam concentrate — Raw chemical compound solution that, when mixed with water and air, produces finished foam
Foam proportioner — Device that injects the correct amount (proportion) of foam concentrate into the water stream to make the foam solution

slides.title: Foam Production
content:
High-quality fire fighting foam requires four elements
Foam concentrate
Water
Air
Mechanical agitation
All elements must be applied in the correct proportions to produce quality foam

slides.title: Portable Fire Extinguishers
content:
Often provide the first line of defense against an incipient fire
To be effective, portable fire extinguishers must be suitable for the protected hazard and of sufficient size to control an incipient fire
Must be readily visible and accessible, properly maintained, and used appropriately

slides.title: Influential Factors for Effectiveness
content:
Potential severity of any resulting fire (size, intensity, and rate of fire spread) 
Personnel available to operate extinguisher (physical abilities, emotional characteristics, any training in extinguisher use)
Environmental conditions may affect extinguisher’s use (temperature, winds, and presence of toxic gases or fumes)
Anticipated adverse chemical reactions between extinguishing agent and burning material
Health/occupational safety concerns (exposure of extinguisher operator to heat, products of combustion, extinguishing agent)
Inspection, maintenance, and service requirements

slides.title: Water
content:
Water fire extinguishers are for Class A fires only
2 1/2-gallon (10 L) model is the most common size
5-gallon (20 L) model is the maximum size to be considered a portable unit
Unless an approved antifreeze agent is added to the water, these extinguishers must be kept in a heated area to prevent freezing
Amount of water carried in the portable unit determines its fire extinguishing capability

slides.title: CO2
content:
Can be used on Class B and Class C fires
Because of its gaseous nature, the CO2 agent may be difficult to project very far from the extinguisher discharge horn
CO2 extinguishers produce a loud noise during discharge
In areas of low humidity, these extinguishers may also discharge static electricity that can shock the operator

slides.title: WARNING3
content: CO2 is an asphyxiant that can cause unconsciousness or death by suffocation. CO2 extinguishers should not be used in a confined space unless the operator has supplied-air respiratory protection.

slides.title: Dry Chemical
content:
Multipurpose dry chemical extinguishers are effective on Class A, B, and C fires
Ordinary dry chemical extinguishers are for Class B and C fires only
Interrupt the chemical reaction of the fire tetrahedron
Small solid particles can be projected more effectively 
Especially suitable for controlling outdoor fires because they do not dissipate into the atmosphere

slides.title: Clean Agent
content:
Halogenated or clean agent extinguishers are effective on Class A, B, and C fires
Halon agents, as well as less ozone-depleting halocarbon agents, leave no residue when discharged
Halon 1211 is frequently used in portable fire extinguishers
Halon 1301, used in some portable extinguishers, is more commonly found in fixed-system applications
Portable extinguishers using halon replacements contain inert gases such as argon or DuPont FE-36™
Clean agent extinguishers, available in several capacities, may cover 5 to 25 square feet (0.45 m2 to 2.25 m2)

slides.title: Methods of Operation
content:
Portable fire extinguishers are also classified by the methods they use to expel the extinguishing agent

These methods include
Stored-pressure extinguisher
Cartridge-operated extinguisher
Pump-operated extinguisher

slides.title: Stored-Pressure Extinguisher
content:
Contain the expellant gas and the extinguishing agent in a single chamber 
Pressure of the gas forces the agent through a siphon tube into the chamber, valve, and nozzle assembly
Normally found in office buildings, department stores, or private residences where a high-use factor is not expected
Often require special charging equipment for pressurization
Usually serviced by licensed distributors
Air-pressurized water (APW) extinguisher is a common type of stored-pressure extinguisher

slides.title: Cartridge-Operated Extinguisher
content:
Stores the expellant gas in a separate cartridge attached to the side of the agent cylinder or tank
During activation, the expellant gas (CO2 or nitrogen) is released into the agent cylinder
Pressure of the gas forces the agent into the application hose
Unit does not contain a pressure gauge
Handheld nozzle/lever controls discharge
Often used in industrial operations, such as paint spraying or solvent manufacturing facilities

slides.title: Cartridge-Operated Extinguisher Recharging
content:
Recharging does not require special equipment
Qualified individuals, often performing this task in-house, replace the gas cartridge and fill the agent cylinder
They also verify the expellant gas cartridge has not been activated and weigh the extinguisher to be sure it has adequate extinguishing agent

slides.title: Pump-Operated Extinguisher
content:
Use manual operation of a pump to discharge the agent
Only water can be used in this type of extinguisher
Primary advantage is that it can be refilled from any available water source
Not generally found outside fire departments or fire brigades
Verify maintenance by checking that 
Extinguisher is full
Pump is operational
Hose and nozzle have no mechanical damage

slides.title: Light Hazard Occupancy
content:
Low amount of ordinary combustible materials or flammable liquids present
Incipient fire of small size may occur
Occupancies include 
Classrooms (but not necessarily all parts of a school)
Churches
Assembly halls
Some parts of an occupancy classified as light hazard, such as the shop or storage areas in a school, may actually be ordinary hazard

slides.title: Ordinary Hazard Occupancy
content:
Moderate amount of ordinary combustibles and flammable liquids
Incipient fire of moderate size may occur
If fire is discovered quickly, fire growth does not rapidly exceed control of fire extinguishers
This classification includes 
Mercantile storage and display
Light manufacturing facilities
Parking garages
Warehouses with storage under 12 feet (3658 mm) in height that are not classified as extra hazard occupancies

slides.title: Extra-Hazard Occupancy
content:
Large amount of ordinary combustible materials and flammable liquids — A rapidly spreading fire may develop

Examples include 
Automotive repair shops
Painting facilities
Manufacturing operations that use flammable liquids
Restaurants with deep fat fryers
Locations with high-piled storage of combustibles

slides.title: Class A Hazards
content:
For each occupancy classification, NFPA 10 recommends the minimum size of extinguisher needed and the maximum floor area to be protected by the extinguisher for Class A fuels
In all occupancies, maximum travel distance to an extinguisher for Class A hazards is 75 feet (22.9 m)

slides.title: Class B Hazards (1 of 2)
content:
Travel distance is the most important factor in determining distribution of Class B extinguishers
Flammable liquid fires develop rapidly and occur in various situations that are fundamentally different 
Fire extinguisher requirements for Class B fire hazards depend on appreciable depth of flammable liquids involved
NFPA 10 defines appreciable depth as a depth of liquid greater than ¼ inch (6.3.mm)

slides.title: Class B Hazards (2 of 2)
content:
Two Class B fire conditions deserve special consideration
Fires that involve flammable liquids in appreciable depth, such as fires involving dip tanks
Fires that do not involve flammable liquids in appreciable depth, such as a fuel spill on an open surface
Individual hazards involving flammable liquids with depth are often protected by fixed extinguishing systems
Systems lessen the requirements for portable fire extinguishers in the area but do not eliminate the need for them
Spill fire could occur beyond the effective reach of a fixed system and require the use of portable extinguishers

slides.title: Class D Hazards
content:
Placement and distribution cannot be generalized
Determining extinguisher placement for Class D fuels involves an analysis of 
Specific metal
Amount of metal present
Configuration of the metal (solid or particulate) 
Characteristics of the extinguishing agent
Extinguishers should be located no more than 75 feet (22.9 m) from a Class D hazard

slides.title: Class K Hazards
content:
Fire is always present in the working environment of commercial kitchens
Employees in such areas are responsible for maintaining appropriate cooking temperatures to ensure safety
Because employees may have various levels of training and because the restaurant seating area may contain fire hazards (light-hazard), NFPA 10 has assigned a more restrictive distance requirement
In areas where Class K fires are likely, the maximum travel distance from the hazard to the extinguisher reduces to 30 feet (9.1 m)

slides.title: Installation and Placement
content:
Proper extinguisher placement is an essential but often overlooked aspect of fire protection
NFPA 10 contains requirements for extinguisher installation and placement
Inspectors should also refer to locally adopted building and fire codes, which may be more restrictive

Portable fire extinguishers must be readily accessible and clearly visible
Located near normal points of travel, egress, or ingress
Arrows, lights, and/or legible signage can be used to more clearly indicate fire extinguisher location

slides.title: Securing Extinguishers
content:
Properly securing extinguishers to the structure avoids injury to building occupants and damage to the extinguisher
Extinguishers are frequently placed in cabinets or wall recesses to protect both the extinguisher and the people who might walk into them
Extinguisher cabinet in a fire-rated wall must have the same fire-resistance rating as the wall assembly or provisions must be made to maintain the wall rating
Must also be installed at an accessible height
Extinguishers placed too high or low can present a lifting and/or handling hazard

slides.title: Standard Installation and Mounting Requirements for Portable Extinguishers
content: Standard Installation and Mounting Requirements for Portable Extinguishers

Clearance between the bottom of the extinguisher and the floor must be at least 4 inches (102 mm)

Extinguishers with a maximum gross weight of 40 pounds (18.14 kg) should be installed so that the top of the extinguisher is not more than 5 feet (1.53 m) above the floor

Extinguishers with a gross weight greater than 40 pounds (18.14 kg), except wheeled types, should be installed so that the top of the extinguisher is not more than 3 1/2 feet (1.07 m) above the floor

slides.title: Personnel Safety
content:
Is the most serious problem involving CO2 fixed suppression systems, especially total flooding systems
By eliminating oxygen from the fire, CO2 also eliminates breathable oxygen from the atmosphere
Total flooding systems deliver at least a 34 percent concentration of CO2 into an enclosed area
Concentrations this high are lethal to humans

slides.title: Alarms for Total Flooding Systems
content:
For safety reasons, total flooding systems must be provided with predischarge and discharge alarms
Alarms alone are not enough to guarantee personnel safety
All affected personnel must be educated about the dangers of CO2 and trained in proper emergency procedures related to system discharge
Both alarm failure and inadequate training can result in fatalities

slides.title: Room Integrity
content:
Critical if total flooding applications are to be effective
Evaluate integrity of a room equipped with a total flooding system
Involves system components such as automatic door closers, door gaskets, HVAC shutdowns, and closing dampers
NFPA 2001 requires annual room integrity tests
Perform a visual inspection of the room on follow-up inspections
Look for obvious issues or changes in the room integrity
Order the room tested if necessary

slides.title: Balanced Pressure Proportioner
content:
Foam concentrate line connected to each fire pump discharge outlet or system riser
Foam concentrate pump (separate from the main pump) supplies concentrate line from a fixed storage tank
Provides pressure equal to pressure at which fire pump is supplying water to riser 
Proportioned correctly because foam concentrate and water are supplied at same pressure, and discharge sizes are proportional
One of most reliable methods of foam proportioning

slides.title: Around-the-Pump Proportioner
content:

Rated for a specific flow and should be used at this rate, although it does have some flexibility
Especially useful when there is low water pressure or when a motor is not available for a separate foam concentrate pump
Most common type of built-in proportioner installed in mobile fire apparatus and some fixed system applications
